articles.title: Sara Duterte has yet to report any threats her and her family – PNP
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) said on Saturday that it has not received any information on any threats against Vice President Sara Duterte and her family amid her woes on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) said on Saturday that it has not received any information on any threats against Vice President Sara Duterte and her family amid her woes on their safety.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said the PNP is monitoring the situation after Duterte said she feared for her and her family’s life.
The vice president further disclosed that she had documented every threat and harassment against her since three years ago.

“To date, however, the vice president has not reported to the PNP any threat to her life or to the safety of her family, including the threats she said date back to 2023,” Nartatez said in a statement.
He added that the PNP has not monitored any legitimate intimidations that pose danger to Duterte or her family.
Nevertheless, the police chief said that they are open to receiving any reported threats, may it be in a “document, report or statement,” for further investigation and verification.

“The PNP respects the right of anyone to raise concerns regarding their safety and treatment. We will allow the verification process to take its course and provide appropriate information once the facts have been established,” he noted.
Nartatez also reiterated that police personnel assisted Duterte as she posted bail at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court early Saturday for three counts of grave threats.
He stressed, “She was able to safely arrive at and leave the court.”
The case stemmed from the vice president’s remarks at an online press conference in 2024.
Duterte then said she had instructed someone to assassinate President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez if she would be killed. /apl

articles.title: Bohol solon seeks social media ban for children below 15
articles.summary: TAGBILARAN CITY, Bohol — Bohol 3rd District Representative Alexie Besas-Tutor has proposed banning children aged 15 and below from creating social media accounts as part of efforts to strengthen…

blocks.text: TAGBILARAN CITY, Bohol — Bohol 3rd District Representative Alexie Besas-Tutor has proposed banning children aged 15 and below from creating social media accounts as part of efforts to strengthen online protection for minors.
Under her proposal, minors aged 16 and 17 will be required to obtain verified consent from a parent or guardian before creating a social media account.

Tutor also wants social media accounts of 16 and 17-year-olds to have parental controls covering privacy settings, contact with strangers, the type of content they can access, online spending and screen time.
“The Philippines should set clear age-based rules to protect children on social media and online gaming platforms,” Tutor said in a statement.
She said similar safeguards should also be applied to online gaming platforms, particularly those where children can communicate or play with people they do not know.
Tutor cited concerns over open chats, user-generated content, contact with strangers, and the possibility of children spending money online without adequate safeguards.

She welcomed commitments from Meta and Roblox to strengthen age verification and parental controls but stressed that children’s online safety should not depend solely on the goodwill of technology companies.
Tutor also called for stronger privacy protections for minors, including limits on the collection, analysis, use and sharing of children’s personal data that could compromise their privacy.
“Strangers, predators, violent content, gambling, manipulation and commercial exploitation can now reach children through a phone,” she said.

She urged the government to strictly enforce existing laws and child-protection mechanisms while calling on Congress to enact additional measures to strengthen online safety, particularly for children and young people. /apl

articles.title: 2 families get aid after sea surge washes away homes in Ilocos Sur
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Two families in Barangay Pantoc, Narvacan in this province whose homes were washed away by a sea surge on Thursday (Sept. 3) received immediate assistance from the…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Two families in Barangay Pantoc, Narvacan in this province whose homes were washed away by a sea surge on Thursday (Sept. 3) received immediate assistance from the provincial government.
The affected homeowners were given hot meals and house-repair materials during an on-site assessment conducted by the provincial government.
The incident came amid unsettled weather in Ilocos Sur, where the southwest monsoon, or habagat, has brought periods of heavy rains and strong winds in recent days.
Several parts of the province were also hit by tornadoes or tornado-like winds on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1.
Strong winds also damaged five beach cottages in Barangay Sulvec, also in Narvacan, while similar weather disturbances were reported in Cabugao, Sinait, San Ildefonso and other areas of the province.
At least 60 houses across Ilocos Sur were reported damaged or destroyed by strong winds.
Gov. Jerry Singson led the relief operation and visited the affected families to assess their needs and provide assistance.

He was joined by Narvacan Mayor Edna Cabalo Sanidad, Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officer Rhon Arquelada, Officer-in-Charge Provincial Engineer Leonard Pascua, and Provincial Social Welfare and Development Officer Kathleen Balbuena.
—Kenneth P. Tabin / Contributor

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock – what comes next?
articles.summary:
District attorney must decide whether to retry case after jury’s failure to reach verdict despite hours of deliberation

Lindsay Clancy, prosecutors, defense lawyers, the judge and millions…

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy, prosecutors, defense lawyers, the judge and millions watching on are back where they started after her five-week trial over the murder of her three children ended in a mistrial.

America’s saddest case has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over, and a second trial could now be on the horizon, prolonging and repeating an agonizing spectacle that has gripped America and the world.
The trial lurched to its conclusion on Friday as jurors in Massachusetts failed to come to a unanimous verdict. A lone male juror holdout appeared to be preventing a conclusion to the case.

That meant the trial ended as it had begun: with no legal certainty about what was in Clancy’s mind when on 24 January 2023 she killed five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson, and eight-month-old Callan, and later cut her wrists and jumped from a bedroom window, sustaining injuries that paralyzed her.

Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, did not deny the killings but pleaded not guilty to the murders. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington blamed postpartum psychosis coupled with overmedication. Prosecutors said she knew what she was doing.

The jury deliberated for six days and over 30 hours, coming back three times in total in a deadlock. The jury foreperson said in a note to the judge on Thursday that a single juror had expressed reasonable doubt but would “not follow the law”.

The mistrial finally came after a nail-biting delay when the judge allowed Clancy’s defense to petition the Massachusetts supreme court to replace the outlying juror with an alternate. Massachusetts justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt took the matter under advisement and soon after issued a decision not to intervene in the proceedings, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.
Reddington stared at the ground and let out a sigh as the judge made the ruling. At the back of the courtroom, largely occupied by supporters, people could be seen wiping away tears.
And now it starts again.

Reddington said he would file a motion for a directed finding of not guilty within days – a ruling that Sullivan could make on grounds that the prosecution failed to present enough evidence to prove the case. A status hearing is set for 29 September when a new trail date could be set.

“This whole case has been unbelievable,” said victims’ rights attorney and survivor advocate Shari Karney. “Eleven jurors believed that Lindsay Clancy did not have criminal intent to commit this crime, understood the consequences of her act, and could not conform her conduct to the law.”

The decision to try Clancy again rests with Plymouth county district attorney Tim Cruz, a prosecutor since 1985 who has served as district attorney for more than 20 years. Before Cruz’s most recent re-election, in 2022, he took aim at progressive district attorneys, saying they have been causing “anarchy and chaos” across the US. “I am against getting rid of life without parole for first-degree homicide people,” said in a debate. “I am against having a list of cases that will not be prosecuted because it does not work.”

Outside court on Thursday, Reddington said he was ready to retry the case. “Bring it on,” he told reporters. But he did not rule out the possibility of a plea deal. “We’ll see what Mr Cruz wants to do, and then we’ll talk about our options,” he said. For now, Clancy returns to Tewksbury hospital, where she has been held since the killings.

According to Karney, the complexity of the Massachusetts law on proving “criminal responsibility” – or what in other states would rest on the defense showing the defendant was insane – is a double standard. “It’s very complicated,” she says.
Part of the difficulty jurors may have had is that mental health issues are not as a transparent as physical issues, and under criminal law there is a bias against them, she says.

Karney said: “Clancy was basically having a mental health stroke, and mental health is the stepsister of the healthcare system. It’s not right. But because we cant see it, that doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist. And the medical healthcare system doesn’t want to recognize and pay for mental healthcare apart from giving out drugs to make them go away.”

During the trial, jurors heard from mental health experts who clashed over Clancy’s medical records. But it was her mother and step mother who may have provided the most powerful testimony when they testified about the steps Clancy had taken to seek help.

Paula Musgrove, Clancy’s mother, testified that she often stayed with her daughter in the months leading up to the killings because Clancy was afraid of sleeping alone, was increasingly paranoid and believed the medications she was taking “were destroying her mind”.
Susan Clancy, Lindsay Clancy’s former mother-in-law, said she was “begging for help” and “was struggling – we were all concerned”.

Forensic psychiatrist Phillip Resnick, for the defense, testified near the end of the trial testimony that that Clancy was “frankly psychotic” the day of the killings, and supported her claim that she heard a voice that ordered her to kill the children and herself.
Resnick said he believed Clancy had experienced “command hallucinations … almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings”.

Avram Mack, a forensic psychiatrist, said he did not believe Clancy was showing signs of psychosis but suffered from a major depressive episode and retained the ability to know right from wrong. “There was the ability to act normally,” he testified.

In theory, prosecutors and defense attorneys could agree on voluntary manslaughter, a lesser charge. “The problem with a jail sentence for this woman is that she’s paraplegic,” said Karney. “How would you incarcerate a woman in a wheelchair with tremendous mental health problems in a woman’s prison, and ensure her safety?”

One takeaway from the Lindsay Clancy trial, says Karney, is the job of getting inside the head of a woman suffering postpartum psychosis is a tough task and that diagnosis and treatment is woefully insufficient.

“Telehealth is good for a sprained ankle or a cold, but not for postpartum depression or psychosis. And then you prescribe more psychotropic drugs via telehealth appointment? It’s crazy and it’s not responsible,” she said.

articles.title: Alberta independence group releases its ‘transition plan’ to become a country
articles.summary: An independence group has released a “transition plan,” sketching out what it sees as a roadmap should Albertans vote in the future to become a sovereign nation. Meanwhile, a federalist leader says…

image.caption: Keith Wilson speaks at the launch of Alberta independence organization Let Alberta Decide in Calgary on June 19. Wilson is also behind the Alberta Transition Council, which launched a ‘transition plan’ on Thursday. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: An independence group has released a “transition plan,” sketching out what it sees as a roadmap should Albertans vote in the future to become a sovereign nation.
The Alberta Transition Council released the 214-page report on Thursday, laying out a series of proposals tied to how life in Alberta might look in the event of a future “yes” vote on independence.
The report also touches on a range of regulations and institutions the group identifies that would need to transition to Alberta’s control through negotiation, including with Ottawa.
Those proposals vary in scope, from the continuity of social programs to air traffic control to the implementation of a new constitution and the relationship with First Nations.

Lawyer Keith Wilson, who leads the Alberta Transition Council and is also a leader with the independence group Let Alberta Decide, says the aim is to outline how Alberta’s exit from Canada could run smoothly.

“What we need to remember is we’re not starting from scratch, right? Those people who work at the airports, we’re not going to blow up the airport. It’s still there,” Wilson said. “All we’re doing is changing the payroll.”
But one critic argued any transition planning is far off and the plan is “unrealistic” about what are certain to be complex negotiations.

“Many of those issues would take many, many years, potentially, to be fully discussed and possibly never come to a conclusion,” said Errol Mendes, a professor of constitutional and international law at the University of Ottawa.
Not all in Alberta's control, report says
Albertans go to the polls on Oct. 19 to vote on whether Alberta should stay with Canada, or hold a second, binding referendum to separate.
Polling suggests a minority of Albertans presently support the idea of secession.

items: Two sides in Alberta separation debate entrenched, with majority wanting to remain in Canada: poll

blocks.text: The guiding idea, according to the group, is to not approach the transition as the creation of a country “from scratch.”

“Alberta independence would not eliminate Alberta’s relationship with the rest of Canada,” the report reads. “It would change the legal and governmental framework within which that relationship operates.”
At the same time, the report acknowledges not all of this is in Alberta’s control.
Debt, mobility, energy infrastructure, pensions, borders, and assets are among the areas where negotiation would be needed with Canada, First Nations and others.
Outcomes cannot be known or guaranteed, the report states.
The document claims 45 Albertans in fields including banking and currency, law, international trade, First Nations and policing contributed to the preparation and review of the package.
However, the identities of those individuals were not made public.
Wilson said confidentiality was put in place to ensure contributors don’t face “cancel culture" or harassment.
“The report will speak for itself. And Canadians, and many people in the world, are growing leery of the ‘experts say’ stuff anyway,” Wilson told CBC News. “People will be able to evaluate it.

“Each one of us have our own level of life experience that we’ll be able to hone in on — something we’re very familiar with — and say, ‘Hey, do the base facts seem accurate? Does this analysis make sense?’”
The document is one of several released recently that explore the various ways Alberta separating from Canada could impact people’s daily lives.

items: Alberta separation too costly with too many uncertainties, warns Calgary think-tank
A president, open-carry gun laws, elected judges: Group floats vision for an independent Alberta

blocks.text: From currency to mortgages to military
In the introductory section of the paper, a series of questions is posed.
“How will laws continue? How will courts operate? How will salaries and pensions continue to be paid? How will money continue to move through banks? How will airplanes continue to fly?”
The group offers some ideas. For instance, take currency. On day one of independence, the group suggests using the Canadian dollar “because it minimizes contract, pricing and consumer disruption.”
“Other possibilities — including use of the U.S. dollar, dual-currency arrangements or a future Alberta currency — remain longer-term or contingency choices,” the report reads.

In many cases, a full resolution isn’t offered yet. On pensions, the group proposes to keep pension payments going for now, leaving the negotiations over future plans for pensions and asset transfers for later.

What would happen to mortgages in the event of a separation vote has been a big question in the run-up to the referendum. Earlier this year, analysts told CBC News there are a lot of unknowns involved in what is likely to be a complicated process.
The plan proposes offering the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation the opportunity to continue its services in an independent Alberta.

“If they’re not interested in that, Alberta would stand up, in advance of independence … the Alberta housing mortgage corporation,” Wilson said. “And a transition would occur where the Alberta entity would agree to transfer the mortgage guarantees … so that the banks remain whole.”

Earlier this week, in a separate report, the Calgary-based public policy think-tank Canada West Foundation calculated that debt per person in Alberta could rise to between $80,000 and $95,000 post-separation, compared to $27,000 per person in 2024, based on the increased debt share Alberta could assume.
The Alberta Transition Council, while not recommending a final federal debt figure, suggests that Canada shouldn’t propose that Alberta assume a share of the debt based primarily on population.
“Such an approach would ignore Albertans’ historical fiscal contributions, which should be taken into account in any fair calculation methodology,” the report reads.
Similarly, the report doesn’t include a detailed costing of the broader dollars and cents tied to the prospect of independence, promising a companion report on those matters in the coming weeks.
The report also acknowledges First Nations have constitutionally-recognized rights and are treaty partners.
“Nothing automatically happens to reserve land merely because Alberta becomes independent,” the report reads.

items: Treaty 6 was signed 150 years ago. First Nations worry a push for Alberta independence puts it at risk

blocks.text: Should an independence vote be successful, the report presents four “relationship pathways” for First Nations, including "Option A," which would allow a First Nation to “keep its current relationship with Canada as much as possible.”

The report also suggests the Alberta Sheriffs could be expanded into a full provincial police force to replace the RCMP, and proposes an initial 2,100-member defence force, which would consist of 300 full-time permanent members and a separate, 1,800-member “territorial force.”
'I don't doubt that it's rosy'
In its report earlier this week, the Canada West Foundation stated that negotiations for Alberta to secede from Canada would be complex, with no guaranteed outcome.
Setting up an independent Alberta would cost more than $200 billion, with ongoing costs of more than $50 billion annually, estimated former Treasury Board senior manager Lennie Kaplan.

items: Alberta separation too costly with too many uncertainties, warns Calgary think-tank

blocks.text: Canada West Foundation President Gary Mar said he has yet to read the Alberta Transition Council’s full report. However, on both the “leave” and “stay” sides, there’s too much certainty, in his view.

“We’ve looked into the complications of both sides, staying and leaving, and have come to conclusions,” Mar said. “I think that Mr. Wilson’s work, I don’t doubt that it’s rosy. But that’s what he’s advocating for.”
Thomas Lukaszuk, leader of the Forever Canadian movement and former deputy premier of Alberta, said he viewed the plan as “ridiculous.”
“He is the guy that thinks that he can divorce and then show up the next day and say, ‘What's for dinner, honey?’” he said. “Well, it doesn't work like that. This is a divorce.”
Wilson said his group’s report was optimistic “in the sense that we assume that the federal government and the provinces and the First Nations would enter into good-faith negotiations.”

“We know each of the services and functions that the federal government provides. We can plan for the transition of them, just as ordinary businesses do when one business acquires another. The customer is not disrupted,” he said.
Over the coming weeks, Albertans can expect even more numbers and predictions about the province’s future.
That includes the University of Calgary's study of the potential costs of Alberta leaving Canada, commissioned by the provincial government.
That report is expected to be released later this month.

articles.title: Palace says PNP followed law as Sara Duterte posted bail
articles.summary: Malacañang said the Philippine National Police implemented the law impartially when police officers secured the Quezon City Hall of Justice on the day Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail over her…

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 7:58pm

Malacañang said the Philippine National Police implemented the law impartially when police officers secured the Quezon City Hall of Justice on the day Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail over her grave threats charges she is facing.

"Ipinatutupad ng PNP ang kanilang mandato ayon sa batas, walang kinikilingan at nang walang halong pulitika kundi para [sa] bawat Filipino lamang. Nanatili silang professional sa pangangalaga sa mga karapatan ng lahat ng taong nasa ilalim ng kanilang pagprotekta,” the Presidential Communications Office said in a statement.

(The PNP carries out its mandate according to the law, impartially and without politics but for [every] Filipino. They have remained professional in safeguarding the rights of all persons under their protection.)
Malacañang expressed its trust in the PNP, as it reminded the public to direct their complaints about police actions through legal processes, and not rumors.

"Buo ang tiwala ng administrasyon sa pamunuan ng PNP at sa hanay nito, at ipinapaalala natin sa publiko na ang anumang agam-agam o reklamo hinggil sa aksyon ng pulisya ay maaari nilang ipaabot sa pamamagitan ng legal na pamamaraan at hindi sa pagsasagawa ng mga usaping walang batayan," the PCO said.

(The administration has full confidence in the leadership of the PNP and its ranks, and we remind the public that any concern or complaint regarding police actions may be raised through legal channels and not by resorting to baseless allegations.)
“Nais din namin ipaalala sa lahat na ang administrasyong ito ay hindi papayag na maging sandata ang kapulisan sa anumang karahasan,” it added.
(We also want to remind everyone that this administration will not allow the police to be used as a weapon in any violence.)
Duterte posted bail at a Quezon City court, a day after the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over her grave threats case.
In a statement, Duterte said she does not feel safe.
"I have documented threats and harassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them," she said.
"Umalis na nga ako kung nasaan ang mga anak ko para pumunta sa korte, pero pumunta pa rin ang pulis," Duterte added.
(I already left the place where my children were to go to court, but the police still went there.)
"I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila ako (I feel they will kill me)," the vice president said.
The QC Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98 set the bail at P120,000 per count. It found that there is probable cause to hold Duterte for trial, prompting it to issue an arrest warrant against her.
Shortly before she posted bail, Duterte’s counsel, Atty. Michael Poa told reporters that Duterte was considered "surrendered." –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-Olongapo mayor apologizes, explains remarks on city’s flooding
articles.summary: OLONGAPO CITY — Former Olongapo City Mayor Rolen Paulino Sr. has apologized for the tone of his response to a resident who asked about the city’s recurring flooding, saying a video of the exchange…

blocks.text: OLONGAPO CITY — Former Olongapo City Mayor Rolen Paulino Sr. has apologized for the tone of his response to a resident who asked about the city’s recurring flooding, saying a video of the exchange was taken out of context.
The statement came after a video circulated on social media showing a resident asking Paulino whether flooding in low-lying areas, particularly Barangay Sta. Rita, would ever end.

Paulino was heard responding: “As long as we’re alive. How can you raise this? Flooding is part of nature. Look at Japan—despite being highly developed, they still experience floods that can reach neck-deep?”
At one point, he added: “Olongapo is below sea level, and water from the mountains flows down into the city. Given the situation there, you should leave Olongapo.”
The video was posted on a local Facebook page and subsequently went viral.
In his statement issued Wednesday (Sept. 2), Paulino said his response should not be interpreted as a promise that flooding in Olongapo would never be addressed.
He explained that the city’s low-lying, below-sea-level areas make it vulnerable to flooding, adding that the forces of nature cannot be completely controlled.

Paulino, who served as Olongapo mayor for two consecutive terms from 2013 to 2019, also cited measures undertaken during his administration to mitigate flooding and hasten the drainage of floodwaters.
He said that they started dredging rivers and constructing drainage systems to mitigate the impact of flooding when he was the city’s mayor.
Paulino, who currently serves as member of the board of directors of the Bases Conversion and Development Authority, apologized for the tone and delivery of his response to the resident.
“To those who know me, you already know that’s just how I answer. It just seems like this secretly recorded video was made with bad intentions,” he claimed.
Paulino also vowed that he and local officials would continue assisting residents affected by flooding despite criticism over the city’s flood-control measures.
“We will never stop extending our assistance,” Paulino said in Filipino.
The former mayor’s remarks came amid weeks of severe flooding in Olongapo, with the city government declaring a state of calamity on Sept. 1.
The prolonged heavy rains caused widespread flooding, landslides, damage to property and infrastructure, and the displacement of residents.
The city, whose mayor is Paulino’s son and namesake, recorded 2,900.5 millimeters of cumulative rainfall in August—about 3.4 times its normal rainfall for the month.
From Aug. 28 to 29 alone, 569.5 mm of rain was recorded, equivalent to about 68 percent of the city’s normal rainfall for the entire month.
—John Patrick Mateo / Contributor

articles.title: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flood disaster
articles.summary:
Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation

Emergency responders rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate…

blocks.text: Emergency responders rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations on Saturday, as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.

The Nepali military said a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.

Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.
Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.
Experts have said that as time passes, the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.

The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.
Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.

Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.
At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

articles.title: How haze from Indonesian fires impacts Southeast Asia
articles.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia—Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago for weeks battles to contain fires that have burned large swathes of Borneo and Sumatra. The hazardous smoke has…

blocks.text: JAKARTA, Indonesia—Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago for weeks battles to contain fires that have burned large swathes of Borneo and Sumatra.
The hazardous smoke has led to an increase in respiratory problems, forced schools to close, and has been drifting to neighboring countries including Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.
Here’s what to know:
Where are the fires?
Most of the fires are concentrated on Borneo island, home to vast tropical jungle that Indonesia shares with Brunei and Malaysia, as well as Sumatra.
So far this year, nearly 300,000 hectares of land have burned in Indonesia, according to an independent estimate from the Nusantara Atlas portal.
Indonesia saw an uptick in carbon emissions since late July.
By the end of last month, the levels were comparable to previous El Nino years of 2015 and 2019, Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) senior scientist Mark Parrington told AFP.

“We’re seeing already now… really extreme fire emissions comparable to those previous strong El Niño years, and also the extent of the smoke and the haze and the air quality impacts,” Parrington said.
Fires in the archipelago have released more than 23 million metric tons of carbon emissions between August 28 and September 3, according to CAMS’ Fire Emission Watch portal.
It was higher than 20.7 million metric tons of emissions from fires over the same period in 2015, which was a strong El Niño year.
What causes the fires?

Analysts said that the El Niño weather phenomenon, which the United Nations said this week could turn out to be the strongest in four decades, has contributed to creating drier conditions in Indonesia and made it easier for fires to spread.
But slash-and-burn land-clearing practices also contributed to the damage, said David Gaveau, founder of the Nusantara Atlas.
“El Niño does not ignite fires. It creates the dry conditions that allow human-started fires to escape and become very large,” he told AFP.
The fires are difficult to extinguish because many occurred on peatlands, a wetland ecosystem with layers of partially decomposed organic materials that become flammable when dry.
Between January and August this year, more than 210,000 hotspots were detected in peatland areas across the country, according to NGO Pantau Gambut.
“Peat is a naturally wet ecosystem and stores large amounts of organic material. When peat is drained, this organic material is converted into fuel,” Pantau Gambut spokesman Wahyu Perdana said.
What is the impact?
More than five million people across Borneo and Sumatra are directly exposed to the health risks from haze, deputy health minister Dante Saksono Harbuwono said last month.
Over 1.4 million students were attending classes remotely, with many schools closed due to worsening air quality, an education ministry official said this week.
In Malaysia, soaring pollution levels prompted the government on Friday to declare an emergency in a region of the Sarawak state in Borneo, with nearly 650 schools closed next week.

In the Philippines, air quality was slowly returning to normal after a week of reaching “very unhealthy” and “severely unhealthy” PM 2.5 levels that saw officials shutter schools in cities and provinces citing the drifting haze.
The haze also drove air quality in Singapore’s central region to an “unhealthy” level on Friday, the country’s National Environment Agency data showed. /apl

articles.title: Nepal tunnel rescue revives hopes 10 days after flood
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal—Rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese alive on Saturday from a tunnel buried by debris, as emergency response teams dug with new vigor in the search for missing people 10 days after…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal—Rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese alive on Saturday from a tunnel buried by debris, as emergency response teams dug with new vigor in the search for missing people 10 days after catastrophic flooding.

A joint rescue team comprising personnel from the Nepal Army and foreign experts rescued the man from 225 meters (738 feet) inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa district, a military statement said.
A picture of the rescue published on the army’s Facebook page shows the man, identified only as Luhaitao, with his arms around the shoulders of two camouflage-clad rescuers.
He looked alert but his hands were covered in thick, slimy mud.
“His health is currently being assessed and further search and rescue operations are continuing,” the army said.

The survivor was among hundreds of hydropower workers who went missing since a tsunami-like wall of water and mud swept through the China-Nepal border following a vast glacial and rock collapse on August 26.
Two Nepali hydropower workers were rescued on Friday at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where searches continued alongside multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects destroyed by the floods.
So far, 1,344 bodies have been recovered in Nepal, according to the national disaster agency, with around 5,000 people missing.
In China, state media said 31 people had been killed and 531 were missing. That takes the overall death toll to 1,375 people, and more than 5,500 missing.
Thousands in relief camps
Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP that “work is underway at the tunnels” to locate any survivors.
The government initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive inside multiple tunnels.
Rescuers called it a “miracle” after the two Nepali men, caked in mud, were pulled out alive on Friday, nine days after being trapped by the flood.
They were taken to hospital and are said to be in a stable condition.
Experts from India, China, Australia and South Korea have been aiding Nepali rescuers in their search of survivors inside blocked tunnels.
With morgues overflowing, some 1,030 bodies hade been buried in mass graves after taking DNA samples for future identification, Nepal Police said Saturday.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah promised to provide “safe and comfortable accommodation” for thousands of people displaced by the diaster and currently living in temporary relief camps.
“We know that staying there (in camps) is not easy for you,” he said in a Friday post on social media.
But he promised to “once again create an environment where you can dream about and build your future.” /apl

articles.title: First professional St Nick with Down’s syndrome inducted into International Santa Claus Hall of Fame
articles.summary:
Atlanta’s Bradley Carlisle first played Kris Kringle for kids with Down’s syndrome and has now completed elite Santa Academy

After recently gaining recognition as the first professional…

blocks.text: After recently gaining recognition as the first professional Santa Claus with Down’s syndrome in the US, Bradley Carlisle has already gotten a lot more than the traditional serving of milk and cookies that is usually left out for Father Christmas each year.

That is because the 37-year-old community theater actor from suburban Atlanta landed an honorary induction into the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame upon completing one of the largest Christmas performer schools in the US in late August – a distinction meant to recognize the important representation his emergence on the holiday scene has brought, according to his supporters.

As his mother, Debbie Chadrix, told it to the Guardian on Friday, Carlisle’s path to his unique place among what she called the Claus family began at the 2023 holiday party of the Down Syndrome Association of Atlanta (DSAA). Chadrix said the organization’s executive director approached her during the gathering and remarked: “We need a Santa with Down’s syndrome who looks like the kids” invited to the party as the guests of honor.
The group’s leader picked Carlisle because of his passion for acting on the local community theater circuit, Chadrix said. Yet Chadrix wasn’t completely sold.

She said her son used to fear Santa growing up because he evidently equated jolly old St Nick’s white gloves with those worn by healthcare providers who took care of him during nonetheless difficult medical experiences. It was only after one Santa in particular slipped his gloves off for Bradley that he warmed up to the concept, she recounted.

Carlisle, however, gamely accepted the offer to transform into Santa for the next DSAA holiday party. He confidently wore the white beard and recognizable red suit, and interacted with more than 200 children involved with the DSAA.

Chadrix said she has never forgotten the looks on many of those children’s faces “when they realized Bradley looked like them – and talked like them, a little bit, too”. And then Bradley declared “he would be our Santa from now on”.

Local news media picked up Carlisle’s story by his second Christmas season as Santa, giving his profile a bump, Chadrix said. And he also appeared on a podcast alongside Rick Rosenthal, who runs Atlanta’s Northern Lights Santa Academy and invited Carlisle to attend a four-day course beginning on 20 August.

At Rosenthal’s academy, which he described as the second largest institution of its kind in the US, Carlisle and others train to carry on in the spirit of figures such as Santa, Mrs Claus and the Christmas elves. Santas in particular receive an education on a wide range of topics, including how to properly dress for the part, adequately maintain their white beards and improvise answers to the heart-wrenching questions children can occasionally ask, especially if grappling with a terminal illness or grieving the loss of a loved one.

Carlisle excelled in that atmosphere, with Chadrix proudly noting that he underwent the same program as all of the other enrollees there. And at a 23 August ceremony on the academy’s final day, Phil Wenz of the Santa Claus Oath Foundation called Carlisle up to a stage.
A video on a social media account for Carlisle showed Wenz complimenting him for the confident style he had displayed while personifying Santa Claus in the lobby outside the ceremony hall.

Wenz alluded to how some of Carlisle’s fellow Claus family members had banded together to cover a completely custom-made Santa suit for him. Carlisle’s photograph would also be shown in New York City’s Times Square as part of the US’s Down Syndrome Awareness Month beginning on 1 October, which is Bradley’s birthday, Wenz continued.

And then Wenz revealed the pièce de résistance: he said he had consulted with a number of Christmas community heavyweights to enshrine him as an honorary member of the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame.
Wenz punctuated the moment with handing Carlisle a badge. Carlisle triumphantly held it up with his right hand while he smiled widely and the audience applauded.

Rosenthal has belonged to that institution in the town of Santa Claus, Indiana, since late 2023. It’s something he considers one of his greatest honors in his 58 years as a Santa. And he said Carlisle merited enshrinement because of his already showing “a magnified sensitivity” to those with Down’s syndrome who are among Santa’s faithful that others in the Claus family simply cannot.

Chadrix said she was notified in advance of the plan to welcome Carlisle to the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame. And she said she made clear, essentially, that she did not want Bradley’s condition to be the only reason he was being enshrined.

She recalled Rosenthal assuring her: “Phil Wenz knows what he’s looking at. And as soon as he saw Bradley as Santa and talking to people and interacting, he knew he has something different and special – and that’s why he got to the hall of fame.”
Among the many to congratulate Carlisle was the DSAA, which shared a link to a television news segment about him published by the Atlanta station WXIA on Thursday.

“Saaaaantaaaaa we know him! So proud of our Santa Bradley,” the organization wrote, adding that those who attend Atlanta’s 3 October Buddy Walk – a DSAA fundraiser at the Kennesaw State University Marietta campus – “might see him incognito”.
Carlisle told WXIA that he enjoyed being Santa “because I like to help with the kids”.
The station also asked him what it feels like to slip into his Santa suit.
He replied: “It feels like love.”

articles.title: Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials say
articles.summary:
Security experts fear Putin may be winning hybrid war with the west amid rise of pro-Kremlin, far-right parties

Defence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out with Russia,…

blocks.text: Defence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out with Russia, Europe could not currently sustain a prolonged war of attrition owing to a public lack of war readiness, a conference on the future of European military coordination heard this week.
The pessimism reflects concern that Russia may be winning a so-called hybrid war with Europe, weakening the options available to Nato war planners in the event of military conflict.

The surge in support for the populist forces in Europe’s main military states is also endangering proposals for a group of five European countries, including the UK, to take on a new coordination role as the US prepares to reduce its commitments to the conventional defence of Europe.

Defence officials, speaking at a forum convened by the Munich Security Conference (MSC), the leading security foundation, said the European public may not have the appetite for a prolonged war, requiring Nato to focus its plans on a relatively quick conflict.

One recent British cabinet member admitted the west had been “crap” at educating its public about the scale of the hybrid conflict with Russia. Another UK diplomat claimed successive British prime ministers had done nothing to explain the scale of the threat.

They said this had left ministers locked in an unenviable task of persuading unprepared voters to cut welfare spending to fund defence. “The level of the debate has been at that of a kindergarten,” the UK diplomat admitted.

blocks.caption: Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, takes part in a wreath laying ceremony in Moscow earlier this year. Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/Reuters

blocks.text: The private criticism has been fuelled by the UK government’s inability to adopt a call in its 2025 strategic defence review to launch a national conversation on the scale of the security threat facing Europe and to build national resilience.

A second diplomat said the collapse of the cold war dividing line with Russia had left Moscow free to exploit the anxieties of European publics on the left and the right. The remarks reveal a wider concern in senior European politicians that they may be losing the so-called hybrid war with Russia, and this may be reflected in rightwing populist surges next year in Poland, France and Italy.
Most populist parties, including Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), are sympathetic to Russia and want an end to the Ukraine conflict.

The MSC discussion – held under rules forbidding identification of the speaker – was given added urgency by the German government this week blaming Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month.

One of the suspected culprits in the attack on 4 August, where an armed drone exploded, has been identified as a Belarusian citizen with a Russian passport who appears to have entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa.

The MSC, an independent but influential foundation, has been promoting the idea of the five main European military powers working much more closely: one means of bringing the UK, outside the EU, to the centre of European defence planning.

Decisions in Washington on its troop deployments that could effectively leave Europe in charge of its own conventional defences are expected in the next few months. But the scale of hybrid war and the potential impact of next year’s elections, as well as the surge by the AfD in Germany, on plans for a stronger European defence coordination was described at the conference as “the elephant in the room”.
One proposal is for the EU to publish a collective statement on the Russian threat that the populist forces would be challenged to accept or decline.

The E5 group of European defence ministers already meet regularly, but they are at the early stages of agreeing of how to jointly procure capabilities such as integrated air and missile defence, deep precision strike and space-based early warning systems that are all currently provided mostly by the US.

“Europe is stagnating at a time when the external threats were assuming a dimension which is really very serious. These are really huge and existential challenges requiring greater integration in defence,” said Wolfgang Ischinger, the chair of the MSC.

He argued the E5 grouping offers a way of including all the European countries with substantial defence industrial capacity and may later be able to incorporate Ukraine in the context of a truce since Kyiv now has the largest and strongest army in Europe.

Advocates of the E5 insist it will neither duplicate nor underline Nato, but fears were expressed that the US would nevertheless block a stronger European pillar inside Nato. “The US are better at talking about burden shifting than power sharing,” said one diplomat.
after newsletter promotion

Italy is one of the E5 states most concerned about the impact of Russia’s hybrid warfare on its domestic politics as Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing administration – which has governed more moderately than many expected, and cultivated a pro-Ukraine image abroad – becomes its longest-running since the second world war.

The Italian foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, warned Italy was suffering daily cyber-attacks, adding it was not immune from potential Russian interference in next year’s national elections, the first time an Italian politicians has warned the election may be manipulated.

blocks.caption: Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, has warned of Russia meddling in his country’s elections next year. Photograph: Mohamed Hossam/EPA

blocks.text: “There are many ways to wage hybrid warfare, it is not done using bombs, planes or tanks,” the minister said.
Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, one of Meloni’s closest political allies, has said it was stupid not to recognise the level of Russian interference.
He warned this summer at the Nato summit in Ankara: “We don’t have the antibodies and we’re penetrable: analyse bots and you’ll see it. The increase occurred thanks to social media.”

His doubts have grown given Moscow’s ability to operate across so many domains, including social media, AI, cybersecurity, databases and critical infrastructure. On Tuesday, he said the Russian threat was growing all the time.

Crosetto also said he recognises Russia is exploiting real problems such as low wages, and so attributing government unpopularity to Russian disinformation risks misidentifying a malaise afflicting western societies, including a general weariness with the cost of the war in Ukraine,

In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the far-right Futuro Nazionale who has challenged the stability of Meloni’s coalition, is widely seen as the most probable carrier of the Russian message in the coming election, that could come as early as April.

Speaking before the investigation into whether his party represents a revival of fascism, Vannacci gloried in the criticism. “Just discovered that I am a ‘Manchurian candidate’ sent by the Russian federation to complain about the unaffordable petrol prices in my country Italy,” he said. “Forgive me, but I still find it hard to accept the idea that dissent from Brussels’ orthodoxy is now, in practical terms, tantamount to disloyalty towards the west.”

In an attempt to shift perceptions so Ukraine is seen not as a financial burden but rather as teaching Europe modern warfare, Crosetto has recruited the former Ukraine defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as his unpaid adviser for innovation. Ischinger praised the decision, describing Ukraine as possessing the best equipped and most modern army in Europe.

In Ukraine, 200,000 drones are being built each month, with the goal of producing more than 7m by 2026. To support this growth, 500 small and medium-sized companies have sprung up, assembling drones even in small workshops, using mostly Chinese components.

articles.title: Trump envoys arrive in Moscow ahead of Ukraine talks, reports say
articles.summary: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to hold talks with Russia before travelling to Ukraine on Sunday.

blocks.text: Two of US President Donald Trump's top envoys have arrived in Moscow, Russian media has said, ahead of a weekend of talks aimed at accelerating efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were due in the Russian capital on Saturday, where they will hold talks before travelling to Kyiv on Sunday for discussions with Ukraine.
Trump told reporters on Friday the pair were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts from the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed to deliver a breakthrough.
US news outlet Axios reported the US envoys would separately meet both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Neither Washington nor the Kremlin confirmed the envoys' arrival, but flight tracking data showed a US government plane landing at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport after flying from Helsinki, Finland. Data showed it had flown into Europe from the US earlier in the day.

Witkoff and Kushner have travelled to Moscow on multiple occasions since Trump returned to office, but Sunday would be their first visit to Kyiv. Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.
Zelensky said on Saturday that Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.

Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.
He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.
Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe.
There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".
Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans.

European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.
In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.
Ukraine said it has struggled to repel attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Sara Duterte not in handcuffs for grave threats arrest; circulating photo is altered
articles.summary: The altered photo was from her visit to Ateneo de Zamboanga University following the August 18 shooting incident

blocks.text: Claim: Vice President Sara Duterte was seen wearing handcuffs before posting bail as the Quezon City Regional Trial Court ordered her arrest on three counts of grave threat on September 4.
Why we fact-checked this: Multiple posts have used the photo and appeared to show that Duterte has finally been arrested and put in handcuffs before posting bail.

Facebook user Atty Joel Rodriguez Dizon, a Baguio-based lawyer, posted the photo with a caption that read, “She made bail. But I have to admit it does give you some measure of quiet satisfaction even for just a tiny moment to see this woman in handcuffs.”
The post has 4,400 reactions and 928 shares as of writing.
Facebook page Trendline PH also wrote in its post, “Be honest, how do you feel seeing her in handcuffs even just for a short while (because she was able to post bail)?”

User Tomboc Urbiztondo Ed posted it in a Facebook group, copied Dizon’s caption, then added: “Guys, nagbayad na ng bail si VP Sara Duterte. Bakit may posas pa siya? Sa mga 32 million na bumoto, guys, anong masasabi ninyo dito?”
(Guys, VP Sara Duterte has already posted bail. Why is she still in handcuffs? To the 32 million who voted for her—guys, what do you have to say about this?)
The other two posts garnered 1,046 reactions, 513 comments, and 78 shares.
The image, accompanied by similar captions, was likewise circulated by various other Facebook accounts and pages.

The facts: The original photo was from Duterte’s visit to Ateneo de Zamboanga University following the August 18 shooting incident. Duterte was not seen wearing handcuffs when she arrived at the Quezon City RTC Branch 98 to post bail.
Duterte shared photos of her school visit in a Facebook post, including the original version of the altered photo where she talked to university president Fr. Guillrey Andal and police officers.
Upon posting bail, Duterte told reporters she does “not feel safe” with the police personnel deployed in the court.

The court ordered Duterte’s arrest for three counts of grave threats in August following complaints from the National Bureau of Investigation over Duterte’s November 23, 2024, midnight press conference.
During that press conference, Duterte said she had already talked to someone who would kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife, and Romualdez if she herself were killed.

Altered through AI: The photo was altered with the use of artificial intelligence (AI). AI detection tool SightEngine flagged it as 99% AI-generated, while HiveDetect said it is 59.7% likely to be AI.
Duterte’s impeachment trial: Duterte’s grave threats case is cited as the fourth article of impeachment, or cases against her, at the Senate impeachment court.
According to experts, Duterte’s case under the Quezon City RTC will not affect the ongoing impeachment trial because the impeachment process is different from criminal proceedings.
– Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.
