articles.title: DILG: PNP accorded VP Sara Duterte respect
articles.summary: Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Saturday said the Philippine National Police (PNP) accorded Vice President Sara Duterte all of the respect warranted of her position, issuing…

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 6:01pm

Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Saturday said the Philippine National Police (PNP) accorded Vice President Sara Duterte all of the respect warranted of her position, issuing the statement following her remarks that she did not feel safe in the presence of policemen.
"It's very unfortunate that all the pressure in her life is affecting her perception. The PNP accorded her all the respect her position deserves," Remulla said in a statement.

When she posted bail Saturday at the Quezon City Hall of Justice over her grave threats case, Duterte said she did not trust the police. The vice president also said lawmen harassed her mother and child.
Remulla said all the deployed cops recorded body cam footage.

"We have all the body cam footages of her warrants being served. We have all the body cam footages of her arrival to post bail. We knew of her whereabouts the night before but we did not force the warrant of arrest," Remulla said.
Duterte posted a P360,000 bail for three counts of grave threats allegedly made against President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez.
The vice president said she preferred civilian protection, wanting to remain in the public eye.
For its part, the PNP said it has taken note of the concerns raised by the vice president, vowing that it would monitor the situation.

"To date, however, the Vice President has not reported to the PNP any threat to her life or to the safety of her family, including the threats she said date back to 2023. Likewise, the PNP has not monitored any verified threat against the Vice President or her family," the PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in a statement.
While she was outside the hall of justice, Duterte said that she has been receiving threats since 2023, the year she broke away from the administration. However, she did not provide further details.
Nartatez also said the police provided security to Duterte when she posted bail. She was able to safely arrive and leave the court.
"The PNP remains open to receiving any document, report, or statement concerning the reported threats," Nartatez said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
articles.summary:
The US defense secretary faces internal dissent and discord at the Pentagon, accused of focusing on culture war issues and his own political ambitions as the Iran war drags on

In a different…

blocks.text: In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile.
But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary.

Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy.
The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more.

Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East.

While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents.

“The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.”

Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.”

After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple.

The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party.

Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation.

The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year

The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long.
The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post.
‘The past six months has failed’

“I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after?

“We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability.

“We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.”

Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade.

“It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength.

As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions.
The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May,
has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination.

In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets.

The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”.

Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts.

A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank.

In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN.

Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis.
The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain.

Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.”

Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said.
‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld

Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war.

Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the International Monetary Fund.

During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein.

But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth.

“Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now.

“But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat.

“If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.”

Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced.
He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa.

“We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.”

Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.”

articles.title: ‘It cost me many friendships’: former Brazil military chief reveals inside struggle to stop Bolsonaro’s coup
articles.summary:
Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior describes 2022 meeting in new book as ex-leader’s son vies with Lula for presidency

The far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro was in his final days as Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro was in his final days as Brazil’s president when, six weeks after losing the election and still refusing to recognise the result, he summoned the heads of the armed forces to a meeting.
The defence minister, Gen Paulo Sérgio Nogueira de Oliveira, took out a document from a plastic folder and handed copies to the commanders of the navy, army and air force.
It was a draft decree proposing to invalidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s election in October 2022 and keep Bolsonaro in power.

“The draft coup decree – which some people still insist to this day never existed – was there, awaiting approval or rejection; consensus or a majority,” writes the then head of the air force, Lt Brig Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior, in a new book coming out this month.

After learning that the document would prevent Lula from taking office, Baptista Júnior told the defence minister he refused even to receive it: “The air force will not take part in this.” He then stood up and left the room.

blocks.caption: Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior.   Photograph: Personal archive, courtesy of Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior

blocks.text: The extensive investigation and trial that convicted Bolsonaro of attempting a coup concluded that the plot failed to move forward mainly because the heads of two of the three armed forces – Baptista Júnior and the army commander, Gen Marco Antônio Freire Gomes – refused to take part.
The navy commander, Adm Almir Garnier Santos, was convicted, as was Nogueira. Both are serving their sentences at military facilities, while Bolsonaro is under house arrest.
Freire Gomes has kept a low profile, but Baptista Júnior, speaking to the Guardian by video call, said he had decided to write a book to help prevent history from repeating itself.
In the book, the 65-year-old former fighter pilot gives a detailed, first-hand account of the various ways in which Bolsonaro tried to cling to power.

Baptista Júnior said he was motivated by the fact that, despite the abundance of evidence presented during the former president’s trial, opinion polls still showed that about a third of the population did not believe there had been an attempted coup.

“Keeping in power someone who lost an election is a coup d’état,” he said, speaking from his home in Brasília, where he was dressed in civilian clothes – having recently retired – and about to pick up his grandson from school.

The book, the Portuguese title of which translates as I Said No! – An Anti-Coup Bulwark, is due to be published on 15 September, about two weeks before the first round of the presidential election, in which Lula will face one of Bolsonaro’s sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

Some Bolsonaro supporters have accused Baptista Júnior of trying to influence the vote, although he makes clear that he will vote for neither Lula nor Flávio, and criticises both in the book. He said the timing of the book was simply the result of the writing and editing process.

blocks.caption: President Lula addressing supporters at a campaign rally in São Bernardo do Campo this month. Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Despite writing that he voted for the far-right populist in the 2018 and 2022 elections, and even recounting a lighthearted moment at a barbecue when he saw the first lady reprimand the president for drinking beer, Baptista Júnior is critical of Bolsonaro, a former army captain who spent 30 largely undistinguished years as a city councillor and then congressman before reaching the presidency.

He describes his former boss as someone with “significant limitations in political, institutional and administrative experience” and an “almost total imperviousness to outside opinions or information that did not conform to the ‘truths’ he had already established as his own” – citing his refusal to accept facts such as the scientific evidence supporting Covid-19 vaccination.

During the election, Bolsonaro became “entirely consumed by his own efforts to remain in office”, writes Baptista Júnior. After repeatedly casting doubt on the vote, the president ordered the armed forces to investigate the electronic voting system, but refused to accept their reports when they found no irregularities.
“He may still not believe the election result even today. Whether that is a matter of character, personality or something pathological, I don’t know,” said Baptista Júnior.

The book touches on, but does not go into detail about, one of the most shocking revelations from the coup investigation: a plan drawn up by army special forces to kidnap or assassinate Lula, the newly elected vice-president and a supreme court justice. Baptista Júnior writes that he was not summoned to those meetings and only learned about them through the press.

He does, however, recount more than a dozen meetings in which Bolsonaro summoned the heads of the armed forces to discuss ways to remain in power. At one of them, he witnessed the army chief tell the president, after hearing a proposal for an institutional rupture: “If you do that, I’ll have to arrest you.”

Baptista Júnior had already given that account in testimony, and during the trial both Freire Gomes and Bolsonaro denied it. But he stands by his account in the book, writing that it was not something anyone present would forget.

Saying no to the coup cost the pilot “many friendships”, he said. Even some military personnel still call him a “traitor” or a “watermelon”, a slur for soldiers seen as green on the outside because of their uniforms, but communist red within.

The attacks started soon after the air force chief refused to join the plot, when the army general Walter Souza Braga Netto, whom Baptista Júnior considered a friend, ordered other military officers to attack him on social media and “make his life and his family’s hell”. Braga Netto, Bolsonaro’s running mate, was also convicted over the attempted coup.

Most of Baptista Júnior’s revelations in the book initially emerged in 2024, when he was summoned to testify to federal police and only then, more than a year after leaving office, revealed that he had witnessed an attempted coup.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Jair Bolsonaro face off with police Brasília in January 2023 in a demonstration calling for the overthrow of President Lula. Photograph: André Borges/EPA

blocks.text: Juliano da Silva Cortinhas, who worked on the civilian side of the defence ministry between 2013 and 2016, before the Bolsonaro administration, said: “It’s positive that he [Baptista Júnior] and the army chief said no to the coup, but as a matter of duty they should have reported it to the police as soon as it happened.”

Cortinhas, who heads a security research group at the University of Brasília, said the armed forces could not present themselves as the “saviours” of democracy because that would be like “tripping society up and then holding out a hand to help it back to its feet”.

“It was the commanders who allowed active-duty officers to take part in politics,” he said, noting that the Bolsonaro administration had by far the largest number of military personnel serving in civilian posts since the end of the brutal 1964–85 military dictatorship.

Cortinhas sees as positive the fact that high-ranking officers were convicted of an attempted coup for the first time, but noted that others involved in the plot escaped justice, and many were not even identified.
“The risk of a new coup is even greater today,” he said.

The new factor, he said, was the US president, Donald Trump, who has sought to influence elections across Latin America in support of far-right candidates such as Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2022, when Joe Biden was in the White House, Bolsonaro’s vice-president acknowledged that attempting a coup would leave Brazil in a “difficult position before the international community”.

Cortinhas said he feared that if Lula was re-elected and Trump refused to recognise the result, some members of Brazil’s military could feel emboldened. “Coup-supporting groups remain within the armed forces,” he said.
Baptista Júnior confirmed that, although it was difficult to know how many, there remained active-duty military personnel who believed a coup d’état would be justified under certain circumstances.
“That’s why eternal vigilance is the best path,” he said.

articles.title: Gaza refugee says sister-in-law ‘would be alive’ if Home Office had let her come to UK
articles.summary:
Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, says Home Office refused visa application despite Maryam having cancer

A man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza…

blocks.text: A man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza would still be alive today if the Home Office had agreed to bring her and her family to Britain.

Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, fled Gaza in 2020 and was granted refugee status in the UK in 2021. After the destruction of large areas of Gaza by Israeli forces following the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023, he applied to bring his brother Hassan, Hassan’s wife, Maryam, their two young children and other family members to the UK in October 2025. He said the Home Office rejected their application.

The process required them to travel to a visa application centre (VAC) for biometric checks, but there was not, and still is not, a VAC in Gaza. It is difficult for Palestinians to leave the territory to access a VAC elsewhere.
In April this year the family asked the Home Office to waive this requirement and grant permission for “predetermination” of their application and “biometric excusal”.
The Home Office is understood to have rejected this request, so the family launched a legal challenge. The Home Office agreed to reconsider its decision but issued a new refusal in July.

Prior to the second Home Office refusal, and shortly after Maryam gave birth to Ismail, who is now seven months old, she was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, which had spread to her lungs. Doctors in Gaza said they did not have the facilities to treat her.

The family provided the Home Office with medical evidence concerning Maryam’s condition, including cancer test results and medical referral reports. They also provided evidence of their living conditions in Gaza, which involved sleeping in tents and shortages of food, medicine and clean water.
Anwar said the Home Office again refused the family’s request for predetermination and biometric excusal but that it accepted the evidence of Maryam’s cancer.
In the Home Office’s letter refusing the visa application on 31 July, seen by the Guardian, officials stated: “Given the current situation in Gaza, reliable healthcare may not be accessible.”

They accepted that Maryam was facing a significant risk of harm because she was in a conflict zone and could not travel to a VAC. Although the Home Office officials found the circumstances relating to travel to a VAC “somewhat compelling”, they concluded that owing to the difficulty in travelling to the VAC, it was “in the best interests of the children to stay with their parents and delay travel to the UK” for the time being.

They concluded the family’s situation did not meet the threshold for “compelling circumstances” and said that pre-entry checks needed to be carried out because the family came from “a territory where terrorists operate”.
In the legal challenge, the family’s lawyers stated: “It is difficult to understand what circumstances would ever qualify as compelling if the present circumstances do not.”
Maryam died from cancer on 28 August.

Gordon McKee, the Labour MP for Glasgow South, raised the family’s case with ministers in June. He warned about Maryam’s deteriorating health and the consequences of the collapse of reliable healthcare in Gaza.
In his letter to Mike Tapp, then a Home Office minister, McKee said the case involved “exceptional humanitarian circumstances”. He asked Tapp to consider reviewing the case personally.

Anwar said: “We believe Maryam’s case raises serious questions about how the UK government deals with Palestinian families in Gaza who are trying to reunite with their families in Britain, particularly when a family member becomes seriously ill while trapped in a conflict zone and unable to safely reach a VAC.
“I believe that if the Home Office had agreed to bring Maryam and her family from Gaza to the UK when we first applied last October, Maryam would still be alive today.

“Maryam is now gone, but her family remains in Gaza. We are now urgently asking the UK government to intervene to protect Maryam’s surviving family members and to find a way to bring them to safety and reunite them with their family in the UK.”
Speaking from Gaza, Maryam’s husband, Hassan, said: “I am struggling to come to terms with losing my wife while I remain trapped in Gaza with our children, including our seven-month-old baby.

“Throughout Maryam’s illness, we were trying to find a way for our family to overcome the biometric requirement and move forward with our applications. The Home Office accepted that Maryam had cancer and acknowledged the evidence, but decided that our circumstances were still not compelling enough to justify biometric deferral or predetermination.
“Now I have lost my wife, and I am left trying to protect our children and find a way to get them out of Gaza and to safety.”
Home Office sources said they did not routinely comment on individual cases.

articles.summary:
Farage, who had earlier suspended two close aides, had his keynote speech interrupted multiple times by protesters on Friday

Morning, and welcome to our UK politics blog. Reform UK’s…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18m agoOpening: turmoil engulfs Reform conference

blocks.text: Reform UK home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf spotted at the conference, taking photos with supporters as the event gets under way.

blocks.caption: Photograph: Will Colebourne/PA

blocks.text: Before we get into today’s events, here’s a look back at the controversy at Reform UK’s conference yesterday.

My colleagues Rowena Mason, Ben Quinn and Pippa Crerar have the full report on a day which saw Nigel Farage attempt to shore up his leadership as the party faced fresh scrutiny over its finances and the suspension of two senior aides.
The report covers the fallout from the undercover investigation, the allegations over potential foreign donations and the divisions emerging within the party. They write:

double quotation markThe row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal. It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.” He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival to Robert Jenrick or Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals. However, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media.
Opening: turmoil engulfs Reform conference

Morning, and welcome to our UK politics blog. Reform UK’s annual conference continues in Birmingham today, with speeches from Lee Anderson, Zia Yusuf, Robert Jenrick and others, before Nigel Farage takes to the stage for the closing remarks.

The conference has been overshadowed by a scandal involving senior Reform figures caught in an undercover sting discussing potential foreign donations, prompting the suspension of two senior aides and renewed scrutiny of the party’s finances.

Jenrick, Reform’s treasury spokesperson, said James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a close aide to Farage, have been “permanently suspended”, telling Times Radio this morning: “There is obviously due process, and so there is going to be an investigation, and we want to learn all the facts, give them obviously a right of reply.” Neither Orr or Jukes have commented on the allegations.

blocks.caption: Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage speaks at the party conference in Birmingham. Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/Reuters

blocks.text: Violence descended on the conference yesterday during Farage’s speech when hecklers were assaulted by a mob of Reform supporters. The New Arab, which published footage of the incident, reported the protesters could be heard raising the issue of an undeclared £5m gift to Reform, which has become a key focus of controversy surrounding the party. Farage appeared to laugh off the incident, according to the news outlet.
We’ll be bringing you the latest from the conference throughout the day, including the key speeches, reaction and any developments.

articles.title: DILG on Duterte: We didn’t arrest her despite knowing her location
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Saturday said they already knew Vice President Sara Duterte’s whereabouts, but chose not to “force the warrant of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Saturday said they already knew Vice President Sara Duterte’s whereabouts, but chose not to “force the warrant of arrest.”
“Its very unfortunate that all the pressure in her life is affecting her perception,” Remulla told reporters in a message.
The statement followed Duterte’s remarks that she does not feel safe in police custody as she posted bail of P360,000 for three counts of grave threats early Saturday.
She also said that she feared for her and her family’s life as the administration had been pressuring and harassing her since 2023.
“The PNP (Philippine National Police) accorded her all the respect her position deserves,” Remulla stressed.
He said that the PNP has surveillance of her warrant being served until the vice president posted bail.
The secretary added that although they knew her location on the night after the Quezon City Regional Trial Court issued the arrest warrant, they did not act upon the order.
“We have all the body cam footages of her warrants being served. We have all the body cam footages of her arrival to post bail,” Remulla said.
“We knew of her whereabouts the night before but we did not force the warrant of arrest,” he pointed out.

The QC RTC issued the warrant of arrest against the vice president on Friday over her alleged death threats to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez in 2024. /apl

articles.title: DA in Davao signs deals to bring Saba bananas to Hong Kong, New Zealand
articles.summary: DAVAO CITY — The Department of Agriculture in Davao Region (DA-11) announced Friday that Philippine Saba (Cardava) bananas are set to reach new international markets. This development comes following…

blocks.text: DAVAO CITY — The Department of Agriculture in Davao Region (DA-11) announced Friday that Philippine Saba (Cardava) bananas are set to reach new international markets.
This development comes following the signing of two Supply and Purchase Agreements during Asia Fruit Logistica Hong Kong 2026 on Sept. 2.
Last month, an initial 20-ton shipment of Cardava bananas bound for Saudi Arabia was sent by accredited exporter GERB Golden Hands Corp.
The shipment, comprising 1,540 boxes at 13 kilograms each, is expected to arrive within 35 days.

DA-11 said the new agreements were signed between Philippine exporter Avante Agri-Products Philippines Inc. and Cozy and Korner Trading Co. of Hong Kong, as well as Fresh Produce Group (FPG) Ltd. of New Zealand.
Cozy and Korner will serve as the exclusive distributor in Hong Kong, while FPG Ltd. will act as the exclusive importer and distributor in New Zealand.

“The new agreement strengthens trade linkages between Philippine exporters and international buyers and creates new market opportunities for Philippine agricultural products, particularly premium export-quality Saba bananas,” DA-11 said in a statement.

The signing was among the highlights of the Philippines’ participation in AFL 2026, where DA led a delegation of fruit industry associations to promote local produce and explore new international markets.
Meanwhile, DA-11 also reported its participation in the Sabah International Expo 2026 (SIE 2026), a biennial trade fair in Kota Kinabalu, Malaysia, running from Sept. 2–6.
The expo serves as a platform for exhibitors across the Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area (BIMP-EAGA) and ASEAN.

DA-11 Regional Technical Director for Operations Marie Ann Constantino said the participation highlights the competitiveness of Philippine products, particularly those from Davao Region, while opening opportunities for Halal-certified enterprises.
“To access the global market, we must know and comply with the market protocols and requirements of the importing country,” Constantino noted.
“Meeting these standards is essential in ensuring that our products can successfully enter and compete in international markets,” he added. /apl

articles.title: Sara Duterte prosecutors weigh dropping bribery article
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors have not made a final decision on whether to drop the bribery article against Vice President Sara Duterte as they consider ways to speed up her impeachment…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors have not made a final decision on whether to drop the bribery article against Vice President Sara Duterte as they consider ways to speed up her impeachment trial, private prosecutor Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr. said Saturday.
Tolosa said prosecutors were reviewing the article alongside their remaining witnesses as part of efforts to finish the trial sooner and avoid extending the proceedings into next year.
“We always say that we don’t want this to extend into next year,” Tolosa said at the Saturday News Forum at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City.

Article III concerns alleged bribery involving Department of Education officials during Duterte’s term as education secretary. Prosecutors had publicly raised the possibility of dropping the article earlier in the week.

Tolosa said prosecutors shared the desire expressed by members of the public and some senator-judges for a faster trial. The panel was reviewing the evidence that still needed to be presented and the number of witnesses necessary to establish its case.
He cited the prosecution’s presentation on grave threats, saying it stopped calling additional witnesses after determining that the evidence it sought to establish had already been presented.
“There were so many witnesses whom we no longer called,” Tolosa said. “When we felt that we were able to meet them already, we stopped there.”

Tolosa said prosecutors had planned to take the same approach when they began presenting evidence concerning confidential funds by reducing the number of witnesses once the necessary testimony had been given.
“And we said from the very start of this discussion on confidential funds that we also wanted, as much as possible, to considerably trim down our witness list,” he said.
The review of Article III is part of that effort, Tolosa said. Prosecutors were considering whether foregoing the presentation of evidence on the article could help shorten the trial.

His remarks followed lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro’s Sept. 3 statement that the panel was reviewing the bribery article and its remaining witnesses, with no final decision yet on dropping the article.
Tolosa said there was precedent for narrowing an impeachment case, citing the 2012 trial of the late Chief Justice Renato Corona, when prosecutors withdrew five of the eight impeachment articles.
“But again, just to be clear, there is no final decision yet on that,” Tolosa said.

articles.title: Expanded free college law to help more Filipino youth earn degrees – Dy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Speaker Faustino “Bojie” G. Dy III said Friday that amendments to the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act would give more Filipino students opportunities to enter…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Speaker Faustino “Bojie” G. Dy III said Friday that amendments to the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act would give more Filipino students opportunities to enter college or technical-vocational training and support them in completing their education.

Dy joined President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., Senate President Sherwin “Win” T. Gatchalian, Education Secretary Juan Edgardo “Sonny” M. Angara, Commission on Higher Education Chairperson Shirley C. Agrupis, Technical Education and Skills Development Authority Secretary Jose Francisco “Kiko” B. Benitez and other congressional leaders at the ceremonial signing of Republic Act No. 12325, or the Act Enhancing the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act.
“For many families, it is not enough for their child to simply enter college. The real success is seeing them graduate, find a decent job and improve the life of the entire family,” Dy said.
Under the law, qualified students from Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program households will receive priority in the grant of tertiary education subsidies.
This will provide support for qualified 4Ps graduates admitted to government-recognized higher education and technical-vocational institutions.

RA 12325 also establishes a Private Education Assistance Program that will provide government grants to poor and deserving students pursuing priority programs in qualified private higher education institutions and technical-vocational institutions.

“When worries about transportation, books, food and other education expenses are reduced, students can focus more on their dreams. This assistance is not only for the student; it is an investment in the future of their family,” Dy said.

The Isabela lawmaker thanked House members and leaders for acting urgently on the measure, which was among the priority bills identified by the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council, and for working with the Senate to reconcile and pass the legislation.

“I thank our leaders and members of the House who acted promptly and united to pass this important measure. We have shown that Congress responds immediately when the future of Filipino youth is at stake,” Dy said.

Dy said Congress’ responsibility does not end with the enactment of the law, adding that the House will exercise oversight and closely monitor the formulation of its implementing rules, distribution of subsidies and concerned agencies’ compliance with its provisions.

“The House will monitor the implementation of this law to ensure that the funds reach students who truly need them properly and quickly. This law will only be meaningful when our people feel its benefits,” he said.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's grave threats case separate from impeachment trial -- Tolosa
articles.summary: House prosecution panel legal spokesperson Atty. Jay Tolosa on Saturday said the arrest warrant issued against Vice President Sara Duterte in connection with her grave threats case is separate from…

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 5:22pm

House prosecution panel legal spokesperson Atty. Jay Tolosa on Saturday said the arrest warrant issued against Vice President Sara Duterte in connection with her grave threats case is separate from the ongoing impeachment proceedings against her.
“Para sa’min, that’s a separate proceeding, judicial proceeding that’s different from the impeachment proceedings. Iba ang nature niyan,” Tolosa told reporters at a news forum.
(For us, that’s a separate judicial proceeding that’s different from the impeachment proceedings. It has a different nature.)

Tolosa was referring to the three counts of grave threats filed by the Department of Justice (DOJ) against Duterte over her remarks that she had hired an individual to kill President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez should an alleged plot against her succeed.
On Friday, the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 ordered Duterte’s arrest after finding probable cause to hold her for trial.
On Saturday, Duterte posted bail of P120,000 per count, prompting the QC court to lift the arrest warrant against her.

“Sa criminal case, ang dine-determine diyan is if may criminal liability, dapat ba siya makulong o hindi. Dito naman sa impeachment proceedings, ang dini-determine is fitness to remain in office,” Tolosa said.

(In a criminal case, what is being determined is whether there is criminal liability and whether she should be jailed. In the impeachment proceedings, what is being determined is her fitness to remain in office.)

In a text message to GMA News, Tolosa reiterated that the criminal case and the impeachment trial are separate proceedings, “governed by different rules and standards, and serving different purposes.”

Tolosa explained that “neither takes precedence over the other,” noting that “the issuance of the warrant does not suspend the impeachment proceedings, nor should it determine the outcome of the impeachment case.”
He also stressed that the issuance of the warrant does not amount to a conviction.

“It only means that the court independently found probable cause to hold the Vice President for trial and to issue a warrant of arrest against her. As to whether the issuance of the warrant has any bearing on the merits of the allegations before the Impeachment Court, I would rather not comment because of the sub judice rule,” the lawyer said.

“As far as the impeachment trial is concerned, our position remains the same: the parties should be allowed to present their evidence, VP Sara should be given every opportunity to answer the evidence against her, and the senator-judges should decide the case based on the evidence properly presented before the Impeachment Court,” he added.— VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit
articles.summary:
Scale of deportations made public for first time amid criticism of hardline approach to UK citizens

Sweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police…

blocks.text: Sweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit.

It is the first time the scale of the deportations of citizens who failed to secure residency in Sweden post-Brexit has been made public and comes amid mounting criticism of a cruel and hardline approach to Britons who had chosen to make the country their home before Brexit.

Some have been told to go after more than 25 years in the country and even vulnerable elderly people with dementia have been affected. One man was deported even though he had lived in the country since he was 10 years old.

Susanna Fonsell, a unit manager and legal expert at the Swedish Migration Agency, told Sverige Radio: “A rejected application does not necessarily result in deportation… and according to the agency statistics, the agency’s rejections of an application for resident status has been accomplished by a deportation decision in only approximately 400 cases,” she told Sweden Radio.

The Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, confirmed to the Guardian that 458 British citizens had been deported since Brexit. “According to the agency’s statistics, the Swedish Migration Agency’s rejection of an application for residence status has been accompanied by a deportation decision in only 458 cases,” a spokesperson said.

David Milstead, who heads up the 9,000-strong activist group Brits in Sweden, said it was important for Sweden to release full and transparent figures in relation to removals and deportations and their circumstances.

“We need to understand exactly what the 458 represents. Does it capture people who gave up and left when they realised their withdrawal agreement application was unlikely to succeed? Does it include people who were refused withdrawal agreement status, subsequently obtained a permit under national law and were only later ordered to leave?
“It certainly does not capture people who are currently managing to remain in Sweden on temporary permits, with little certainty about their long-term future.”

He said the figures illustrated a “broader problem” in that the data was issued piecemeal and sometimes in an opaque manner. “We still do not have basic published figures showing how many people submitted a missed-deadline application and the fraction of these which succeeded,” he said.

The last available data shows that there were 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency, which included family members joining British citizens after the deadline by 2024. Of those, just under 4,000 were rejected, a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%, according to Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) analysis.
Deportations are still happening. This week, the Swedish wife of a former business director from Cambridge told how her husband was detained in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a forced removal.
She said they had been fighting to overturn the decision by the migration authorities for five years and felt that they had been “hunted”.

Earlier this week, the Guardian revealed a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, who had lived in Sweden since he was 10, had been deported, separating him from his wife, Caroline, in Gothenburg, who said people needed to know how Brexit had “crushed families”.

blocks.caption: Joyce Thomas, 78, is facing removal from Sweden as a result of its hardline Brexit policy. Photograph: Felix Andler

blocks.text: Another woman, 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, has been told to remove herself from the country before next Wednesday. Friends are trying to get an injunction and have appealed to the European Commission for help.
after newsletter promotion

If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and be “registered on a watchlist” preventing potential entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”.

The Swedish Migration Agency told the Guardian it had “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. The Swedish Migration Agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions.”
Late applications for post-Brexit residency are allowed under the Brexit withdrawal agreement, both in the EU and the UK, but applicants have to show “reasonable grounds” for missing the deadline.
The FCDO has said that “in practice” late applicants in Sweden “are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”.

Earlier this week, Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, said his government had followed the rules but that it was willing to look into the matter. “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future,” he said.
A spokesperson for the FCDO said: “We continue to raise this with the Swedish authorities and welcome their statement that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so.”

Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for Sweden’s opposition Centre party, said the government needed to go much further. He pledged to bring in new laws if his party won power at the next general election to allow British to reapply for post-Brexit residence, saying “a touch of humanity” was needed.

articles.title: Trump signs order to remove endangered species protection for grey wolves
articles.summary: The US president says the move will help ranchers, but conservationists say it could derail efforts to recover populations.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has signed an executive order to remove endangered species protection for the grey wolf and a subspecies, the Mexican wolf.

The US president's decision could pave the way for pastoral farmers to kill the canines to protect their livestock. His order said ranchers played a "vital role" in the food supply chain and American cultural heritage.
But conservation groups have criticised the move, saying it could derail long-term efforts to recover the endangered wolf populations.
There were 319 Mexican wolves in the wild in the US in 2025, up from just four when they were reintroduced in 1998, US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) figures show.
Meanwhile, there are roughly 18,000 grey wolves across the US, though they are still considered endangered as most of their habitat has been destroyed by humans.

An attempt to de-list them at a federal level in 2022 became tied up in litigation, and some campaigners have indicated they intend to do the same of the US Department of Interior acts on Trump's order.

The executive order does not give ranchers immediate license to shoot wolves preying on livestock, but instead gives Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to determine whether the grey and Mexican wolf populations had recovered enough to warrant being taken off the endangered species list.
Noting that US livestock herds were at a 75-year low while demand for beef had risen by 10% in the past decade, the order added: "More can and should be done to support this critical industry."
However, environmental groups pointed to studies that suggested wolf attacks on livestock were rare and had little impact on ranchers' income.

"This is a huge distraction to placate a handful of ranchers and make them believe that wolves are a greater threat than President Trump's own policies," said Greta Anderson, deputy director of Western Watersheds Project, which works to conserve wildlife in western US states.

The Wolf Conservation Center noted that ranchers were entitled to up to 100% compensation for any livestock losses caused by wolves under the current system, with individual states providing funding for programmes to deter attacks.

"The Mexican grey wolf is not recovered simply because the population has grown," said Claire Musser, executive director of the Grand Canyon Wolf Recovery Project. "Weakening federal protections now would put decades of recovery work at risk."
The executive order comes as the Trump administration is seeking to lower record-high beef prices for consumers, driven by drought and an outbreak of parasites in US beef stocks.
Ranchers have been frustrated by Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on beef imports to address price rises, putting pressure on their already tight margins.

The US government launched a campaign to systematically exterminate wolves towards the end of the 19th Century. This, along with farmers and landowners trapping and killing wolves, pushed them to the brink of eradication.
Ranchers still view them as a nuisance, which tackling lethally constitutes a federal crime.

articles.title: How might Lindsay Clancy’s case have unfolded in another country?
articles.summary: The US mother was on trial for strangling her three children. In other western countries, there’s a specific law for mums who kill their young children.

articles.title: 'A surreal moment': Lunenburg's Logan Taylor reflects on making NFL's Chargers
articles.summary: Logan Taylor spent last Sunday hoping his telephone wouldn't ring. The Lunenburg, N.S., native now lives in Los Angeles and Sunday marked the day NFL teams had to make their final roster cuts. The…

image.caption: Los Angeles Chargers guard Logan Taylor stands for the national anthem before an NFL pre-season football game against the San Francisco 49ers in Inglewood, Calif., on Aug. 20, 2026. (Kyusung Gong/AP Photo)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

Logan Taylor spent last Sunday hoping his telephone wouldn't ring. The Lunenburg, N.S., native now lives in Los Angeles and Sunday marked the day NFL teams had to make their final roster cuts. The deadline was 3 p.m. PT and if players were getting cut, they'd get a call.
The 6-7, 312-pound offensive lineman is one of few born-and-raised Nova Scotians to make an NFL team
Logan Taylor spent last Sunday hoping his telephone wouldn't ring.

The Lunenburg, N.S., native now lives in Los Angeles and Sunday marked the day NFL teams had to make their final roster cuts. The deadline was 3 p.m. PT and if players were getting cut, they'd get a call.
When the clock hit 3 p.m., Taylor, a sixth-round selection in this year's draft by the Los Angeles Chargers, finally breathed a sigh of relief.
"It was a surreal moment … it's a very small percentage of people that are able to say they've made a 53-man roster, so [I'm] just very honoured," he said.
The list of born-and-raised Bluenosers who have played in a regular-season game in the NFL is short: Tyrone Williams and Steve Morley.
How Taylor celebrated making the team
After learning he made the team, Taylor said he went out for dinner with his wife and was in bed early to get a good night's rest, so he could report for work the next day.

Making the Chargers is the culmination of a lifelong dream that meant moving away at 14 from his home in the tiny seaside South Shore community. This has included stops in Timberlea, N.S., Virginia and Massachusetts to chase his dream.
Taylor, a six-foot-seven-inch, 312-pound offensive lineman, recognizes his journey is only beginning.
"It's never over, so that's one nice thing about this job is you can never be content, and you got to show up and be the same person every single day and strive to get better," he said.
The Chargers' season starts Sunday, Sept. 13.
Sam Dickens is the president of Seahawks Minor Football, the organization where Taylor started. She said his success is inspiring current players.

"They've been watching him every game, the pre-season games and we have banter all over the field every practice night," she said. "I'm on the field five nights a week and it's always a topic of conversation."

items: Lunenburg to La-La Land: Logan Taylor chases lifelong NFL dream

blocks.text: Taylor has put on a few free football camps with Seahawks Minor Football, and the lessons he's taught are sticking with the players, said Dickens.
"The older kids see that he's somebody to aspire to, they're putting in extra work, extra time, extra efforts, always taking the extra reps," she said.

At the most recent camp, which was held shortly after April's NFL Draft, Dickens said Taylor led drills, signed autographs for the kids, and the organization raffled off some signed merchandise to raise money for Seahawks Minor Football.
"He is one of the most humble kids I've ever met," she said. "He would rather be out there playing with the kids out on the football field than doing anything media-related, basically.
"But he absolutely enjoys coming out, seeing the kids, showing them what they can do, teaching them and then turning it around and seeing what they're doing later on."
For Taylor, coming from a province where most professional athletes play hockey, there wasn't much of a blueprint for how to get to the NFL. He wants to be a resource to help others achieve that.
"I was in their shoes at one point and I know it's difficult to get here," he said.
