articles.title: Black-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in Kent
articles.summary:
Traffic on A20 in and out of port grinds to halt as Kent police say they are in attendance and engaging with group

A large group of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas have…

blocks.text: A large group of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas have blocked the road at the port of Dover in Kent, forcing closures in both directions.
Kent police said they were aware of the protest, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. Officers were in attendance and engaging with protesters, they said.
Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 has been stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways.
Videos and pictures shared online show masked people in black standing on the road in a large group as lorries wait in traffic next to police cars.
Some have estimated that about 300 people have gathered, although this has not been confirmed by police.
The Port of Dover confirmed in a statement that the disruption was affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town, and that it was in touch with the police.

It said: “The Port of Dover can confirm that there is an ongoing public order incident happening around the town of Dover. This situation is impacting our local community and our customers, so of course we are hoping for a swift resolution.”

Nathan Ditchburn, who was on his way to work when he saw the group arrive at about 6.45am, told KentOnline: “I would say there are around 300 men, maybe more. Nobody will speak; they just handed me a piece of paper to look at. They have blocked off every entrance and exit of the Dover port area, and Jubilee Way is blocked as well. It will be causing huge delays for the ferries today.”
The far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted a video of the blockade, highlighting a livestream of the protest.

The local parkrun group cancelled its Dover Waterfront run, telling runners the course was unsafe or blocked. A spokesperson told KentOnline: “I am afraid we are going to cancel this morning. We have mass disruption with some protesters.”

Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, criticised what he described as “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. In a post on Facebook, he said: “Parkrun cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption. I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”

A local Reform UK councillor, Paul King, told residents to avoid the port area. He said: “I’ve been told it’s a stop the boats protest. Speaking to local women, they felt frightened by such a large group of men walking up the street. We don’t condone causing public disturbance by protest. But it’s a very good example of what is happening daily with the boats coming in.”
The shipping company DFDS said: “We are aware of the current traffic disruption affecting access to the port. Rest assured we will accommodate you on to the next departure once you arrive.”
P&O Ferries said its sailings were still going ahead as scheduled, adding that those who missed their departure would be offered the next available crossing.

articles.title: Angara honors 2 teachers in 2026 Outstanding Filipinos awards
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Education Secretary Sonny Angara honored two public school teachers at the 2026 Metrobank Foundation Outstanding Filipinos awards on Friday for their leadership and…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Education Secretary Sonny Angara honored two public school teachers at the 2026 Metrobank Foundation Outstanding Filipinos awards on Friday for their leadership and compassionate teaching in basic education.
Angara co-presented the awards with Metrobank senior management, highlighting the work of educators who go beyond their duties to help their students and communities.

“Our teachers are the heart and foundation of our education system. What Dr. Emmanuel Guarde and Engr. Sheila Marie Amigo have demonstrated proves that when a teacher’s love extends beyond the classroom, an entire community can be transformed and uplifted,” Angara said, translated from Filipino.
Citing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive to care for teachers and improve basic education, Angara said the awardees served as “steady beacons of hope, compassion, and innovation.”
“They remind us every day that behind every child who dreams is a teacher who first believed in them, sacrificed for them, and gave them the tools to succeed,” he added.

Guarde, a Master Teacher III at Cornelio Lintawagin Memorial Elementary School in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, is a member of the Alangan Mangyan indigenous community who has spent 17 years promoting culture-based education.

He developed localized early-grade learning resources and the Mangyan Alangan Community-Based Competencies framework. He also helped establish a primary school, solar lighting and basic facilities in the remote community of Sitio Begnay.
Guarde also initiated the Adult Education and Livelihood Strategy Management Plan, which provides community members with functional literacy and vocational skills.
“I believe that quality education must be both accessible and meaningful,” Guarde said.

“Through my extensive research on the traditions and values of the Alangan Mangyan, I seek to contribute to the integration of indigenous knowledge into the curriculum so that education can become more inclusive, relevant, and respectful of cultural diversity,” he added.
Amigo, a Master Teacher I and licensed electrical engineer at Siay National High School in Siay, Zamboanga Sibugay, has served for 11 years.
She developed DULA, or Dynamic Utilization of Learning by Amusement, an initiative that uses low-cost, hands-on learning tools to make science more accessible to high school students.
Through the initiative, students’ average test scores increased from 22.67 percent to a post-intervention average of 70.40 percent.
What started as a lesson plan concept later developed into an instructional strategy, with Amigo’s findings published in 2023 and gaining institutional support at the district and division levels.
Her DULA Eco Havens initiative also established hands-on learning spaces in local barangays.
“As an engineer, I used to find joy in designing systems and solving technical problems. But nothing compares to the immense joy of building a learner’s confidence,” Amigo said.
“My heart fills up whenever a student who used to hide at the back of the classroom out of fear suddenly smiles because they finally understand a difficult lesson,” she added.
Angara also reaffirmed the Department of Education’s commitment to supporting teachers through professional development and welfare initiatives.
Eight other public servants — two higher education professors, three military officers and three police officers — were also honored at the event.
Each awardee received a P1-million cash prize, the Metrobank Foundation “Flame” trophy and a Medallion of Excellence.

The Metrobank Foundation Outstanding Filipinos program was established in 1985 by the late Metrobank Group Chairman George S.K. Ty. It has honored more than 700 public servants for integrity, service and excellence in nation-building.

articles.title: DepEd moves to strengthen Scouting policies in schools
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) is pushing to revise and strengthen school-based Scouting policies to make programs more inclusive, focused on character formation and…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) is pushing to revise and strengthen school-based Scouting policies to make programs more inclusive, focused on character formation and responsive to learners’ current needs.

DepEd recently gathered Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts leaders and education partners for the Stakeholders’ Convergence on the Harmonization of Scouting Programs in Basic Education, where participants discussed revisions to guidelines under DepEd Order Nos. 76 and 86, series of 2012.
The convergence was held on Aug. 25.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara said Scouting provides learners with practical skills beyond classroom instruction.

“Scouting is not just a co-curricular activity; it is a cornerstone of character building. It’s about giving our learners practical tools like discipline, teamwork, and crisis management that ground them for life and directly enrich what they learn in class,” Angara said.
“We are modernizing these policies to ensure every learner gains access to real-world leadership skills, resilience, and a strong sense of civic duty in a safe, supportive environment,” he added.
DepEd said the initiative is aligned with its Quality Basic Education Development Plan and Five-Point Reform Agenda.

The agency considers Scouting a co-curricular activity that can help develop character, leadership and community service while supporting learners’ physical and mental well-being and curbing school-based violence.
The policy review is also part of broader DepEd reforms intended to protect schools from learning disruptions and safety risks.

Officials from the Boy Scouts of the Philippines (BSP), Girl Scouts of the Philippines (GSP), Ten Outstanding Boy Scouts of the Philippines, Chief Girl Scout Medalists, Association of Top Achievers Scout–Philippine Chapter and National Eagle Scouts Association of the Philippines attended the convergence.
Representatives from the National Youth Commission and National Federation of Supreme Secondary Learner Government, as well as veteran DepEd Scouting advisers, also participated.
BSP Senior Vice President Jose Mari G. Pelaez said challenges encountered in implementing Scouting programs in schools underscored the need to update existing policies.
Pelaez also emphasized the long-standing partnership between DepEd and Scouting organizations in providing activities aimed at developing well-rounded learners.

GSP National President Cristina Lim-Yuson, meanwhile, said collaboration among DepEd and community partners helps ensure that education goes beyond academics to develop confident, resilient, compassionate and active learners.

Lim-Yuson said the initiative was not merely about funding but also about shared responsibility, with schools identifying learners’ needs and partner organizations providing the necessary resources and training.
Participants agreed to promote Scouting as a leading co-curricular activity for building character and fostering peace and safety inside and outside schools.
DepEd said the finalized policy framework is expected to help institutionalize Scouting as a major component of its efforts to provide learners with a safe and meaningful learning environment.

articles.title: Your cat can now fly with you on Philippine Airlines domestic flights
articles.summary: Fur parents, rejoice! Both small cats and dogs are now cleared for takeoff on all local PAL flights

blocks.text: TAKE-OFF. Philippine Airlines' first A350-1000 plane takes flight.
Airbus
Fur parents, rejoice! Both small cats and dogs are now cleared for takeoff on all local PAL flights

MANILA, Philippines – Philippine Airlines (PAL) passengers can now bring their cats along for domestic trips, with the flag carrier expanding its FurPAL in-cabin pet program to include both small cats and dogs.
For P2,500 one way, passengers may bring one small dog or cat inside the cabin on PAL domestic flights, subject to aircraft availability and the airline’s pet limits.
There are a few things to remember before you book your cat’s next flight.

Pets must be at least 12 weeks old and fully weaned, while the combined weight of the animal and its carrier cannot exceed 10 kilograms. They must be inside a soft-sided carrier, measuring no more than 45 x 25 x 28 centimeters, that can fit beneath the seat and be roomy enough for the pet to stand, turn around, and lie down comfortably.
Pet parents also have some paperwork to prepare. At check-in, PAL requires:

items: A signed declaration and waiver
A veterinary health certificate issued within five days of departure
A valid anti-rabies vaccination certificate
A Bureau of Animal Industry local shipping permit

blocks.text: Once aboard, cats and dogs must stay inside their carriers under the seat for the entire flight. So, sorry, hooman, no lap time or mid-flight photoshoots allowed. Buying your pet its own seat is also not an option.
Pets may drink water but can’t be fed airline food, so owners are advised to feed them before departure. Dogs must also have diapers on, while cats must have absorbent pads in their carriers.

FurPAL is limited to approved aircraft, including PAL’s Q400, A320, A321ceo, certain A330s, Boeing 777s and A350s. Space is also scarce. Most approved aircraft can carry only up to three pets per flight, so you need to be book and pay at least 48 hours before departure.
Travelers can check PAL’s full FurPAL terms and FAQs for the complete rules before booking. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Duterte: I was advised that posting bail is better than being detained
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday said her lawyers advised her to post bail as this situation will be safer than being in police custody, following an arrest warrant…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday said her lawyers advised her to post bail as this situation will be safer than being in police custody, following an arrest warrant issued against her.
The arrest order was in connection with the charges of three counts of grave threats filed against her in court.
“My lawyers spoke with me and advised me to post bail, instead of remaining in a separate confinement while in police custody,” she said in a statement posted on Facebook.

Her legal counsel further advised that it will be best to be protected by civilians who can watch her every move, instead of being isolated inside a detention cell, where her security will be less guaranteed.
Duterte said she has been pressured and harassed by the administration since 2023. She added that she feared for her mother and children’s security.
“I do not feel that my mother and children will be safe if I stayed with them, and I am deeply concerned about their safety and well-being,” she said.

Her statements came after the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (QC RTC) on Friday issued an arrest warrant against the vice president in relation to her reported threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Her bail was set at P120,000 for each count.

Duterte, together with her lawyers Atty. Paul Lawrence Lim and Atty. Michael Poa, appeared before the QC RTC Branch 98 early Saturday to post bail, where she told the media how she feared for her life.
“My fears are shared by the majority of citizens,” Duterte said.

“They worry, not only about the safety of their families, their lives and their dignity, but also about their property and livelihoods, given the lack of adequate public services and rampant corruption,” she added. /apl

articles.title: Abante wants Sara Duterte subpoenaed over P612.5-M confidential funds
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Rep. Bienvenido “Benny” Abante Jr. on Friday called for Vice President Sara Duterte to be subpoenaed in her impeachment trial to personally explain what happened to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Rep. Bienvenido “Benny” Abante Jr. on Friday called for Vice President Sara Duterte to be subpoenaed in her impeachment trial to personally explain what happened to P612.5 million in confidential funds after witnesses disclaimed knowledge of how the money was ultimately spent.

Abante, chairperson of the House Committee on Human Rights and an endorser of one of the impeachment complaints against Duterte, said the Vice President should face the impeachment court herself rather than leave the task of answering the allegations to her subordinates and lawyers.
“The Vice President should really be subpoenaed now. She should personally appear,” Abante said during an online press briefing.
House impeachment team adviser and spokesperson Ace Barbers, meanwhile, said the evidence and unanswered questions surrounding the confidential funds ultimately point to Duterte.

“The allegations in this article have already been substantiated, but if there are questions about where the money really went, and all roads lead to Vice President Sara, then perhaps she should explain it to the people,” Barbers said.
Abante stressed that calling Duterte to testify would give her an opportunity to directly answer the allegations and would not amount to a presumption of guilt.
“This is good for the Vice President. It is also good for her because she will be able to answer all the allegations against her,” Abante said.
“And if she is subpoenaed, it does not mean she is guilty. We’re not actually saying that she is guilty,” he added.
Abante said he was personally among those pushing for Duterte to be called to testify.
“I’ll say it: I’m the one suggesting that she be summoned. Let’s go to the jugular. Let’s see. She is the impeachable officer, so she should really face the court,” he said.
Abante said there was little reason to continue relying on Duterte’s subordinates when the central questions concern her own accountability as the impeachable official.
“Let’s not make it harder for her deputies, her staff,” he said.
“Why? Because she is the only one who can actually answer all of those allegations against her,” he added.

The confidential fund article covers P500 million spent by the Office of the Vice President (OVP) in 2022 and 2023 and another P112.5 million spent by the Department of Education (DepEd) in 2023 when Duterte was education secretary.

Former OVP special disbursing officer Gina Acosta testified as a hostile prosecution witness that Duterte instructed her to turn over four P125-million tranches of confidential funds to then-security chief Colonel Raymund Dante Lachica.
Acosta said she had no personal knowledge of how the money was ultimately distributed after it was turned over to Lachica.
OVP Assistant Secretary and Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio similarly testified that only Duterte and Lachica knew how the confidential funds were implemented.

Former DepEd undersecretary, chief of staff and spokesperson Michael Wesley Poa, who is now part of Duterte’s defense team, likewise testified that he had no personal knowledge of DepEd’s confidential fund operations.
Barbers said the testimony left unanswered the central question of who actually knew where the money went.
“If you go back to everyone who appeared, none of them knew. The question is, who knows?” Barbers said.
“So who else could better explain where it was placed?” he added.
Barbers later summed up what he described as the unanswered questions arising from the prosecution’s presentation of evidence.
“Bigger questions have been left in the minds of our countrymen: Where is the money? Where is the proof of its proper use or the receipts? And third, who should be held accountable?” he said.
Barbers, however, stressed that the prosecution panel has made no final decision on whether to seek a subpoena for Duterte, saying the matter was still being discussed.
“We’re not at that point yet, and it is still being discussed. Someone is merely suggesting it. But there is no final decision yet on whether she will be summoned,” he said.
He said the prosecution could eventually ask the impeachment court to subpoena Duterte if her presence becomes necessary to resolve questions left unanswered by the evidence.
“If her presence is really required and the questions that are left hanging remain unanswered, perhaps that’s the time that we will ask the court to subpoena her,” Barbers said.
Barbers also acknowledged that the impeachment rules do not compel Duterte to personally attend the trial because she is represented by lawyers.
“The rules of impeachment do not compel the respondent to appear. That is why she has lawyers,” he said.

articles.title: Sharing story of 9/11 'only way I can survive,' says first responder visiting Gander
articles.summary: Gordon Huie, who witnessed the explosion of the Twin Towers, lost his sister in Tower 1 and helped the injured in the hours that followed, visited Gander this week to tell his story and thank…

image.caption: Gordon Huie was working as an orthopedic surgeon in New York on Sept. 11, 2001 and when the Twin Towers were struck, he rushed to the nearest hospital to begin helping people affected. (Troy Turner/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

Gordon Huie, who witnessed the explosion of the Twin Towers, lost his sister in Tower 1 and helped the injured in the hours that followed, visited Gander this week to tell his story and thank residents of Gander for their help and support.
Gordon Huie lost his sister in attack, and helped others in the immediate aftermath
Gordon Huie calls himself the only “triple” survivor of the terrorism attack on Sept. 11, 2001 — a survivor who lost a family member and worked to help others in the immediate aftermath.
He's found sharing the details makes it easier to cope with. It brought him to Gander — the Newfoundland and Labrador town intertwined with the relief effort — this week.
"I noticed I decompressed a little bit each time when I spoke at these [events]," Huie told CBC News on Tuesday.
"I realized I need to tell my narrative, because that's the only way I can survive."
Huie was a working orthopedic surgeon in New York on Sept. 11. He was working on a research paper that was supposed to bring him to a hospital in Chinatown, he said.
That changed quickly.

"I left my office on 35th and Park Avenue, started heading downtown to my meeting. But when I looked up and I saw the towers on fire … Instead of heading to my meeting, I went to the right and started heading toward the World Trade Center," Huie said.
"When I got to the base of Tower 2, Tower 2 came exploding down."

items: "Heritage Minute" immortalizes Gander's 9/11 kindness
U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to visit Newfoundland for 25th anniversary of 9/11

blocks.text: Huie survived the explosion from the street, but quickly realized there wasn't much he'd be able to do at Ground Zero. That's when he decided to find the nearest emergency room.
"I went to Beekman Hospital. I don't work there, don't have privileges there. I identified who I was … [and] they trusted me at my word," he said.
"They gave me the fourth-floor conference room. There was no one up there. It was just myself, and they sent up one patient at a time."
9/11 survivor, rescue worker recounts what he did to help others on tragic day
From there, Huie worked to sew up patients' injuries, armed with only a conference room table and three pieces of equipment he was constantly trying to sterilize.
But hours later, he got a call he wasn't expecting. His sister, Susan, had died while inside Tower 1.
"When I called her office that morning, I got the usual, you know, recording. 'Hi, this is Susan Huie, I'm not going to be in the office September 11th, September 12th,' Huie said.
Susan often travelled for work, he said, and was in a meeting at the Windows on the World Restaurant inside the World Trade Center.
"She was on the 106th floor of Tower 1. The planes hit 86th to 96th floor … We had no idea she was up there."

Huie said he didn't plan to talk about the tragedy in the immediate aftermath. He realized the healing power it had when he spoke of the attack during a medical speaking commitment in Philadelphia a month later.
It would be years before Huie learned of Gander's piece in the history of the tragedy, when he was approached by producers of Come From Away, the hit Broadway musical detailing it.

He said he was most blown away by how the community came together, and how residents continue to say it was no big deal to this day. He spoke at a series of talks at the North Atlantic Aviation Museum in Gander this week.
"The day after the planes left, they went back to their normal lives and did not expect anything different," Huie said.
"They'll come out and say, 'we're not heroes'. Yes they are, OK? Because they have that moral compass. They care about people, they took in total strangers."
The community will continue its annual commemoration event held each Sept. 11 next week.

articles.title: Sara Duterte wants civilian protection over police detention
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte said Saturday she preferred to post bail and seek civilian protection rather than stay under the watch of the police.

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 4:26pm
Vice President Sara Duterte said Saturday she preferred to post bail and seek civilian protection rather than stay under the watch of the police.

Duterte showed up at the Quezon City Hall of Justice to post bail together with her lawyers, a day after a court issued an arrest warrant against her over the alleged grave threats she made against President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez.

"Nakipag-usap sa akin ang aking mga abogado at pinayuhan nila akong magpiyansa sa halip na manatili sa hiwalay na pagkakakulong habang nasa kustodiya ng pulisya. Ipinaliwanag nila na mas maaari akong maprotektahan ng mga sibilyan na makakakita at makakapansin sa aking kalagayan, kumpara sa pananatili sa detensyon kung saan ako ay nakahiwalay at mas mahina ang proteksiyon," Duterte said in a statement.

(My lawyers spoke to me and they advised me to post bail instead of remaining in separate detention in police custody. They explained to me that I can be better protected by civilians where I can be seen and my condition can be monitored, compared to remaining in detention where I am separated with weakened protection.)
While she was outside the hall, her counsel could be seen attempting to explain her legal options. The vice president, however, was visibly upset.

Duterte was insistent on bringing the media with her inside the building because she wants to be seen. She repeatedly said that she did not feel safe, accusing the police of harassing her mother and her child.
She also claimed to have been harassed by the government since 2023, but did not elaborate in what manner.

"Ang aking pangamba ay siya ring pangamba ng nakararaming mamamayan. Hindi lamang kaligtasan ng kanilang pamilya, buhay at pagkatao ang kanilang ipinag-aalala, kundi pati na rin ang kanilang mga ari-arian at kabuhayan dahil sa kawalan ng sapat at tamang serbisyo publiko at talamak na kurapsyon," she said.

(My worry is also the worry of everyone. It is not just the safety of their families, lives, and character they are worried about, but their belongings and livelihood because of the lack of adequate public services and rampant corruption.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
articles.summary: Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

image.caption: A statue in the port of Bremerhaven commemorates the millions of Germans who emigrated abroadImage: S. Ziese/blickwinkel/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, warned against accepting German immigrantsImage: Public Domain

blocks.text: The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven. "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."
A journey into the unknown

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

blocks.caption: Many European immigrants who came to the US in the 20th century arrived by boat in New YorkImage: Raimund Franken/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.
An invitation from Russia

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

blocks.caption: Catherine the Great officially invited Germans to immigrate to Russia in the late 18th centuryImage: akg-images/picture-alliance

blocks.text: However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.
"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.
Migration: A burden or an asset?
Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

blocks.caption: Migration researcher Jochen Oltmer has studied the immigration waves to and from Europe in the 19th and 20th centuriesImage: Michael Gründel/NOZ

blocks.text: In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.
By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

blocks.caption: Between 1956 and 1973, around 14 million 'guest workers' came to Germany from other European countriesImage: Hans Heckmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.
Who's welcome – and who isn't?
These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

blocks.caption: Germany took in hundreds of thousands of refugees in 2015, above all people fleeing the civil war in SyriaImage: Johannes Simon/Getty Images

blocks.text: Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.
"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."
Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet

articles.title: Why many Syrians feel Assad death sentence isn't enough
articles.summary: In July, a Syrian court sentenced former dictator Bashar Assad to death for crimes against his own people. But after 14 years of civil war, many survivors are demanding more when it comes to…

image.caption: Despite terrible memories of death during the war, including that of her brother, Huda Khayti now often returns to her hometown of DoumaImage: privat

blocks.text: Huda Khayti often finds herself returning to the place where she lost almost everything. Khayti, a Syrian women's rights activist, survived a 2013 chemical weapons attack on the east Ghouta region by forces of the former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad.

Her brother was killed by the bombs of the Assad regime and its allies. Her women's center was destroyed along with her home and in 2018, she had to leave her hometown of Douma — a major city in Ghouta — and flee to Idlib, a rebel stronghold in northern Syria.

Today, Khayti regularly visits her hometown, which is about 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) northeast of the country's capital, Damascus. Since the Assad regime was overthrown in late 2024, Khayti has traveled regularly between Idlib and Douma, where she's even working on opening a new women's center.

"Ghouta means so much to me emotionally," she told DW. But every time she returns there, she is also confronted with remnants of the civil war. "When I'm traveling through the country I see traces of war everywhere, so many houses and so much infrastructure destroyed. So much suffering. So much trauma."

blocks.caption: In Douma, Huda Khayti visits the grave of her murdered brotherImage: privat

blocks.text: Almost two years since the overthrow of the Assad regime, Syria has started a process to examine the crimes of the regime in court. In mid-August a Damascus court sentenced Bashar Assad and other high-ranking members of his regime to death in absentia. Assad is currently living in Russia, where he fled after his government was overthrown. Many senior officials are also there or hiding elsewhere.
Among other things, Assad was found guilty of premeditated murder, torture and depriving individuals of their liberty. The court said these were war crimes and crimes against humanity.

"Of course, this conviction of Assad is a good thing," Khayti said. "Even if it's only on paper. Bashar Assad may have been convicted but he just continues to live his life in Russia — like so many other Syrian criminals who fled to Russia."
Justice served in Syria?

The court's conviction had a big impact in Syria anyway. "The verdict had a lot of echoes by people, they were so happy," said Lina Chawaf, a Syrian journalist, media expert and researcher at Harvard University's Center for Middle Eastern Studies. "Many media celebrated the verdict on the statement day as a victory and consider it as part of transitional justice."

Still, it remains unclear whether there will be any actual punishment following the conviction. Although Russia and Syria agreed on an extradition treaty in 2023, observers say it's unlikely Russia would send Assad, a long-time ally, back to Syria. Additionally, according to the treaty, if the death penalty is likely, that could prevent extradition too.

In August, Syria's Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem said the country had established a commission to cooperate with Interpol and that cooperation with other countries in extraditing fugitive suspects would speed up legal proceedings.
Syria still scarred after 14-year civil war

Rana Sheikh-Ali, founder of Daret Salam (Peace Circuit in English), which uses technology to build peace and empower women, believes the Assad trial in August should be seen as largely symbolic. From a human rights perspective, she opposes the death penalty, but at the same time she says many locals saw the death sentences as just.
But the prosecution of high-ranking regime members is only one aspect of the transitional justice process.

Transitional justice isn't just about criminal trials. Other aspects include searching for missing people, investigating crimes, deciding on reparations and formulating institutional reforms. With all that, the focus should be on victims and survivors.

Numbers supplied by the Syrian Network for Human Rights indicate just how big the task is. In an article, the advocacy network reports that over 234,805 civilians were killed during the civil war, at least 202,000 of them by the Assad regime and its allies.

In addition, there are also at least 181,312 cases of arbitrary arrest and enforced disappearance to investigate as well as 45,339 deaths resulting from torture. It's thought that the actual numbers are likely far higher. The network has also documented 217 chemical weapons attacks by the Assad regime.
Victim-centered process needed

Women's rights activist Khayti was just a few kilometers from the epicenter of one of those attacks in eastern Ghouta in 2013. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she recounted. "I can't forget the screams of the victims. I kept thinking we were next. I felt that scratchiness in my throat, that burning in my eyes."

For a system of transitional justice that is truly victim-centered, it's not enough to just have survivors act as witnesses in court. "Victims must also participate in every detail related to the transitional justice process," she explained.

Additionally, those who were impacted by the crimes must be able to participate voluntarily and be protected as they do, Sheikh-Ali added. They should be able to talk about their experiences and should also be heard on topics like compensation, financial support and public recognition.
For survivors like Khayti, this means not just making Assad and a few top regime officials the primary targets of justice.

"I also want to see convictions for individuals who wrote reports that led to people ending up in the Saydnaya torture prison," Khayti said. "These individuals are just as guilty as the torturers themselves."

blocks.caption: Huda Khayti also runs a women's center in Idlib and works with people in refugee camps on the Turkish borderImage: privat

blocks.text: At the moment, though, it's unclear exactly how thoroughly Syria will confront its past.

"Convictions in absentia against Assad and other officials send an important signal after decades of impunity," said Sophie Bischoff, managing director of Adopt a Revolution, a German-Syrian human rights organization that supports civil society initiatives. "But for survivors like Huda Khayti, these sentences remain symbolic as long as those convicted are not actually held accountable — and it's also still not transparent exactly who is to be held accountable and on what legal basis, and who would be granted immunity."
Bischoff also noted that the new Syrian state has yet to fully and comprehensively investigate crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Syria.

"So far it's primarily been Syrian civil society organizations and human rights activists who have been researching and documenting these cases for years," she told DW. "Systematic state documentation of violent crimes committed during the Assad regime era is only just beginning."

The new Syrian government has created two commissions to work on issues of transitional justice. In late August, one of these — the National Commission for Missing Persons — launched a platform called Athar, where families of the missing can submit information.

The other organization, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, was established in May 2025 but has so far dealt only with crimes committed by the Assad regime. It has not dealt with crimes committed by militias fighting the war or the extremist group known as the "Islamic State".
Return to Syria: Rebuilding and seeking justice in Yarmouk
Investigating all war crimes
"This falls far short," said Bischoff. "For a comprehensive reckoning and a new beginning in a Syria for all, the war crimes of all warring parties must be included."

For Khayti, the requirement to place victims at the center of the process of transitional justice also has another difficult aspect. Her testimony is being heard, but at the same time she is forced to return to the original trauma.
"It's difficult for me to talk about it and I often feel like I'm reliving it," Khayti explained.
Sheikh-Ali said centering the victims means those impacted play a meaningful role in the process. But as they do so, she added, they should also be protected.

It's also important to remember these events, Khayti added. In Douma, she is working on ways to preserve recollections of the war. "We need to inform younger people about it so that the memory doesn't fade," she said.
In Syria, she said now it's about finding the missing, holding all perpetrators to account, fully investigating all crimes and giving survivors a voice.
"We will continue to be loud," Khayti said. "And we will continue to demand justice."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Cayetano on Lacson’s alleged slow release of charges: It’s like striptease
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano criticized Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson over the latter’s alleged gradual release of allegations against him. Cayetano…

image.caption: Senator Alan Peter Cayetano (left) and Senator Panfilo Lacson (Photos by NIÑO JESUS ORBETA)

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano criticized Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson over the latter’s alleged gradual release of allegations against him.
Cayetano particularly cited those accusations involving infrastructure and reclamation projects in Taguig City.
The senator likened Lacson’s actions to a “striptease” without evidence.

The lawmaker made the pronouncement during another Facebook livestream after Lacson noted that his office’s probe into the alleged anomalies in Taguig’s infrastructure and reclamation projects is making the minority leader “quake while quacking.”
“Every day for the last three months, it’s like a striptease, but there’s no real evidence. Just constant accusations,” said Cayetano on Friday.
“Why did I say witch hunt? Just looking for everything, even if there is none. It’s like you’re looking for a ghost. It’s not there. You’re making up a story,” Cayetano told Lacson.
He then dared Lacson to end the “trial by publicity” by allowing the Office of the Ombudsman to do its job.
According to Cayetano, he himself is cooperating “one hundred percent” with the Ombudsman.
“No one is above the law. We welcome an honest-to-goodness, fair investigation,” he said.
Cayetano then expressed confidence that the investigation will not only clear him, but will eventually reveal Lacson’s motive for repeatedly attacking him.
“We are confident that once everything is submitted, we will not only be cleared, but the intention of Senator Ping will be seen,” he said.
Meanwhile, on Saturday, Lacson responded to Cayetano, stating that he was right in mentioning that there were “ghosts” in Taguig.
“True. There are so many ‘ghosts’ in the slope protection and flood mitigation projects along Taguig River. The Ombudsman is now investigating,” said Lacson in a social media post.
The senator also bared that officials of the Taguig city hall reportedly tried to block investigators probing the reclamation project in the city alleged to be illegal.
“The illegal reclamation is a separate case that they are also looking into, but they were blocked by city hall, so the SAF arrested them yesterday,” he disclosed. /apl
