articles.title: How ‘Filipiñana’s’ slow burn exposes the Philippines’ class divide
articles.summary: Heat and thirst establish the class divide in ‘Filipiñana,’ Rafael Manuel’s satirical debut featuring a 17-year-old ‘tee girl’

items: Filipinos face a complex relationship with extreme heat, which has significant social and economic impacts, as highlighted in the film 'Filipiñana'.

The film explores themes of class disparity and personal fulfillment through the story of Isabel, a young tee girl at an exclusive country club, juxtaposing her experiences with those of residents in a water-scarce neighborhood.
Despite critiques of its slow pace, 'Filipiñana' is praised for its visual storytelling and deeper commentary on Philippine society, colonialism, and the quest for identity.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Content warning: Minor spoilers ahead.
Filipinos have a complex relationship with the tropical heat.

We’re used to getting sweaty all our lives, even during the times we don’t even move that much: sitting in random establishments, wandering idly in our homes, or standing in line, waiting for something (an activity Filipinos have been well accustomed to, because everything feels ironically slow in our fast-paced society).

But as mundane as it may seem, the extreme temperature isn’t to be underestimated. A Greenpeace report shows that heat stress is pushing Filipinos into a “climate poverty trap.” Heat has lingered in our lives so much that it has caused class suspensions and economical disruptions, among other things.

In the Filipino film Filipiñana, though, heat isn’t only a villain; it’s a catalyst to expose bigger evils. The satirical debut feature of Rafael Manuel — who also wrote and edited the film — follows Isabel (played by Jorrybell Agoto), a 17-year-old “tee girl” who’s new to the job in an exclusive country club. Her responsibilities include assisting golfers in setting up golf balls at the hitting bay. One of them is Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman), the club’s president, whom Isabel gets strangely drawn to.

blocks.caption: Jorrybell Agoto stars as a 17-year-old tee girl. Filipiñana film still

blocks.text: Before hitting the local cinemas, Filipiñana graced the international festival circuit through the Sundance Film Festival — where it took home the Special Jury Award for Creative Vision — and the 76th Berlinale.

Bianca Balbuena, one of the film’s producers and CEO of Epicmedia Productions Inc., shared in an interview with Rappler: “This is the project where I got to deal with big studios mostly doing English-speaking films, the complicated but rewarding UK system of legal, financing, and closing.”

“We also have a UK distributor, BFI [Distribution], so I am excited to discover a wider UK audience. I am also learning a lot from our Oscar-winning distributor Kino Lorber and our PR companies in North America, Divergent and Cinetic, on how to push and market our local films to the Western market.”

Filipiñana happens over the course of one day. It starts off strong with its juxtaposition of two contrasting scenes, showing class disparity. There’s a cramped Manila neighborhood where residents scurry to fill their jugs with water, a scarce resource. Their chaotic state gets even more rattling when they almost get hit by a tourist van, ridden by the country club visitors, who are protected from the drought thanks to their air conditioning.

Meanwhile, the golf course catering to high society has an abundance of water — sprinklers and water fountains are for everyone’s convenience, even to the rich who can’t seem to stop complaining: “Grabe, ang init, parang galit na galit ang Diyos sa atin (Wow, it’s so hot, it’s like God is so angry at us).”

Thirst is a strong emotion in the film, and is experienced by almost everyone — whether it’s for a new discovery, self-expression, or personal fulfillment. Everyone can’t seem to feel satisfied with what they have now, and are always left wanting more.
But you’ll have more empathy for the tee girls who’d put themselves in discomfort, just to catch some cold air conditioning because their electric fans won’t cut it in the sweltering heat.
For a relatively quiet film, it told a lot.

Filipiñana had its Cinemalaya 2026 run as the festival’s closing film, its Philippine premiere, with some critics pointing out how it’s awfully slow, that you could easily fall asleep before the credits roll.

While its slow pace is heavily felt, it’s intelligently done, as it lies in intention. Its slowness probably means lethargy — how the extreme heat pushes you to take things in slowly, or discourages you to take action.

“As our great cinema icon Lav Diaz says: ‘It’s just cinema.’ We feel that to group a film into a category just based on the pace of the film would do a great disservice to the audience,” Balbuena said.

“There are so many kinds of films to explore and discover. We would say don’t be fooled by the term ‘slow cinema’. It can move you with incredible emotion and even overwhelming violence. Pacing and technique are just ways to tell a story,” she added.

“Filipiñana is different from most films we’re used to as [a] general audience, because the film is more formalist than narrative. It takes a certain kind of openness to accept that. And that is, in fact, counterflow cinema.”

Since the POV we’re following is Isabel’s, the slow burn also makes sense. It’s her first day on the job, and for someone so young in that disposition, it would take some time to absorb (and revisit) some horrors.
“For us, it’s always been about the portrayal of innocence — about innocence lost but ultimately, humanity gained,” Balbuena stated.

“The film is a coming-of-age. Her growing up has a lot to do with her turning inward into memories, which she has suppressed or forgotten. This is a representative of a malaise plaguing our country — we have a short collective memory as people.”

Even if the film’s audience is torn between liking or disliking its pace, what they can probably agree on is that it’s the epitome of picturesque. Every frame packs striking color palettes, flawless blocking, and overall jaw dropping production design. This reflects the team’s ambitious creative choices.

“I’ve also learned that when we have big support, we can do production the proper way. We shot for over 50 days in eight golf courses and took care of the well-being of the staff and cast. We do rehearsals in the morning and shoot in the afternoon. It was a breath of fresh air — how this production was run,” said Balbuena.
Does this make perfectionism a healthy trait to cultivate in filmmaking?

“[It] depends on the goal and purpose. If it’s perfectionism with the goal of doing things the right way based on a moral stance, then yes. But we also believe perfectionism is the enemy of creativity,” argued Balbuena.

Perfectionism also spilled over to the movie. There’s an eerie kind of synchronization in the actions made by the swimming pool cleaners to the staffers fixing the chairs and tables. Everything is well-choreographed, as if to cover something dark and twisted.

As both Isabel and Dr. Palanca hail from Ilocos, you’d initially think that this becomes a sacred similarity. However, this profound (one-sided) connection also becomes Isabel’s portal to a wakeup call, as exhibited to the timing of when “Manang Biday,” a traditional Ilocano folk song, plays in the film.

“Ilocos, as you already know, is a rural northern region in the Philippines that is of immense political significance — it’s where infamous dictator Ferdinand Marcos hails from,” explained Balbuena. “And now, less than 40 years after he was ousted from power, his son is the current president of the Philippines. Ilocos is also where Jorrybell Agoto, who plays Isabel, was born. So it was a very natural choice.”
Ultimately, Filipiñana portrays Philippine society rooted in American colonialism. And it’s a clever creative choice to inject it right in the title.

“When you look up ‘Filipiñana’ in a dictionary, it’s defined as anything that relates to Filipino culture and I liked the juxtaposition of matching that with the image of a golf course,” Manuel tells Rappler. “Because although it’s not the first thing that comes to mind when one thinks of the Philippines, I think a golf course encapsulates our country quite well. I also think of it as a play on Americana but with an “ñ” (which is used in Spanish) so with one word — “Filipiñana” — you allude to both our colonial histories.”

But zooming into the film, you’ll feel that this isn’t where it all ends. When a default Mandarin greeting gets repeatedly taught to the tee girls to welcome Chinese tourists — to the point that it almost feels robotic — you could sense how Isabel suddenly wants to take control of what she can, even in ways you can’t explain.
So, you almost completely get it when she hits a mango with a golf club, or jumps into unknown waters, just to feel something. – Rappler.com

articles.title: As Canada-U.S. relations sour, border towns of upstate New York fear damage will be permanent
articles.summary: As U.S. President Donald Trump fights with Canada on tariffs and his decision to rename Lake Ontario, Americans along the border in upstate New York fear the heightened fight could spell the end of…

image.caption: People watch the sun set over Lake Ontario in Olcott, N.Y., on Aug. 25. (AP Photo/Adrian Kraus)

blocks.text: At his marina in Sackets Harbor, N.Y., on a cloudy Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Alex Morgia looks toward the water and paints a vivid picture of the beauty he often sees, even on an overcast day.

"Sometimes those are the best sunsets because the sun will peek through underneath and then you get all of the cascading colours on the underside of the clouds," Morgia says, looking out over what has recently become North America's most controversial lake.
"We get sunsets over the lake year-round," Morgia says, before clarifying: "Over Lake Ontario, not to be vague."

Sackets Harbor, located on the lake's eastern shore around a 40-minute drive from the Canadian border, finds itself caught up in a war of words and wares, as the United States and Canada feud over tariffs and U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America."

items: Ontario premier unveils Lake Ontario sign in Hamilton as tensions with U.S. escalate

blocks.text: The harbour, Morgia points out, was even mentioned in Trump's executive order.
It's not the first time the quaint village has been at the front lines of a fight between these two nations: Sackets Harbor was the site of two major battles during the War of 1812, Morgia says.
"People find cannonballs in their yard all the time," he said. "People use them as doorstops."

While Morgia downplayed how much support Trump has for renaming the lake, he — along with other U.S. residents and officials living near the border in upstate New York — is concerned this heightened fight could spell the end of close Canadian ties, to the detriment of their communities.

"We had a brief period of time where I thought he was distracted with other problems and was going to leave the Canadians alone and we could be friends again. Obviously, that ship has sailed," Morgia said.
'It hits in the heart'

About a half-hour drive north of Sackets Harbor, on the U.S. side of the Thousand Islands Bridge over the St. Lawrence River, Corey Fram is fretting that the already difficult situation he faces is about to get much worse.

As director of the Thousand Islands Regional Tourism Development Corporation, Fram is responsible for marketing on both sides of the border. But after Trump got elected for a second time, there was a substantial decline in Canadian spending and border crossing, he said.
"It hurts to lose that economic impact of Canadian visitors on the New York side. But in a border community, it hits in the heart," Fram added.
Decline in Canadian cross-border travel continues

While he understands there may be a strategy Washington and Ottawa are each pursuing that buoys their countries' economic standpoints, those efforts have the opposite effect on border communities, he said.
"There's almost a sense that those of us along the border are having to pay the price for what is a supposed economic benefit for the greater good of each of the respective countries," Fram said.

items: U.S. border city residents put their 'Elbows Up' for Canada amid trade war

blocks.text: Anthony Adamczyk is facing the same issue in Ogdensburg, N.Y., about 45-minute drive northeast. He's the executive director of the Ogdensburg Bridge and Port Authority, which owns and manages the local bridge spanning the St. Lawrence.
Despite a slight uptick in border crossings from Canada in January 2025 compared to the previous year, they declined the following month and have never recovered, Adamczyk said.

Overall, traffic volume decreased 23 per cent in 2025 compared to 2024, equating to about 136,000 vehicles. The bridge's toll revenue went down 35 per cent, representing about $536,000 in lost revenue.

Fram's longer-term concern is that the number of Canadian tourists will permanently remain lower. He told CBC's The House that each time a major crisis affects border crossings — like the COVID-19 pandemic or the 9/11 terrorist attacks — the numbers fall and never return.
"My concern is this is yet another step, a big jump down that we're not going to get back to where we were in 2024 anytime soon, and maybe not ever."
Residents divided over Trump's tactics

The ongoing fight over tariffs and Lake Ontario's name puts residents of Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor in a complicated position. The two areas fall within St. Lawrence County and Jefferson County, respectively — both of which Trump has won by more than 10 points in previous presidential elections.

Outside a Walmart in Ogdensburg, Greg Barr told The House he visits Canada all the time and has never had any issues with Canadians. But when asked about the trade war, he said he thinks the U.S. has been "way too generous."

items: Carney dismisses 'unelected' Trump officials' explanation for why trade talks fell apart

blocks.text: "Not [just] to Canada but to other countries," Barr said. "[Trump's] getting things more even, to me. Maybe he has a different way of doing it, but he does get results."
Jim Rupert, who runs a taxi service that takes clients back and forth from Canada all the time, echoed Barr's view that Trump's tactics are a means of equalizing the playing field.
"I hate to listen to [Trump] half the time because he rambles, he rants, he does this and that, but the policies are solid."
But Carol and Gary Davis, who say they've noticed how much more their groceries cost nowadays, say they can't make sense of Trump's actions.
"When he got elected, gas was going to be cheap, food was going to be cheap," Gary said. "It's just the opposite."
Carol, who voted for Trump in the last election, said she's disappointed with the president — though she felt there weren't better options when she cast her ballot.
"So, yeah, I guess I do have regrets now."
Local Republican lawmaker weighs in

Scott Gray, a Republican assemblyman who represents Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor, is aware of residents' concerns. He told The House he's not opposed to tariffs, but doesn't want them to harm either his residents or Canadians.
"We have enjoyed a long-time exchange in our economy and our trade, and I think we should try to maintain that," Gray said.
He said he hopes some key irritants, like U.S. access to the Canadian dairy market, can be corrected through trade negotiations. But tariffs, he added, can be disruptive — as are counter-tariffs.
Gray pushed back on behaviour from the White House, including Trump repeatedly calling Canada the 51st state and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth belittling two female Canadian cadets.
Hegseth's comments on Canadian military 'stupid,' says U.S. Democratic senator
But he also placed some blame at Canada's feet, like when Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Trump could "kiss my ass" in response to tariff threats.

"We need to make sure there's a fair trade deal, and we need to do it without creating animosity and friction, which is largely caused by whatever antics that you want to describe out there," Gray said.

Back at the marina in Sackets Harbor, Morgia questions whether the U.S. government will stop antagonizing its northern neighbour. He's sympathetic to Canadians' calls for Americans to step up and pressure their leaders to back off on punishing their country.

"I guess not until [midterm elections in] November. People are trying, but right now the Republicans control most of the government. And until that changes, I don't think he's going to be held to account."

articles.title: How public institutions — like schools and transit — are handling Quebec's new secularism law
articles.summary: From university halls to Metro garages, public institutions across Quebec are quietly locking prayer rooms and rewriting employee guidelines as the province’s expanded secularism law takes full…

image.caption: Vanier College in Montreal is among schools that have locked the campus prayer room. A notice on the door says Muslim students can head across the street to a mosque to pray. (Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: From university halls to garages in Montreal's Metro network, public institutions across Quebec are quietly locking prayer rooms and rewriting employee guidelines as the province’s expanded secularism law takes full effect.
Law 9 significantly broadens the reach of Bill 21 and extends restrictions.

The religious symbols ban passed into law in 2019 now applies to daycare staff and prayer spaces are now forbidden in places like university campuses, or the facilities of a transit agency like Montreal's Société de transport de Montréal.

But as institutions rush to comply with the changes, administrators and legal experts warn that the government has left them navigating a complex legal grey zone with few clear guidelines on how to actually enforce the rules.
Law 9 took effect on Sept. 1.
Prayer rooms closed, chapels can stay
Concordia University — which had a large prayer room, according to the Muslim Student Association — says it no longer has any places set aside for prayer.
McGill University says it intends to comply with its legal obligations as well. Dawson College declined to comment.
“All the signs have been taken down,” said Ezekiel Montoya Desjardins, the vice-president of external affairs at the Dawson Student Union, who managed the prayer rooms there.

Signage and some furnishings, like carpeting, have been removed and the rooms are empty now. Montoya Desjardins said he understands the government’s position, but secularism doesn’t need to be defined as no religious activity.
“I think that it means there is neutrality in all religions at school,” he said, noting that the prayer rooms were mostly used by the Muslim community, but were open to everyone.

As for Vanier College, Benoit Morin, the school’s director general, said the small prayer room has been locked since the start of August. A notice on the door says Muslim students can head across the street to a mosque to pray.
While prayer rooms like that one close, religious practice in chapels, like the one at Université Laval, Concordia, McGill and Bishop’s University, is allowed.
Vanier catching up with the law

Morin said the school is still working on two important steps included in the law. The first is establishing a process whereby religious accommodations can be requested and determined by management, and initiating a complaints process as well.
Before, students would ask professors for religious accommodations. Now that request will go up to Morin's office, for him or someone he delegates to decide.

And when it comes to complaints about someone not operating in line with the multiple existing secularism laws, there needs to be a new, separate registry for Law 9 complaints that can be audited by the ministry, he said.
The school also created new training for security guards to teach them about Law 9 and give warnings to people if they see something that isn't in line with the law, he said.
LISTEN | Exploring some of the effects of Quebec's expanded secularism law:
Let's Go10:08Secularism law expansion goes into effect for STM, daycare workers
Morin said the new measures are affecting Vanier's ability to teach students the importance of living peacefully together.

“It was and still is fairly complex to determine the fine print as to how it should live within the walls of Vanier,” he said. “And we've been working hard throughout the summer to make sure that we can be compliant.”
The hope is schools like Vanier will be consulted more before such laws are adopted in the future as “it has a deep impact on communities that have been built over several years,” he said.
Daycare union keeping close eye on enforcement
The law also bars workers in subsidized daycares and private schools from wearing religious symbols. Those already in their positions are exempt.
A spokesperson for the federation representing health and social service workers is looking into the impact on its 13,000 daycare workers across 400 subsidized daycares.

In a statement, Lucie Longchamp, the spokesperson for the Fédération de la santé et des services sociaux-CSN, said it has asked its member daycares to identify Law 9's impacts and the federation “will closely monitor developments in the coming weeks.”
She said the federation expects to hear about a breakdown of services, departures and hiring difficulties. From there, the federation will have more to say on the matter.
The spokesperson also said the FSSS-CSN will continue to “advocate for an open, pluralistic model of secularism that does not further jeopardize the provision of non-profit educational services.”
STM closes prayer space, adjusts policies
Montreal's public transit agency is telling employees they can no longer pray on workplace property.
The Société de transport de Montréal (STM) says it has four rooms that employees can use for silent activities such as meditation and yoga but can no longer be used for prayer.
The agency says signs have been posted outside the rooms to remind people of the ban, and said supervisors who witness religious practices should address the matter with the employee.
The STM union representing maintenance workers declined to comment.

items: STM tells employees they can no longer pray at work as Quebec secularism law takes effect

blocks.text: Inside the transit network, musicians can still sing about their beliefs and wear whatever they want, but they can't "manifest any religious practice" or lead a worship service with music in the Metro.
STM spokesperson Amélie Régis said the agency’s special constables, with new training, will be intervening if any Metro performers are praying or evangelizing.

Groups like Jehovah's Witnesses will still be allowed to operate, even talking to people about their beliefs. Since they aren’t forcing their beliefs on people, but instead waiting to be engaged by passersby, the STM isn’t going to prohibit the practice.
“It is our understanding that discussing a belief is not a religious practice,” she said.
Régis said constables will intervene by "prioritizing an awareness-raising approach," so warnings will be given to those who don’t follow the rules.
Lawyer says there’s a ‘grey zone’
The penalties laid out in Law 9 are fines that, in general, range between $125 and $1,125.
The law outlines how the province is going to enforce the law, with inspectors who can go into an institution, take photos and report back.
However, the onus is still on employers to ensure compliance.

items: Quebec passes expanded secularism law targeting daycare workers, public prayer

blocks.text: Constitutional lawyer Frédéric Bérard said Law 9 represents a significant expansion of both where government oversight applies and what measures are enforced.
"You can say that it goes, you know, way beyond Bill 21," Bérard said. "One should ask the following question: What was the objective behind that?"

He argued the government cannot point to concrete examples of public prayer in places in the Metro causing disruptions, calling the legislation political pandering rather than a response to real needs.

While Bill 21 targeted authority figures like teachers and police to prevent state influence, Bérard said extending restrictions to cafeteria workers, janitors and transit employees reveals a shift toward removing visible religious presence entirely.
"So what's the next step, actually?" he asked. "Are we going to ban Muslim women from wearing veils in public, on the street? Are we going to go that far?"

items: Quebec talking with chief electoral officer over mailing of French-only voter info: premier

blocks.text: Bérard added that public institutions are left navigating a legal grey zone without clear rules on enforcement or handling non-compliant employees.
It offers no guidance on what to do if an employee refuses to comply.

"What do we do with people who keep wearing their religious symbols? Do we fire them? How do we do that?" Bérard said. "Those institutions are not quite clear about what they have to do in order to respect the new bill."
CBC News reached out to the office of the minister responsible for secularism and was told they would respond soon. The story will be updated.

articles.title: Some Great Lakes sturgeon may be 400 years old. Scientists are rethinking how to save them
articles.summary: New research suggests Great Lake sturgeon may live more than 400 years — far longer than previously thought. The discovery is forcing scientists to rethink the already-generations-long effort to…

image.caption: University of Windsor biology Prof. Trevor Pitcher, right, holds an adult lake sturgeon with the help of graduate student Olivia Galloway on the Detroit River, a place where the fish is making a comeback thanks to restoration efforts. (Dane Roberts)

blocks.text: Some of the lake sturgeon swimming around in the Great Lakes today may have been alive when Samuel de Champlain first reached Lake Huron more than four centuries ago.
New research suggests these ancient-looking, armoured fish may live far longer than scientists previously thought — in some cases, more than 400 years.

But despite their extraordinary longevity, lake sturgeon — which can weigh up to 180 kilograms and grow up to two metres long — have barely survived us. In Ontario, lake sturgeon are listed as a species at risk, and endangered in the Great Lakes specifically.

Overfishing and destruction of their spawning habitat wiped out an estimated 99 per cent of the lake sturgeon's historic population. More than a century later, populations in parts of the Great Lakes still rely on human beings raising and releasing young fish to help them recover.
The new study uses more than four decades of data from lake sturgeon caught and recaptured across the Great Lakes, suggesting recovery could be a much longer project than scientists anticipated.
A new way to count sturgeon birthdays

"We're pretty comfortable saying that there are potentially 400-year-old lake sturgeon swimming around," said Ed Baker, a fisheries scientist with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources who led the study.
Traditional estimates suggest lake sturgeon can live for as long as 150 years. But figuring out how many birthdays a sturgeon has had isn't as easy as counting candles on a cake.
Meet the ancient giants of the Great Lakes

Scientists have typically estimated a sturgeon's age by counting annual growth rings in a cross-section of its fin ray. But the older a sturgeon gets, the more slowly it grows — and the harder those rings become to distinguish.

Instead of counting growth rings, Baker and his colleagues used 44 years of capture data to calculate how much individual sturgeon grew between one capture and the next — then modelled how long it would take them to reach adult size.

In one remarkable case, a male sturgeon measured 117 centimetres when researchers caught the fish in 1990. When the same fish was caught again 34 years later, it had grown just seven centimetres, or about 0.21 centimetres per year.
When researchers used those real-world growth rates to calculate how long it would take a fish to reach full size, some of the resulting ages stretched into centuries.
"It's a completely unexpected result," Baker said. "But it's one that's supported by the data, for sure."
The very long game of saving sturgeon

For Trevor Pitcher, a University of Windsor biologist who has spent years trying to rebuild lake sturgeon populations, the finding raises a much bigger question: What does it mean to conserve an animal whose lifespan may be measured in centuries?
"I think it changes everything," he said. "Assuming they do live, let's say 200 to 400 years, we need to reframe the way we do conservation."

Canada's existing conservation plan is a century long, Pitcher said, with the expectation the work will outlast the individuals who started it. If the new longevity estimates hold up, the assumptions behind that plan may have to change, he said.
"We would have to readjust some of our plans about restoration, and some of the habitat work would certainly be different."

Pitcher said sturgeon eat large numbers of invasive quagga mussels and gobies, helping hold those populations down. Because historic overfishing and habitat destruction by humans reduced sturgeon to roughly one per cent of their former population, he said, "we kind of shot ourselves twice in the foot."
"When you take out a key species like sturgeon, it changes everything in the food web."

Pitcher's work is already extending beyond his own lab. His team is helping train people in Georgian Bay and Walpole Island First Nation to raise lake sturgeon themselves — spreading the expertise needed to rebuild populations around the Great Lakes.
A spiritual connection that runs deep

For Perry McLeod-Shabogesic, an elder and knowledge keeper from Nipissing First Nation, about 40 kilometres west of North Bay, Ont., the importance of lake sturgeon extends far beyond their role in the ecosystem.
"Because of their longevity, they were considered like a grandfather fish."
A fish that can live for centuries experiences and witnesses things across generations, he said, and it's the reason sturgeon are regarded as elders in Anishinaabe tradition.
"They're seen as elders — fish elders, if you will," he said.
Their appearance adds to that sense of age. Lake sturgeon belong to a lineage of fish that stretches back more than 150 million years — long before humans appeared.
It was only relatively recently that their numbers collapsed, as habitat destruction and commercial fishing nearly wiped them out across the Great Lakes.

Lake Nipissing once teemed with sturgeon. McLeod-Shabogesic remembers older fishermen describing spring spawning runs, when the fish crowded the Sturgeon and French rivers so thickly that their backs broke the surface.
"You could walk across the river, they were so thick," he said.
'Duh'
For McLeod-Shabogesic, the unusual traits also place the fish in another category; he describes sturgeon as beings that live "in between" — neither like other fish nor anything else in the lake.

In Anishinaabe teachings, he said, things do not always fall on one side or the other; between male and female is two-spirit, between hot and cold, there is warm. Sturgeon, he said, occupy a similar space.

That idea appears in an old Nipissing story McLeod-Shabogesic learned from his father. A family staying on the Manitou Islands caught and ate a mysterious black fish. By the next morning, they had transformed into serpent-like beings and disappeared beneath the ice.
The story, he said, speaks to the sturgeon's place in between worlds, and to its power and medicine.
"They weren't a fish completely and they weren't a snake completely. And then their age — they were different from the other fish."
So when McLeod-Shabogesic heard scientists now believe lake sturgeon may live for centuries, he wasn't surprised. "Duh," he said, laughing.

"It validates things to a certain degree," he said. "These are things that we already knew that our teachers and my ancestors — my grandparents and those fishermen that have fished this lake for a long time — they all knew these things already."

articles.title: A Michigan Democrat wants to put Canada on the ballot during the midterms. Are voters listening?
articles.summary: CBC News recently travelled to Michigan to get a temperature check on how Americans are feeling about U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff war with Canada — the state's largest export market.

image.caption: Lisa McFadden, left, and Peggy Banks take part in a women's bowling league in Flint, Mich. They're frustrated by tariffs and voting Democrat in the midterms. (Gian Paolo Mendoza/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics·New
CBC News recently travelled to Michigan to get a temperature check on how Americans are feeling about U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff war with Canada — the state's largest export market.
State's open Senate seat is shaping up to be a tight race in the shadow of a trade war
It's just past noon at Richfield Bowl on the outskirts of Flint, Mich., and already the sounds of rolling bowling balls and crashing pins fill the large hall.
Here, strikes and spares are serious. So are splits. And not just when two pins are left standing.
"President [Donald] Trump's trying to keep American people working instead of sending it overseas," said Scott Holmes, moments before his turn to bowl.
"My son just lost his job a few months ago because they sent it over to Africa."
His teammate Dick Hunt sees the U.S. president's tariffs another way.
"The people, we end up paying for it," he said.
How the Canada-U.S. trade war is playing out in Michigan
CBC News recently travelled to Michigan to get a temperature check on how Americans are feeling about the tariff war with Canada — the state's largest export market.
MAGA supporter Tina Bentley says she trusts the president's handling of the economy.
"I think he's a smart man. And I think that he cares 100 per cent about America," she said.
"The way I look at it is God didn't use perfect people to do his work. He used people like Trump to do his work."
A few lanes down, longtime bowler Peggy Banks can't disagree more.
"Our tariffs have not done anything for the people except make everything more expensive," she said.
Bowling league-mate Lisa McFadden nodded along.
"I think now everybody is starting to see it regardless of if you're a Democrat or a Republican because now it's affecting everybody's pocket," she said.
Trump's tariffs on the ballot

Michigan, heart of the auto industry, is one of the states hardest hit by the trade dispute. Just this month the U.S. National Taxpayers Union Foundation published a study suggesting Michigan households face the highest per-household tariff costs in the country.

items: Whitmer told Trump in private that Michigan auto jobs depend on a tariff change of course
Sault Ste. Marie in Ontario and Michigan share a border — and now a very big tariff threat

blocks.text: That puts the already hotly contested race for U.S. Senate this November in the shadow of an escalating trade war.

Winning Michigan's open seat is crucial for the Democratic Party if they want to regain control of the Senate during the second half of Trump's term. The Republicans are hoping to flip the seat red. So far, polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck.

Abdul El-Sayed, considered a progressive-left choice for this party, is hoping to capitalize on Michiganders' frustrations with the trade war. He's been pushing Canada into the conversation while campaigning, repeatedly calling Trump an "asshole" for starting a trade war with the country's northern neighbour.

"People don't want to have to keep paying more for stuff that they need to buy. And this is the logical outcome of an illogical trade war. So here we are," El-Sayed told CBC News during a campaign stop in Waterford, Mich., on Thursday.
Abdul El-Sayed says Michigan voters not happy with Trump's 'vanity trade war'
The Democrat — who was quick to raise his childhood memories of watching Hockey Night in Canada and his love of lacrosse, Canada's actual national sport — isn't ruling out all tariffs.
He cited duties on windmill parts or solar rigs as an example of tariffs he would keep if it would help build up his state's renewable energy industry.
"But it's because you're being very particular about exactly what kind of industries you're trying to protect. This is just across the board, ridiculousness, for no particular reason," El-Sayed said.
"So I can't quite explain it. Except for that everything Donald Trump does is ham-fisted, chaotic and self-serving."
His Republican rival has largely stayed away from talking about Trump's tariffs on the campaign.

Mike Rogers's camp didn't respond to CBC's request for an interview, but was recently asked by Fox News if he supports Trump's handing of the trade deal with Canada and backed the president's objectives.

"The Canadians have not been good partners on this," Rogers said in an interview on Fox & Friends on Monday. "I think they think that the Republicans are going to lose in the midterms, and then that the Democrats are going to open up the borders again and absolutely undercut the people who build cars and car parts right here in Michigan."
Voters mixed on if tariffs play into their vote
Residents in Genesee County were mixed on whether the tariffs will impact their votes.
Carl Olson, teammates with Holmes and Hunt, offered a quick "no."
"I think eventually everything will level out and everything will go back to normal," he said.
"If anything, it made it stronger that I will never vote Republican," said Joan Castor, when stopped in the Flint downtown core.
Down the street, Matt Zastrow said work and housing are his main concerns. If he votes, it will be for the Republican candidate.
"I think Trump's doing a good enough job right now. I'm not sure where we would be if we had somebody else in there," he said.
So far, industry in the region is largely staying out of politics. Businesses CBC contacted didn't want to speak on the record, citing the atmosphere.
Glenn Stevens Jr., executive director of MichAuto at the Detroit Regional Chamber, said businesses he speaks to want to see the cloud of uncertainty this trade war has brought cleared.
"Politics is not what this is about," Stevens Jr. said. "This is about making cars, in our perspective, moving lumber, moving energy, moving agriculture to the market and employing people.
"So the politics and the rhetoric are one thing, and that's at a crescendo right now, but the economics really are what speaks."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catharine Tunney is a reporter with CBC's Parliament Hill bureau, where she covers national security and the RCMP. She worked previously for CBC in Nova Scotia. You can reach her at catharine.tunney@cbc.ca
With files from Sylvia Thomson

articles.title: A month after migrants surged into Ceuta, thousands of kids are still stranded on the streets
articles.summary: Ikram, 17, left the Moroccan border town of Fnideq at the end of July, when an estimated 80,000 Moroccans and migrants from countries further south travelled travelled to the northern border city,…

image.caption: Ikram left the Moroccan border town of Fnideq at the end of July, when an estimated 80,000 Moroccans and migrants from countries further south travelled to the northern border city, hoping to cross into Ceuta. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

blocks.text: "I'm back on the street," 17-year-old Ikram wrote in a text message to CBC on Monday.

For a brief period, Ikram had felt relief in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. After spending almost a month sleeping in a forest, an abandoned bathhouse and on the street, the young Moroccan had finally found somewhere to stay. For three days, a family had hosted her as she helped look after their young children.
Then the work ran out.

Ikram left the Moroccan coastal town of Fnideq at the end of July, when an estimated 80,000 Moroccans and migrants from countries further south travelled to the north, hoping to cross into Ceuta. For many, the Spanish territory represents a possible route toward legal residency in Europe.
"In Morocco we are living, but not living the life we want," she said. Her father works as a tailor but earns little.

Most of the migrants who arrived during the July surge returned to Morocco within hours. But Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said 5,000 remain in Ceuta. Local authorities estimate 9,000 remain in and around the small enclave, whose population is roughly 80,000.

items: A Moroccan soccer player dreamed of Europe — but died on her way to Ceuta
Hundreds of migrants in Spain's Ceuta enclave protest for asylum, against deportation to Morocco

blocks.text: Among those who remain are hundreds of unaccompanied minors, including Ikram, living in extremely vulnerable conditions.
Many minors under 13, Spain says
According to Jennifer Zuppiroli, a migration specialist at Save the Children Spain, the Spanish Ministry of the Interior has registered 2,500 "children and adolescents" in Ceuta so far.
The actual number could be considerably higher.

"Various social and neighborhood organizations estimate that there could still be thousands of minors awaiting identification and referral to protection services," Zuppiroli told CBC News. Spain's Minister for Youth and Children, Sira Rego, said many of the minors are under the age of 13 and that around 700 of the migrant minors were girls.
Ceuta faces humanitarian challenge after surge of migrants
Most of the children and adolescents in Ceuta are from Morocco, Zuppiroli says, although minors from other countries are also there, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa, including Sudan.
(CBC is not using the last names of the migrants in this story because they fear deportation and reprisals from locals. For this reason, CBC is also not showing the faces of some of the migrants.)

Rego has reiterated that family reunification is the priority while acknowledging that "in most cases, there is no possibility of return." Under international law, the removal of unaccompanied minors is subject to strict safeguards, including the requirement to consider the child's best interests.
Ikram had tried to reach Ceuta alone during a previous mass crossing attempt in 2024. This time, however, she hadn't actually planned to go.

"My mom told me in the morning that people were crossing. Then, on my way to work, I met a friend who told me to go. I told her, 'No, I have a job.' She said, 'Let's just go and see.' And then I said, 'OK, let's go,' and we went."
At the border, they were confronted with a scene of chaos, with hundreds of people trying to swim around the border fence.
"We saw so many dead people," Ikram said. "Still I said, let me try my luck, and I went in. I almost died, too. I kept crying, and then I couldn't go on anymore."
One boy helped keep her afloat. "He kept pushing me, pushing me until I reached the shore."
When Ikram eventually reached the beach, she fainted and was taken to hospital. She was released the following day.
Her 15-year-old brother, Marwan, had crossed the land border earlier that day but left shortly afterward.
"He couldn't handle it," Ikram said, referring to the dire situation for migrants in Ceuta.
Ikram, however, insists she'll stay in Ceuta despite not having a place in any official accommodation or child-protection facility.
"I wish to build my future abroad, so I can help my mom and dad," she said. "Because right now, they're the ones counting on me."
For unaccompanied minors, Ceuta is 'a war zone'
Khadija Toufik, a French independent journalist who has reported for France Télévisions and TV5Monde, has seen how many minors are on the streets of Ceuta.

"They sleep alone outside," she said. "Every night is a night of terror, as soldiers come to wake them up, and very often, they are beaten with batons. Most of the minors I encountered in the streets were scarred and injured. For them, this is a war zone."
This vulnerability extends beyond unaccompanied minors. Some parents who have arrived in Ceuta with their children have also found themselves without stable shelter.

A man named Anouar crossed with his nine-year-old son, Wael, leaving his wife and three other children behind in Morocco. Since arriving, he and his son have moved between the streets and the homes of people who occasionally offer them a place to sleep, charge their phones or take a shower.
Meanwhile, tensions on the streets of Ceuta have escalated in recent weeks.

"There has been a rise in demonstrations by fascists calling for attacks against migrants," Toufik said. Last week, dozens of residents blocked Red Cross workers from distributing food and water to migrants. Later, fires were set at migrant encampments on a beach.
The unrest came after the arrest of 12 migrants accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, smashing its windows and injuring four people inside.
'The soldier hit me with a stick'
A 17-year-old named Abdo told CBC News that about three weeks ago, some 30 Spanish soldiers used violence to force him and other migrants out of an abandoned hospital where they had been sleeping.
"The soldier hit me with a stick. He broke my phone and my power bank," Abdo said in a video call with CBC News. He held up his hand, which was in a cast.
Medical volunteers with No Name Kitchen (NNK), a humanitarian organization established in Ceuta, treated Abdo's injured hand.

Ric Fernández, co-ordinator of NNK, says the group has collected more than 150 testimonies from migrants reporting violence by "uniformed agents, from the National Police, the military or civilians in disguise."
Abdo has been in Ceuta for more than a month. It was his ninth attempt to reach Europe.

In the previous two years, he had tried crossing the Mediterranean by boat, by hiding inside a truck on a ferry bound for Spain and by trying to enter through Melilla, Spain's other North African exclave.
"In Morocco, there aren't opportunities to work," he said. Youth unemployment in Morocco is around 36 per cent, according to the pan-African research institution Afrobarometer.

Abdo's father, a taxi driver, died in a car accident 10 years ago. His mother, who has five children and suffers from a uterine condition, is unable to work. His sister has a master's degree in law but has also been unable to find employment.

This year, Abdo completed Morocco's baccalaureate, a national qualification students can get at the end of high school, and says he was among the three top students at his school. He dreams of becoming a writer or journalist.
In the meantime, his main preoccupation is finding a safe place to sleep.

For the past three days, Toufik, who helps minors wherever she can, has arranged temporary accommodation for Abdo and another migrant in a hotel room. But with hotel prices rising, they will soon have to leave.
As for Ikram, she has become friends with an 18-year-old named Hasna, also from Morocco.

Members of NNK informed Ikram and Hasna they had received notice that a local organization had set up a safe camp for girls. The two told CBC News they walked together through the night looking for the camp but eventually decided it was safer to wait in a park.
"Honestly, we are scared, but it's night. We'll go in early in the morning."
The next day, Ikram was accepted into the camp. Hasna, who is not a minor, was not — and is still living on the streets of Ceuta.

articles.title: As Carney advances Vancouver port expansion, environmentalists raise concern for at-risk species
articles.summary: Canada's federal government is taking steps to designate the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 port expansion in Vancouver as a project of national interest. Environmentalists are concerned that fast-tracking…

image.caption: A rendering of the proposed Roberts Bank Terminal 2 project in Vancouver. The federal government has issued a mandatory notice that it intends to designate the port expansion as a project of national interest. (Port Metro Vancouver)

blocks.text: Politics

Canada's federal government is taking steps to designate the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 port expansion in Vancouver as a project of national interest. Environmentalists are concerned that fast-tracking the project could damage the Fraser River Estuary, an area integral to the survival of orcas and salmon.
Aug. 29 notice part of larger push by federal government to fast-track projects amid trade war with U.S.
The federal government is advancing the process to potentially designate the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 port expansion in Vancouver as a project of national interest.

A notice published in the Canada Gazette on Aug. 29 marks the start of a 30-day consultation period on whether to list the port expansion as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act.
The law allows projects deemed to be in the national interest to have their approval process, including environmental assessments, expedited.

In announcing the potential listing of both the terminal and the Mackenzie Valley Highway project in the Northwest Territories, the Liberal government said the projects "have the potential to strengthen Canada's transportation and trade networks ... and support Canada's long-term economic sovereignty."
However, environmental groups are concerned that potentially fast-tracking the port expansion could allow the government to bypass environmental protections.

The Roberts Bank Terminal 2 (RBT2) port expansion project, led by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority, is a proposed three-berth container terminal that would increase the port's capacity by nearly 50 per cent and generate approximately $100 billion in annual trade capacity, according to the port authority.

The federal government approved the project in 2023, imposing 370 legally binding conditions intended to address environmental concerns. That same year, B.C. issued the project an environmental assessment certificate that included 16 additional conditions.
In their decisions, both levels of government acknowledged that the project would likely cause significant adverse environmental effects, but were "justified in the circumstances."
The RBT2 project is still in the process of securing final environmental permits, including legal approval from Fisheries and Oceans Canada related to compliance with the Species at Risk Act (SARA).
However, if the project is granted national-interest status, Carney's cabinet could obtain the discretionary power to grant it exemption from SARA.
In July, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced $10 billion in federal support for the expansion project as part of a broader agreement with British Columbia.

items: George Massey Tunnel, mines and LNG: what's in the Ottawa-B.C. MOU

blocks.text: The expansion would be built in the Fraser River estuary, a location that environmentalists say is integral to the survival of hundreds of species, many of them endangered.
'Mega port' in an 'incredibly important breeding ground'

"This is an incredibly important breeding ground ecosystem for over a hundred at-risk species," said Julia Levin, associate director of national climate with Environmental Defence, a Canadian environmental advocacy group. "It's putting a mega port in the middle of that, destroying nearly 200 hectares of this really biodiverse estuary."

Last year, a Federal Court judge dismissed a lawsuit launched by multiple environmental groups who said the project would destroy vital chinook salmon habitat and threaten the survival of southern resident killer whales.
Southern resident killer whales — also known as orcas — are among more than 600 wildlife species listed under the Species at Risk Act. Only 75 southern residents remain.

Chinook salmon, currently under consideration for listing under SARA, are one of the southern resident's main food sources. But the area has lost approximately 85 per cent of its salmon habitat due to development and infrastructure, according to a 2021 study.

In response to environmental concerns, the port authority said in an emailed statement to CBC News that it plans to restore 102 hectares of habitat in collaboration with First Nations to "support key species like juvenile Chinook salmon and Dungeness crab."
The port authority said it is also advancing protections for southern resident killer whales, including requiring ships to participate in slowdown programs designed to reduce underwater noise.

B.C.'s Environmental Assessment office pointed to the legally binding conditions, saying in an emailed statement to CBC News that when construction begins, officers would "monitor the project for compliance with all provincial requirements over the life of the project."

Last spring, the federal government also proposed $258 million over five years to protect whales and their habitats, including $95 million over five years and $16.5 million annually thereafter specifically for the protection of southern resident killer whales.
But Levin and other environmental groups say the government's potential fast-tracking of these projects is a way to get them built at "any cost," including at the southern resident's expense.
Getting projects built at 'any cost'
"The federal government is clearly pursuing multiple avenues to bypass environmental safeguards," said Levin.

Along with potentially fast-tracking several major projects, including a new West Coast pipeline that would end in Roberts Bank, the Carney government is considering further changes to environmental regulations, including the Species at Risk Act, that it says would allow for quicker approval and construction of major projects.
"All of this is about overriding environmental protections, environmental laws and species protections to get certain projects built at any cost," Levin said.
The changes the government is considering would render the Species at Risk Act — and the protection it provides — "meaningless," wrote multiple scientists in a press release last month.

In May, two federal discussion papers proposed a number of possible changes, including exempting certain projects from the "jeopardy test" in the Species at Risk Act. Following criticism from First Nations and environmental groups, the government extended the engagement period, which ended in July.

"We're suggesting, rather strongly and bluntly to the minister, maybe this is not the way you want to do this," said David Green, a biologist and professor emeritus at McGill University who is one of the former COSEWIC chairs behind the letter.
"You don't have to just give yourself carte blanche to do whatever you want without mulling it over."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brock Wilson is a senior writer and producer for CBC News, based in Toronto. He produces episodes for Rosemary Barton Live and About That with Andrew Chang and writes digital stories. You can reach him at brock.wilson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Why was no mugshot taken of Sara Duterte in the grave threats case
articles.summary: A day after an arrest warrant was issued against Vice President Sara Duterte, she appeared before a court on Saturday to voluntarily surrender and post bail.

blocks.text: A day after an arrest warrant was issued against Vice President Sara Duterte, she appeared before a court on Saturday to voluntarily surrender and post bail.
On Friday, the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 issued a warrant of arrest against Duterte for three counts of grave threats after finding probable cause to hold her for trial.

The case stemmed from Duterte’s November 2024 remarks that she had ordered a person to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife, Liza Araneta Marcos, and then-Speaker Martin Romualdez if she were killed.
Bail was set at P120,000 for each count, requiring Duterte to post a total of P360,000.

Duterte’s legal counsel said her appearance before the court constituted a voluntary surrender. They also confirmed that the arrest warrant had been lifted following her appearance and the posting of bail.
However, Duterte did not have an official mugshot taken during the booking process. Instead, her camp submitted photos of her to the court.
Duterte’s counsel, Atty. Paul Lawrence Lim, said a mugshot was unnecessary because such photographs are typically taken by police when a person is arrested.
“Hindi kailangan, kasi yung mugshot, yung kinukuha ng mga pulis 'yun lang ay pag inaresto. Again, the Vice President voluntarily appeared,” Lim said.
(It wasn't necessary because mugshots are only taken by police when a person is arrested. Again, the Vice President voluntarily appeared.)
Lim said Duterte nevertheless underwent the standard booking procedures for an accused person, including fingerprinting.
“Kasama lahat ng mga usual, yung picture, yung fingerprint,” he said.
(It included all the usual steps, such as taking her picture and fingerprints.)
"She went through the same process as any accused individual. There was no special treatment—she submitted all the requirements and posted bail."
The court order lifting the arrest warrant also acknowledged receipt of the documents submitted by Duterte.
The documents included four copies each of photos showing Duterte from the left, right, and front.
Requirements
In November 2022, the Office of the Court Administrator outlined the minimum documentary requirements for posting different types of bail bonds.
For cash bail, the requirements are as follows:

items: Certified true copy or official court copy of the Information;
Four sets of the accused’s photographs showing the front, left and right profiles, with the accused’s name and signature on the back of each photo;
The accused’s left and right handprints or fingerprints;
Barangay certification for bail purposes indicating the accused’s real name and residence;
Location plan or house sketch of the accused’s residence, certified by the barangay;

Certificate of Detention, if the accused is detained or voluntarily surrenders to police in a location different from the court where the case is pending. The certificate must indicate the name, designation and signature of the authorized personnel at the detention facility.

blocks.text: However, the certificate is not required if the accused chooses to post bail before the court where the case is pending and has not voluntarily surrendered to the police or is otherwise not in police custody.

items: Accused’s Undertaking and Waiver of Appearance in accordance with Rule 114 of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure, notarized or sworn before the Clerk of Court or before the Warden, in case the accused is detained or imprisoned; and
Bail amount recommended or imposed by the Court

blocks.text: Jurisdiction
Duterte’s camp said it would continue to challenge the court’s jurisdiction over the case, even as proceedings move forward.
“Siyempre habang tuloy na nililitis yung kaso rito tuloy din naman na kinukwestyon namin 'yung jurisdiction. Again, we are awaiting the action of the Supreme Court,” Lim told reporters.
(Of course, while the trial is ongoing here, we will continue to question the court’s jurisdiction. Again, we are awaiting the Supreme Court’s action.)
In early August, the Department of Justice filed three counts of grave threats against Duterte.

Duterte later filed a motion to quash the charges on jurisdictional grounds, arguing that, as an impeachable officer, she enjoys limited procedural immunity from criminal prosecution while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
The DOJ said the court denied Duterte’s motion for lack of merit.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Lim said in an earlier statement.
Duterte’s alleged grave threats against Marcos and other officials are also cited in one of the Articles of Impeachment being heard by the Senate impeachment court. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Tate brothers officially indicted with trafficking and sex crimes in Romania
articles.summary: Andrew and Tristan Tate are currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges and deny all the allegations.

blocks.text: The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022.
They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.
Romanian prosecutors described a case as centring on a vulnerable female who was 15 at the time of the alleged offence, in information released on Friday.

She is alleged to have been recruited by Andrew and housed in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, so he could sexually exploit her. Tristan is alleged to have been an accessory, prosecutors say, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.
DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression, and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.
Andrew is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.
He is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.
Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 be confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.
The two brothers were previously indicted in Romania on trafficking charges, but in 2024 an appeals court in Bucharest sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible.
It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can begin.
The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities.

Their lawyer in Romania, Eugen Constantin Vidineac, said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial.

"The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial.

"DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process.

"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."

Correction 5 September: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that the Tate brothers were charged with further offences. The article has been updated to make clear they have been officially indicted with offences of which they had already been accused. It has also been updated to reflect that Andrew, not Tristan, was alleged to have recruited the 15-year-old.

articles.summary: Official estimates say that 275 Indians continue to be unaccounted for in Nepal's flood catastrophe. Meanwhile, no Indian travelers are said to be stranded in flood-affected Tibet. DW has more.

Official estimates say that 275 Indians continue to be unaccounted for in Nepal's flood catastrophe. Meanwhile, no Indian travelers are said to be stranded in flood-affected Tibet. DW has more.

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: India's Ministry of External Affairs says 275 Indians are missing while 169 have been rescued following the August 26 Nepal-Tibet floods
India is celebrating Teachers' Day
Preparations for the18th BRICS summit in New Delhi are entering the final phase, with a week left to go

blocks.text: Here is our rolling coverage from India on Saturday, September 5.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 5, 2026
Nepal floods: India says tally of missing Indians at 275
India has said that 275 of its nationals remain missing, ten days after flash floods ravaged areas along the Nepal-Tibet border.
A total of 169 Indians have been rescued so far from the flood-affected areas in Nepal, India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Friday evening.
Jaiswal said that in the latest rescue three Indians, including a five-year-old, were pulled to safety from Trishuli Bazaar in Nepal.
"Our Embassy in Nepal is assisting in their return to India by air," he said on X.
The spokesperson told a press conference in New Delhi that 1,907 Indian nationals have safely crossed over to Nepal from China.
No Indian travelers are now stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region, Jaiswal announced, citing official Chinese sources.
Nepal's official death toll from the deluge now stands at 1,294, with 5,053 still missing.
A frantic rescue effort has gone on for days to search for survivors, especially at mud-filled hydropower tunnels, where hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped.
Indian team assists in Rasuwa tunnel rescue
On Saturday, New Delhi's envoy to Kathmandu said that an Indian tunnel rescue team, working with Nepal's defense forces at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, had stepped up operations.

"The Indian tunnel rescue team working alongside with Nepali Army dug deeper into Chilime tunnel yesterday draining out water. A temporary track is also being made to allow more heavy equipment to reach tunnel," Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava said.
He added that doctors accompanying the Indian rescuers had also held a health camp for the local community.
India has also supplied nearly 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal since the floods hit the country on August 26, Jaiswal said on Friday.

articles.title: Gamified abuse: How a PH forum rewards submissions of non-consensual intimate content
articles.summary: The forum’s gamified system rewards users for uploading intimate content, while traffic and advertising turn exploitation into profit

image.caption: — Dana Batnag, data privacy lawyer

blocks.text: Content Warning
The following story contains descriptions and discussions of sexual violence, image-based abuse, and the non-consensual sharing and explicit sexualization of women. Reader discretion is advised.
Second of two parts
Shortly after discovering that intimate videos of her had been uploaded online, Mishy kept returning to a question.
"I am hurt by the fact that they took something so private, deeply private, to gain attention or to make money," she said.
"Why would someone share something that was never theirs in the first place?"
It's because there is something to gain. For the operators of NSFWPH, it is traffic.

The forum, which now boasts more than 430,000 registered members, has evolved into far more than a repository of intimate images and videos. It is a structured online community where users are rewarded for posting content, climbing membership ranks through participation, and, in some cases, monetizing the very intimate images they upload.
Rewarding exploitation
Unlike a conventional pornographic website, NSFWPH is an internet forum.
Members create threads. They comment. They react to posts. They earn points. And every interaction contributes toward a merit system that unlocks additional privileges.
Users who accumulate enough points are promoted through ranks such as "Established Member," "Elite," "Contributor," and eventually "Legendary," the forum's highest status.
Higher-ranked members may gain access to locked content, including additional information attached to posts such as the names of victims or links to their Facebook and Instagram accounts.
Participation and contribution are rewarded.
On NSFWPH, however, those incentives revolve around something more concerning: the non-consensual sharing of intimate content.

By its structure, the system has the effect of encouraging members to find material worth posting, whether by obtaining videos from former partners, redistributing Telegram content, or manipulating women into sending intimate images. The more active a member becomes, the more they stand to gain within the community.
It is a structure that transforms participation into exploitation.
“A person can consent to documentation, but not for posting.”
From internet points to real money
The rewards do not end with forum status.
Rappler identified one of the platform's most prolific contributors: a user known as Mikey Kun.

Kun holds the rank of "Legendary," the highest attainable status in the forum. He has amassed 4,902 posts — the third-highest post count on the site. Included among those uploads are sexually explicit videos of Filipina women, ranging from livestreamers on livestreaming platform BIGO to content described as "leaks" and "scandals."
Majority of Kun's posts use a service called shrinkme.io for monetization.

To download one of Kun's videos, a user clicks on a shrinkme.io link associated with a specific post. The user is then redirected to a series of pop-up ads before they eventually reach the actual download link. For every 1,000 users that click the link, Kun is given a payout.
Shrinkme.io's official payout rates vary by country. In the Philippines, the rate is US$4 per 1,000 views.

In our scan, Kun had more than 200 posts with corresponding shrinkme.io links just in July and August 2026. In our random sampling of these posts, the majority reach at least 1,000 views on the forum, with one post reaching at least 12,000, while a few reach only 600 or 700 views.
Theoretically, if 100 of those 200 posts reach at least 1,000 clicks on shrinkme.io links, that would mean Kun earned $400 or roughly P24,000 (at $1 = P60).
What this illustrates is that content is not simply exchanged; it also generates income for some, in this case, Mikey Kun.
“Why would someone share something that was never theirs in the first place?”
Beyond that, Kun also redirects audiences outside NSFWPH.

Under the same identity, he maintains Facebook pages and Discord communities where followers are directed toward additional content. In one Facebook post, he reminded users he had referred to NSFWPH to follow the forum's rules because violations could affect his own account. In another, he told followers he would focus less on updating NSFWPH and instead devote more attention to his Discord server, The Nowhere.

His two Discord servers — Mikey's Vault and The Nowhere — collectively host nearly 6,000 members. One advertises a VIP-only section offering "Exclusive" and "SHS" (senior high school) sets to paying members. His Facebook page has 4,400 followers.
Access costs P500, according to a post by Mikeykun on his Discord channel called Mikey's Vault, payable through GCash. In return, members receive download links to additional content.
The result is a multi-layered monetization model.
Users gain prestige in the forum. They earn advertising revenue through download links and also by selling access to the seller's collections directly on other channels.
The forum profits too
The NSFWPH platform itself is designed to capitalize on traffic.
According to analytics service Semrush, NSFWPH receives more than 10 million page views each month, with users viewing an average of 25 pages per visit and remaining on the site for over 14 minutes.

The website displays multiple advertisements on every page using ExoClick, an advertising network commonly used by adult websites. ExoClick estimates earnings of roughly $500 for every 3-5 million ad views, although actual revenues vary, depending on factors such as location and conversion rates. Each page on NSFWPH displays around five advertisements.
The figures do not reveal exactly how much the site earns but they do show that this amount of traffic has commercial value.
Together, they sustain a platform whose popularity depends on the continued circulation of intimate content — the origin of which are often questionable.
What the law says
Despite the apparent business built around these images and videos, Philippine law already prohibits much of the conduct taking place.

The Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act of 2009 makes it illegal not only to record sexual acts or private parts without consent, but also to copy, distribute, publish, sell, or broadcast such recordings without the written consent of everyone involved — even if the recording itself was initially consensual.

The later Safe Spaces Act further strengthened protections by penalizing gender-based online harassment, including the non-consensual uploading or sharing of photos, audio, or videos with sexual content.

Lawyer Dana Batnag, data privacy expert and human rights advocate, discussed further the elements of proper consent. "First, consent has to be informed. You need to tell me your purpose [for recording or documenting]. Consent has to be specific. A person can consent to documentation, but not for posting. If you were manipulated [to share intimate content], then was that consent freely given? Consent must also be freely given."

Consent to take a photo or record a video doesn't mean that the person has also given consent to have the content distributed, shared, or posted by any means. Persons also have the right to retract that right at any time they want.

Respicio Law also states: "A person who receives leaked private photos and forwards them may also face liability. 'I only shared it' is not always a defense… Group chat members, page admins, channel operators, and social media users should not repost, save, mock, or circulate intimate images."

Based on data privacy laws, Batnag said that since the forum is trafficking sensitive personal information in the form of intimate photos and videos, the administrators and owners of the site should be identified.

"For example, I'm one of those women. I have the right to know, under the data subjects right, who looked at my picture, who gave it to you, how you got it, your source of information. And I have the right to know to whom you shared those. As the data subject, I can demand that right. I can demand it from the owner of the website," the lawyer explained.

The site allows users to request for a content takedown, but since these are intimate images that are considered sensitive personal information, that would also mean that when the thousands of users get to see them without the clear and express permission of the subject, it can be argued that a violative breach of privacy has occurred.

Batnag also said that even if the website was hosted in another country, the owners of the website would face consequences under the Data Privacy Act, as the site deals with information of Filipinos, not just of the potential women victims, but also the very users registered on the site.

According to Liza Garcia, executive director of the Foundation for Media Alternatives, who advocates against the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, a massive platform like NSFWPH inflicts "a lot of harm" on victims, particularly young women, who often suffer profound "emotional harm" and "psychological harm."

Beyond the immediate trauma, victims face severe "harm to reputation" and even "financial harm" because the public nature of the exploitation can result in a victim being unable to work: "hindi ka na makapagtrabaho, ayaw mo na kasing lumabas ng bahay, nahiya ka na" (you can no longer work, you no longer want to leave the house, you are already ashamed).
This "profound shame" often causes victims to "tend to isolate" themselves, which means the "economic aspect of [their] life" is deeply affected.
This is the potential damage that can be caused by the operation of such a website.
For Garcia, those harms are not hypothetical. They are the foreseeable consequence of a platform built around the circulation of intimate content.
For the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group (PNP-ACG), NSFWPH is part of a broader landscape of online sexual exploitation and non-consensual sharing of intimate material.

The police have been actively pursuing perpetrators. From 2025 through August 2026, the PNP-ACG conducted 138 operations involving cyber warrants, entrapment operations, arrest warrants, and rescue operations, resulting in the arrest of 160 individuals involved in violations of the Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act.
Authorities also rescued minors and apprehended seven children in conflict with the law (CICL) related to these cases.
But going after NSFWPH itself presents a different challenge: jurisdiction.

A quick check on forensic tool Domaintools.com showed that the IP address of NSFWPH is connected to a Cloudflare server in San Francisco, California. Asueta said since the forum is hosted outside the Philippines, it is difficult for Philippine authorities to directly compel the platform to act. "So this is a jurisdictional issue," he said.
Requests for takedowns can also be circumvented through new sites and VPNs.

Asueta said these activities have existed for "medyo matagal-tagal na rin" (for quite a long time already). Recently, the PNP-ACG has seen fewer reports about the non-consensual spread of intimate images within its unit but cautioned that this does not necessarily mean the problem is declining because some victims may simply not be reporting.
Server accountability

Victims still have some recourse with content found on NSFWPH. The PNP-ACG said victims can file a complaint, and investigators can attempt to trace the source of the material found on the forum, identify an individual suspect, and pursue a case.
The police can also apply for a cyber warrant to search and examine the suspect's cellphone or computer for evidence.

But again, going after the actual platform is harder. Right now, if investigators can gather sufficient evidence, Asueta said they can coordinate with the relevant jurisdiction through Interpol and the International Mutual Legal Assistance mechanism — a formal method for international cooperation under the Department of Justice.

However, in the longer term, Asueta called for laws requiring foreign platforms operating in the Philippines to establish local offices and submit to Philippine court processes such as warrants and subpoenas.

To other women who may one day find themselves in the same position, Mishy offered fighting words: "Your body is not your shame. You deserve to take up space in this world without apologizing for what someone else did to you. There are countless women standing beside you, silently carrying the same wounds — but all of us are still worthy of every beautiful thing life has to offer. What happened to you is not a reflection of your worth."
Mishy said that if she had enough proof or evidence on who leaked the videos, she would attempt to pursue a legal case. — Rappler.com
Lance Ariel Bustos is an Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, currently studying at the De La Salle University Manila.
