image.caption: Police estimate that 6,000 people turned out at one demonstration in MagdeburgImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 5, 2026
Thousands turn out at 'Democracy Festival' in Saxony-Anhalt

blocks.caption: Police estimated that 6,000 people turned out at the demo in MagdeburgImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of people joined a "march for democracy" on Saturday in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.

Organized by a coalition called "Saxony-Anhalt: Open to the World," the march was called to uphold values of democracy, diversity and inclusivity ahead of a state election in which the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is comfortably leading opinion polls.
Germany's federal intelligence service has labeled the AfD state branch in Saxony-Anhalt as a right-wing extremist organization.
At the demo on Saturday, attendees carried signs that read "more love, less hate," "a better life without Nazis," and "the potato is also of foreign origin," among other slogans.

blocks.caption: Signs included slogans such as: 'A better life without Nazis'Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police estimated that some 6,000 people participated in the march from Magdeburg's central station to Cathedral Square, where another 3,000 people joined them.
Among them were contingents from trade unions, church groups and other civic organizations.
"As initiatives, clubs, associations, and individuals, we are taking a stand and advocating for respectful coexistence in our state," the organizers stated in their call to action.
According to police, eight gatherings had been registered to take place in Magdeburg on Saturday. Others included a human chain for democracy and a democracy-themed cycling tour.

In an interview with German daily the Tagesspiegel, right-wing extremism expert Heike Kleffner praised the organizers' "paradoxical confidence" in being able to mobilize democratic masses despite being under attack.

blocks.caption: The demonstrators marched to Magdeburg's Cathedral SquareImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal
articles.summary: Some say the case shed light on the mental health struggles of mothers, while others argue it's no excuse for murder.
articles.byline: Ana Faguy, Brandon Drenon, Sheila Flynn

blocks.text: Inside court as judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case
ByAna FaguyReporting fromreporting from court in MassachusettsBrandon Drenon and Sheila Flynn
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

Jodi Fournier spent 15 days at the courthouse - sitting, listening and waiting. It was a personal duty, she felt, to show support for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three children.
Katelyn Kazmirci, from North Carolina, convinced her mother to make a detour to the courthouse in Plymouth on their way to a family funeral, intrigued by the case she had followed on TikTok.

All around them, dozens of women wearing pink rallied in support of Clancy. Not everyone felt the same and across the country, on social media and at dinner tables, Americans have been debating the case with passion.
For nearly seven weeks, the trial transfixed and divided the nation on whether Clancy was a victim or a criminal who deserved to be behind bars.

The 36-year-old nurse's defence team argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis when she strangled her young children and so could not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution alleged the killings were intentional and calculated.
The judge declared a mistrial on Friday after jurors - who had heard the testimony of dozens of witnesses and deliberated for 40 hours - failed to come to a uninanimous decision.
Their inability to agree mirrored the wider discourse around the trial - one that trial attendee Maryanne Drysdale, 65, saw play out within her own family.
She and her 28-year-old daughter believe Clancy needs mental health treatment, not prison, while her three adult sons, who have children of similar age to Clancy's, completely disagree.
"It's black and white for them, [Clancy] killed the kids and that's that," she said. "I brought these kids up - how can we think so differently about this?"

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jodi Fournier spent more than two weeks outside the courthouse to show support for Clancy

blocks.text: Jodi Fournier spent more than two weeks outside the courthouse to show support for Clancy
Fournier believes Clancy was wronged by the US health system and felt compelled, as a woman and a mother, to show up for a case that has given a spotlight to postpartum struggles.
"It only takes one person to change the narrative," she said. "This is a global issue. This isn't just Massachusetts-small-town. This is... women everywhere."

Clancy claims she experienced hallucinations and delusions before strangling her three children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months old - and then jumping from a second-floor window, leaving her paralysed.
The court heard testimony from more than 10 expert witnesses on Clancy's mental and postpartum health during the trial.
But some of them seemed to dispute the defence's claim that postpartum psychosis - a rare post-childbirth condition characterised by mania and depression - precluded Clancy from criminal liability.
Jennifer Tufts, who treated Clancy during more than a dozen sessions over five months, testified that she had not shown signs of psychosis.
Psychiatrist Avram Mack later testified that the American Psychiatric Association did not recognise postpartum psychosis as a diagnosis.
These declarations only deepened staunch opinions for many - on both sides.

Texas mother-of-four Nicole Russell, who followed the trial remotely, noted the prosecution's presentation of how much medical care and support Clancy had received - from doctors, her husband, nanny and family - calling it "way more help" than most mothers receive.

Clancy's struggles were said to have begun following the birth of her youngest child. She repeatedly sought care, visiting a hospital emergency room, different medical professionals and even calling a suicide hotline.
Many observers took that as evidence that Clancy had been proactive and done everything within her power to heal but had been failed by the system, prompting sympathy from some.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Melissa Merrill says she, like Clancy, suffered suicidal ideation after giving birth

blocks.text: Melissa Merrill says she, like Clancy, suffered suicidal ideation after giving birth
Melissa Merrill had been treated at the same hospital as Clancy after the birth of her son.
"I see myself in her, as a mum who had suicidal ideation," she told the BBC outside the Plymouth courthouse.

Throughout the weeks of emotional testimony, the now wheelchair-bound Clancy could be seen crying, holding her attorney's hand and making agonised utterances in court as sometimes harrowing details were shared.

After one of the trial days, Merrill rushed to Clancy's defence attorney outside the court and gave him a pink envelope holding a message of support and hope for his client, believing Clancy was a "sad, defeated woman".
But other parents, like Texas mother Russell, railed against "toxic empathy", insisting Clancy was "not a martyr or a symbol for tired mums".

"Lindsay Clancy cannot be the poster child of what difficult motherhood looks like, because millions of mothers give birth to children and endure all kinds of hardship, and they do not hurt their children," Russell argued.
The moment judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case

The discourse around the Clancy trial was prominent on social media, with many users being hard-pressed to find a platform where the case was not being mentioned, if not being subject to myriad conspiracy theories.

Clancy's mother, sister and former husband all testified to her deteriorating mental state in the run-up to the murders, but her ex Patrick Clancy was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.

There were claims that he was to blame for the murders, despite his wife never denying killing their children, nor that she had been the only adult at home at the time. This thrust him into the limelight, with tabloids snapping photos of him travelling and with his new wife.
His lawyers issued a statement to CNN in August calling the facts "indisputable".

"Patrick Clancy has suffered an unspeakable and unimaginable loss," they said. "Unfortunately, the tragedy Patrick has experienced has been compounded by patently false, defamatory and injurious public statements."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Clancy supporters - many wearing pink - huddled outside the courthouse

blocks.text: Image source, The Boston Globe via Getty Images
Clancy supporters - many wearing pink - huddled outside the courthouse

blocks.caption: Image caption, Those who believed Clancy should be held accountable for the killings also had a presence outside the court

blocks.text: Those who believed Clancy should be held accountable for the killings also had a presence outside the court
The case became a flashpoint for gender discussion, too, with opinions often divided along gender lines.

Father-of-three Vincenzo Vazquez, who followed the trial from Illinois, believes gender has a lot to do with Clancy's treatment, doubting that the public would show similar sympathy if a father were on trial for the same charges.
"Whatever someone is dealing with, I don't think there's ever an appropriate time or an excuse or a justification to, you know, kill children of your own, or kill any children," he said.

He said he felt "very sad and a little disgusted to see how many people are rallying behind her", adding: "I think people should be out there rallying for justice for the children. They're three beautiful kids that had a future in front of them."

The decision to declare a mistrial after seven days of deadlocked jury deliberations has left the status of the case - and Clancy's future - unclear. A hearing at the end of the month could establish whether prosecutors will move ahead with second trial or attempt to reach a plea deal.
For now, the debates elsewhere will no doubt continue.

articles.title: Value of kush haul found in yacht at Subic port rises to P366.65M
articles.summary: OLONGAPO CITY — The total value of high-end kush seized from a yacht at the Port of Subic has risen to P366.65 million after authorities discovered an additional 123.91 kilograms of the illegal drug…

blocks.text: OLONGAPO CITY — The total value of high-end kush seized from a yacht at the Port of Subic has risen to P366.65 million after authorities discovered an additional 123.91 kilograms of the illegal drug during a continuing inspection of the vessel.

The Bureau of Customs (BOC)-Port of Subic confirmed on Saturday, Sept. 5, that its composite team found 109 more packages of kush worth an estimated P204.44 million as authorities continued stripping and examining the yacht.
The latest discovery brought the total haul from the vessel to 198 packages of kush, with a combined estimated street value of P366.65 million.

The continuing inspection was conducted by the BOC in coordination with the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA), Department of Justice (DOJ), Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), Philippine National Police (PNP) and Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority Law Enforcement Department (SBMA-LED).
Authorities had earlier seized packages of kush from the same yacht during an enforcement operation at the Port of Subic.
BOC-Port of Subic District Collector Geniefelle P. Lagmay said the latest discovery showed that the agency’s work did not end with the initial seizure.

“This additional discovery shows that our work does not stop with the initial apprehension,” Lagmay said, adding that authorities would continue to thoroughly examine and strip vessels to ensure that possible hiding places were checked.
BOC Commissioner Ariel F. Nepomuceno said the operation was part of the agency’s efforts to strengthen border security and disrupt the illegal drug trade.
The seized items were turned over to the PDEA for proper custody and disposition, while the BOC and its partner agencies continued their enforcement and investigation into the seizure. INQ /mr

articles.title: No final decision yet to drop bribery article in Sara Duterte impeachment trial, says Tolosa
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel has yet to make a final decision whether or not it will be dropping the bribery charge under Article III of the Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 2:30pm

The House prosecution panel has yet to make a final decision whether or not it will be dropping the bribery charge under Article III of the Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte.

At a news forum on Saturday, House prosecution legal spokesperson Atty. Jay Tolosa said the prosecutors are still deliberating on the matter as they consider both the sentiments of the senator-judges and the public to expedite the impeachment proceedings and not let it continue up to next year.
“To be clear, wala pa namang ganung pinal na desisyon kasama po yan sa pinaguusapan, pinagdedesisyunan ng panel of prosecutors sa ngayon,” Tolosa said.
“Sabin naman natin mula noon kaisa kami doon sa hangad na as much as possible i-expedite natin ‘tong proceedings,” he said.

(To be clear, there has been no final decision, it is included in the discussions of the panel right now. We've said that since the beginning, we are one in the objective of having the proceedings expedited.)

The Article III refers to the allegation that the Vice President must be impeached for committing bribery by giving monetary gifts or payments to Department of Education (DepEd) officials to induce the violation and circumvention of procurement and other related laws.

So far, the prosecution has presented Article IV —which alleges that Duterte committed an impeachable offense by contracting for the assassination of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos, Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former speaker of the House and incumbent Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez, by making grave threats, and by actively inciting sedition against the republic— and Article I which alleges that the Vice President committed an impeachable offense due to systematic misuse, misappropriation, and irregular liquidation of confidential funds amounting to P500 million released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and P112.5 million released to the DepEd during her tenure as Education chief.
“Dalawa na lang ang matitira bribery and unexplained wealth (Only two remains, bribery and unexplained wealth),” Tolosa said.

He said that the House prosecution team has already collated records from the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the Anti-Money Laundering Council for the Article II, which argues that Duterte amassed unexplained wealth.
“Meron tayong nakuhang maraming dokumento na sa tingin namin talagang importanteng maipakita to sa proceedings and it will go to waste kung ‘yun naman ang hindi namin mapu-pursue,” Tolosa said.
(We have many documents which we think are really important and it will go to waste if we cannot pursue it.)
However, he said that the prosecution may opt to present first Article II to be followed by Article III. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?
articles.summary: Detention centers for deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, vigilante groups — the AfD wants to drastically overhaul Saxony-Anhalt. What does the party have planned?

image.caption: Ulrich Siegmund, top candidate for the far-right AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, is confident he will get the mandate to form a governmentImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) could bring in massive changes should it form a government in Saxony-Anhalt. The far-right party, currently way ahead in opinion polls, is hoping to form a single-party government and have its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, serve as state premier.
The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the AfD is classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed far-right."
Radical tightening of asylum laws

In its draft government program, the AfD has promised "deportation from minute one!" if it wins the election in Saxony-Anhalt. The stated goal, according to the party's election program, is simply to deport as many immigrants who have no residency permits as possible.

The party has also pledged much stricter asylum rules at all levels: It wants more detention pending deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, and intends to cut all state funding for integration programs, which it refers to as an "asylum industry."
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?

Furthermore, it wants to exclude children and adolescents who do not have permanent residency in Germany from attending regular schools. On top of that, a "Remigration Task Force" is to be established within the state government to coordinate the state's asylum policy.

Exactly how many of these measures an AfD state government would be legally able to implement remains unclear. Creating special classes for refugees could, for example, be a violation of international and European law.
And the question of who can and can't be deported falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government, not that of an individual state.
Anti-immigration policy

The AfD opposes immigration to Germany. In its government platform, the party calls for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy," and its stated goal is to reduce the number of immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt.

However, the region has been suffering for years from a shortage of skilled workers, particularly in nursing and care for the elderly. The AfD's plan to end this shortage is to encourage Germans who live abroad to come back.

To this end, it plans to launch a "return program," including a proposed "return bonus" to help find housing and daycare spots for children. It is unclear how many returnees the AfD anticipates and how much money it has budgeted for the "return program."
Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage

Saxony-Anhalt has been severely affected by depopulation for over 30 years. No other German state population has shrunk more since reunification in 1990 — from around 2.9 million people then to 2.1 million today.
Economic researchers like Reint Gropp, president of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, have warned that an AfD government is likely to exacerbate the skilled worker shortage.
"Highly qualified professionals, in particular, have options," he told Die Welt newspaper on Tuesday. "If they feel they are unwelcome or can expect hostility, they will choose other regions."
Rapprochement with Russia

The 16 state governments have virtually no authority over Germany's foreign and defense policy, though they can influence political debates via the Bundesrat, the chamber of parliament that represents the states. In that context, an AfD state premier would carry considerable political weight.

For example, since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, Germany has largely halted oil imports, but the AfD's election platform calls for a rapprochement with Russia and an end to sanctions.
The call is largely symbolic, as Saxony-Anhalt is bound by federal sanctions, but an AfD state premier could set a new tone in the Bundesrat.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?
The AfD also wants to expand Russian language instruction in schools and specifically recruit native Russian speakers for this purpose.

On Ukraine, meanwhile, the AfD is taking a harder line, calling for a "return offensive" for Ukrainian refugees. Again, a state government cannot deport Ukrainians from Germany — that is regulated by federal policy.
Establishing citizen patrols

Particularly controversial is the AfD's call for a kind of auxiliary police force. The regular police are "overwhelmed" by the task of ensuring security, according to the AfD's program for Saxony-Anhalt: "We will therefore establish a voluntary citizen patrol as a third pillar of the local security architecture."

Legal scholar and criminologist Thomas Feltes, of Ruhr University Bochum, warns against the idea. "It is the police's duty to ward off dangers and ensure the protection of the public. Only the police are authorized to use force in doing so," he wrote in a column for the outlet Legal Tribune Online.
Germany's freedom of art under threat?

A "citizen patrol," he said, would basically be a vigilante group that would have a negative effect on public safety: "Where such groups are active, the fear of crime is only stoked — not only among the participants, but above all among everyone else, and not just among 'concerned' citizens," he wrote.
Radical change in social policy

A central tenet of the AfD's governing platform is so-called identity politics. It aims to promote a positive image of German history, and advocates a fundamentally different view of the country's past. The party describes the process of coming to terms with German crimes during the Nazi era as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" and wants to change school curricula accordingly.

It has also declared war on social diversity: Rainbow flags, as symbols of diversity, are to be banned in schools. It rejects the world-famous Bauhaus architecture — which flourished in Saxony-Anhalt — as "too globalist" and calls for a "patriotic cultural policy."

To that end, it wants to redirect funding away from the many pro-democracy projects that receive state funding for their work. In its platform, the AfD has rejected any continuation of these payments.
Between homemaking and hate: Undercover with far-right women
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: 3rd missing passenger in Tarlac SUV plunge found dead in Pangasinan
articles.summary: TARLAC CITY — The body of the third missing passenger of the SUV that plunged from the Agana Bridge in Tarlac City was found in Bayambang, Pangasinan, on Saturday, Sept. 5, according to Tarlac City…

blocks.text: TARLAC CITY — The body of the third missing passenger of the SUV that plunged from the Agana Bridge in Tarlac City was found in Bayambang, Pangasinan, on Saturday, Sept. 5, according to Tarlac City Mayor Susan Yap.

Yap said rescuers found the body of Shiela Mae Taborlupa, 25, a teacher, partly buried in mud and among banana trunks. She was wearing black shorts, matching the description of what she was wearing when the accident occurred.
Taborlupa was a cum laude graduate of the Technological University of the Philippines.
Yap said she and city officials were on their way to Bayambang to claim the body.

Earlier Saturday, Yap held a briefing with the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO), Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO), Armed Forces of the Philippines, Philippine Air Force, Philippine National Police and other rescue teams to coordinate the search and rescue operation.
The teams used drones and a helicopter in the aerial search for the missing passengers.
Meanwhile, the family of Paul Harvey Collado, a nurse supervisor at Jecsons Medical Center and the owner of the SUV, continued to hope that he would be found alive.
Collado’s family came from the United States and immediately traveled to Tarlac City after learning about the accident.
Yap provided the family with a place to stay in Tarlac City while they wait for updates and coordinate with rescue teams. INQ /mr

articles.title: Passenger arrested at Tacloban airport for bringing handgun bullets
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — Police arrested a 59-year-old businessman after airport security personnel allegedly found a magazine and 30 rounds of .45-caliber live ammunition concealed in his backpack at the…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — Police arrested a 59-year-old businessman after airport security personnel allegedly found a magazine and 30 rounds of .45-caliber live ammunition concealed in his backpack at the Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport here Friday night, the Police Regional Office 8 (PRO 8) reported.

The suspect, identified only as alias “Mak,” a resident of Barangay Copocawayan, Sto. Niño, Samar, was arrested at about 7:21 p.m. at the Central Security Screening Checkpoint of the airport, according to PR0 8.
Police said Mak was a departing passenger booked on a flight to Manila when an X-ray operator detected the items inside his backpack at about 7:15 p.m.
The bag was subjected to manual inspection in the presence of police personnel, witnesses and the passenger, resulting in the recovery of one magazine and 30 rounds of live .45-caliber ammunition.

Police personnel assigned at the Tacloban Airport Police Station then conducted verification and profiling to determine the circumstances surrounding the passenger’s possession of the ammunition and whether it constituted a violation of Republic Act No. 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act.
Police said the passenger was asked to present documents showing his legal authority to possess the ammunition but allegedly failed to do so.
He was subsequently arrested and informed of the reason for his arrest and his constitutional rights under the Miranda doctrine in a language he understood.
The recovered ammunition and magazine were secured and turned over to the duty investigator for proper disposition and examination.
The suspect remains under the custody of the airport police station as police gather additional evidence and prepare the appropriate complaint for possible violation of RA 10591. INQ /mr

articles.title: Palawan heirloom rice gets new lease on life
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — In the indigenous communities of Palawan, rice varieties passed down through generations are getting another chance to survive. The Department of Agriculture (DA) has collected…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — In the indigenous communities of Palawan, rice varieties passed down through generations are getting another chance to survive.
The Department of Agriculture (DA) has collected 300 rice varieties from these communities in an effort to preserve heirloom seeds that have long been grown across the province.

Eleanor Lotivo, officer-in-charge of the Agriculture Program Coordinating Office, said the seeds were sent to the Philippine Rice Research Institute (PhilRice), where more than 180 were found to be original varieties.
Some of the other varieties, she said, may actually be similar rice types that were simply given different names by different indigenous communities.

“These are their heirloom varieties, the old varieties that are really resilient. We have already sent these varieties to PhilRice after collecting them from indigenous communities. We are trying to preserve these seeds and distribute them back to the communities,” Lotivo said in Filipino.
Beyond their value as heirloom varieties, the seeds have also caught the attention of agriculture officials because of their resistance to pests.
The DA said varieties that can withstand pests will eventually be returned to Palawan, allowing indigenous communities to continue planting them.
The agency began collecting rice seeds in the province in 2025 as part of its effort to preserve heirloom varieties for future generations.

“We are also studying these unusual rice varieties so that they can still benefit future generations because these are resistant to pests. We now have many pests because we are using different hybrids,” Lotivo said in Filipino.
The preservation effort also forms part of the DA’s broader assistance to indigenous communities through the Kabuhayan at Kaunlaran ng Kababayang Katutubo, or 4K, program.

The program supports farmers and fishers living within ancestral domains through production and post-harvest machinery and equipment, as well as assistance identified through community needs assessments.
In Palawan, indigenous communities have received vegetable and corn seeds, garden tools and livestock.
They have also undergone agricultural skills training to help them operate and manage the machinery provided to their communities.
For Lotivo, preserving traditional rice varieties goes hand in hand with ensuring that indigenous farmers are not left behind in agricultural development.
“We cannot forget our brothers and sisters in the mountains, our indigenous peoples,” she said in Filipino. /dm /mr

articles.title: LOOK: Court order lifting arrest warrant vs VP Sara Duterte
articles.summary: The Regional Trial Court Branch 98 of Quezon City lifted the arrest warrant against Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday after she posted bail for her grave threats case.

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 1:56pm
The Regional Trial Court Branch 98 of Quezon City lifted the arrest warrant against Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday after she posted bail for her grave threats case.
Duterte's lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim showed media a copy of the court order for the lifting of the arrest warrant, according to GMA News reporter Bea Pinlac.
According to the court document, Duterte posted bail in the amount of P120,000 for each count of grave threat. Duterte is facing charges for three counts of grave threat.
The court order also acknowledged receipt of the following documents submitted by Duterte:

1. barangay certification2. photos of Duterte — left side, right side, and front (4 pieces each)3. affidavit of undertaking dated Sept. 5, 2026 signed by Duterte4. Duterte's profile5. sketch and vicinity of Duterte's residence6. photocopy of Duterte's PhilHealth ID
Duterte went to the court on Saturday morning, a day after it issued the arrest warrant.
In its order for her arrest, the court said it found probable cause to hold Duterte for trial.

“Together with its supporting evidence, and after due consideration of the arguments raised by both parties in their oral arguments, the Court finds that there is probable cause to hold the accused for trial for the crimes charged in the Informations,” it said.

In early August, the Department of Justice filed three counts of grave threats against the vice president over her remarks that she hired an individual to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez, should an alleged plot against her succeed.
Duterte's lawyer on Friday said the vice president would face the charges head on.

articles.title: Sara Duterte posts bail for grave threats case
articles.summary: The Vice President posts bail a day after a Quezon City court issued warrants for her arrest over three counts of grave threats

blocks.text: POSTING BAIL. Vice President Sara Duterte, along with legal counsels, arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over a grave threats case, on September 5, 2026.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The Vice President posts bail a day after a Quezon City court issued warrants for her arrest over three counts of grave threats

items: Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail of P360,000 after being charged with three counts of grave threats related to alleged assassination threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and others.
The Quezon City Regional Trial Court issued warrants for her arrest, which were upheld despite her legal team's arguments regarding her status as an impeachable official.
Duterte expressed concerns for her safety and that of her children, citing documented threats and harassment since 2023.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday, September 5, in connection with the three counts of grave threats filed against her over her alleged assassination threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.
Her lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, confirmed that Duterte posted P120,000 bail for each count of grave threats before Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98.
Lim said Duterte underwent booking process inside the court, which includes taking of her fingerprints.
“Kailangan pa rin (It’s necessary)…. [She did the booking process] in front of court staff,” Lim told reporters outside the court.
Duterte’s impeachment lawyer and spokesperson Michael Poa was also present in court with Duterte and Lim.
Before entering the hall, Duterte talked to journalists where she aired concerns over her security.

“I have documented threats and harassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them. Umalis na nga ako kung nasaan mga anak ko para pumunta sa korte pero pumunta pa rin ang pulis. I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila ako,” Duterte said in a statement.
(I left the place where my children are to go to the court but the police still came… I feel like they will kill me.)

On September 4, the court issued a warrant after it found probable cause to hold Duterte for trial. It also denied her motion to defer or recall the warrants and quash the information for lack of merit.

Duterte’s camp had argued that she could not face a criminal case while serving as Vice President because she is an impeachable official. Several legal experts, however, have said that unlike the President, the Vice President is not immune from suit.
The Department of Justice filed the three counts of grave threats in August following complaints from the National Bureau of Investigation over Duterte’s November 23, 2024, midnight press conference.

During that press conference, Duterte said she had already talked to someone who would kill Marcos, his wife, and Romualdez if she herself were killed. Duterte said at the time that she was not joking. – Rappler.com

articles.title: The market eats its own: How a UP Visayas student turned Iloilo’s palengke into a horror film
articles.summary: ‘Kanibal,’ a 16-minute Hiligaynon short film written and directed by Michael Baylon, turns body horror into a commentary on the redevelopment of an Iloilo City public market

blocks.text: ‘Kanibal,’ a 16-minute Hiligaynon short film written and directed by Michael Baylon, turns body horror into a commentary on the redevelopment of an Iloilo City public market

There is a shot in Kanibal that looks like nothing at all until you notice it. A woman in an orange apron works her stall. Slabs of pork hang from hooks above her head. Taped to the post behind her is a prayer card to St. Martha, patron of cooks and servants. On her chest, printed across a white campaign shirt, is the smiling face of the mayor she voted for.
By the end of the film, the meat and the woman will be difficult to tell apart.

Kanibal is a 16-minute-and-52-second Hiligaynon short film written and directed by Michael A. Baylon, a Communication and Media Studies student at the University of the Philippines Visayas. It is his debut as a director. It is also one of 20 shorts selected for the Puregold CinePanalo Film Festival 2026, each carrying a P200,000 production grant, screening in the Shorts Category (Set A) when the festival runs from September 23 to October 4 across Gateway Cineplex 18, TriNoma, Fairview Terraces, Ayala Malls Feliz, Ayala Malls Circuit, Ayala Malls Manila Bay, and Market! Market!

The premise is deceptively small. Lea (Rowen Jean Ledesma, in her introducing credit) is a meat vendor who runs her stall with her daughter Anne (Lia Sophia Sajonia) underfoot, in a public market loud with the ordinary business of a town buying and selling. One morning, her neighbor at the next stall, Anecita (Ma. Lourdes Maculada), brings news: Mayor Lin (Roselle Lao) is coming to visit. Lea has been a diehard supporter since the campaign. She is thrilled. She prepares a cut of meat as a gift.

articles.title: Sara Duterte posts bail for grave threats case at QC court
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday posted bail at a Quezon City court, a day after the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over her grave threats case.

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 12:54pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday posted bail at a Quezon City court, a day after the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over her grave threats case.
The QC Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98 set the bail at P120,000 per count.
It found that there is probable cause to hold Duterte for trial, thus issuing an arrest warrant against her.
In a statement, Duterte said she does not feel safe.
"I have documented threats and harassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them," she said.
"Umalis na nga ako kung nasaan mga anak ko para pumunta sa korte pero pumunta pa rin ang pulis," Duterte added.
"I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila ako," the vice president said.

Duterte did not to appear before the Quezon City court on Friday, the day that the warrant was issued. Additional police forces had been deployed at the Hall of Justice, with cops bringing inside the building a backdrop used for taking mugshots.

Policemen were securing the area on Saturday morning as well. The vice president's counsels, Michael Poa and Paul Lawrence Lim, arrived at the Hall of Justice ahead of her. They did not entertain questions from the media upon their arrival.
Lim had issued a statement Friday, saying that, "Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies."

To recall, the DOJ filed three counts of grave threats against the vice president over her remarks that she hired an individual to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez, should an alleged plot against her succeeds.

Following this, Duterte filed a motion to quash on the ground of jurisdiction, arguing that she and other impeachable officers have limited procedural immunity while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
The court held the oral arguments on Duterte’s motion in late August.
For her part, Duterte previously said her remarks were "maliciously taken out of logical context."
The vice president's alleged grave threats against Marcos is also the basis of one of the Articles of Impeachment against her in the ongoing trial before the Senate impeachment court. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Resil B. Mojares, National Artist for Literature, dies at 83
articles.summary: Mojares was an award-winning writer, historian, and literary critic who had contributed greatly to the promotion of regional and Filipino literature

blocks.text: REST IN PEACE. National Artist for Literature Resil B. Mojares dies at 83.
Leigh Go Mojares' Facebook
Mojares was an award-winning writer, historian, and literary critic who had contributed greatly to the promotion of regional and Filipino literature

items: Resil B. Mojares, a renowned writer and National Artist for Literature, passed away on September 5, just a day after celebrating his 83rd birthday.
He was known for significant works such as 'House of Memory' and 'Interrogations in Philippine Cultural History,' and had a profound impact on Filipino and Cebuano literature.
Mojares was honored by various literary circles and government agencies for his contributions, and his passing is mourned by the literary community, including fellow writers and organizations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Renowned writer, historian, and literary critic Resil B. Mojares died on the morning of September 5, his family confirmed. Mojares had just celebrated his 83rd birthday a day earlier.

“Papa Resil was a pillar of our family, and although we will miss him dearly every day, we find comfort in knowing that he is now reunited with our dear mother, Sally, who left us in 2022. Together once again, resting peacefully in eternity,” his daughter Leigh Go Mojares wrote.
Mojares was named National Artist for Literature in 2018 alongside six other big names in arts and culture, including composer Ryan Cayabyab and cartoonist Larry Alcala.

Among the late writer’s most impactful works is the 1997 book House of Memory, a personal and cultural essay collection for which he received a Philippine National Book Award. He also authored The Feast of the Santo Niño: An Introduction to the History of a Cebuano Devotion, and Interrogations in Philippine Cultural History and The War Against the Americans: Resistance and Collaboration in Cebu, 1899-1906, to name a few.
Interrogations in Philippine Cultural History (2017) and Enigmatic Objects: Notes Towards a History of the Museum in the Philippines (2023) would be the last of his published works before his death.
In 1971, he also became a Carlos Palanca Memorial awardee, having received the second prize in the English Short Story for his work Beast in the Fields.

Mojares hails from Polanco, Zamboanga del Norte, but later moved to Cebu City, where he obtained his bachelor of arts and masters degrees from the University of San Carlos. He had served as Professor Emeritus in the same university.
The Origins and Rise of the Filipino Novel author was also the founding director of the Cebuano Studies Center, a research center on all things Cebuano culture.
Throughout his career, he was also a visiting professor at several universities across Singapore, the US, and Japan.

Acclaimed writer Jose “Butch” Dalisay Jr. had regarded Mojares as one of his personal heroes. The late literary great had written the blurbs for Dalisay’s short story collection Voyager and Other Fictions.

“We were friends in that rather formal way aging men assume when they sit across a table over coffee — no backslapping, no intimacies exchanged, just a wry understanding of how things work. I think the most personal we ever got was when I sent him a message condoling with him on the passing of his wife Sally a few years ago,” Dalisay wrote in a Facebook post.
“Rest up, Resil, now you can smoke and scribble all you want in that great coffeeshop in the sky.”

“Naku. Laking kawalan para sa history ng Bisayan lit. Nakikidalamhati kami sa pamilya ni Resil (What a huge loss to the history of Bisaya literature. We are grieving with Resil’s family),” fellow National Artist for Literature Virgilio “Rio Alma” Almario said in a Facebook comment.

Literary circles and organizations also joined in mourning Mojares’ death, including the Unyon ng mga Manunulat sa Pilipinas (UMPIL), which honored him with the Gawad Pambansang Alagad ni Balagtas in 1997.

Government agencies had also joined in to pay their respects for Mojares — with the National Historical Commission of the Philippines and the National Commission for Culture and the Arts remembering him for his extensive contributions to Filipino and Cebuano cultural history and literature.
Mojares was married to Salvacion “Sally” Ouano Go, with whom he shared four children. His wife passed away in 2022. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte considered 'surrendered' as she appears before court over grave threats case
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte is considered surrendered to authorities as she prepares to comply with the process to post bail for her grave threats case, her lawyer Michael Poa said Saturday.

blocks.text: POA SAYS
Published September 5, 2026 12:44pm
Vice President Sara Duterte is considered surrendered to authorities as she prepares to comply with the process to post bail for her grave threats case, her lawyer Michael Poa said Saturday.
"Well, yeah. Kapag ganito naman talagang surrendered," Poa told reporters at the Quezon City Hall of Justice.
(Well, yeah. In these situations, it's really surrendered.)
Quezon City (QC) Regional Trial Court Branch 98 on Friday issued the arrest warrant against Duterte over three counts of grave threats after finding probable cause to hold her for trial.
She did not appear before the Quezon City court on Friday, the day that the arrest warrant was issued.

Amid a police deployment to the site, the vice president was reluctant to enter the QC Hall of Justice upon her arrival on Saturday morning, repeatedly saying she feared for her safety. After much discussion with her lawyers, Duterte eventually entered the building.

In early August, the DOJ filed three counts of grave threats against the vice president over her remarks that she hired an individual to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez, should an alleged plot against her succeeds.

Following this, Duterte filed a motion to quash on the ground of jurisdiction, arguing that she and other impeachable officers have limited procedural immunity while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
The court held the oral arguments on the motion in August.
In its order, the QC Regional Trial Court Branch 98 said it found probable cause to hold Duterte for trial.

"Together with its supporting evidence, and after due consideration of the arguments raised by both parties in their oral arguments, the Court finds that there is probable cause to hold the accused for trial for the crimes charged in the Informations," it said.
Bail was set at P120,000 per count. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Alarm foils pawnshop break-in, 8 suspects arrested in Tarlac
articles.summary: MABALACAT CITY, Pampanga — A concerned citizen’s report of a triggered security alarm led to the arrest of eight suspected robbers who allegedly attempted to break into a pawnshop in Santa Ignacia…

blocks.text: MABALACAT CITY, Pampanga — A concerned citizen’s report of a triggered security alarm led to the arrest of eight suspected robbers who allegedly attempted to break into a pawnshop in Santa Ignacia town, Tarlac, on Friday, Sept. 4.

In a statement Saturday, the Tarlac Police Provincial Office (TPPO) said the suspects attempted to burglarize the ML Lhuillier pawnshop along Romulo Highway in Barangay Poblacion West at around 10:30 a.m.

The TPPO Tactical Operations Center received a 911 call reporting the activation of the establishment’s alarm system. Responding police officers discovered a small hole in the floor near the roll-up door, which was believed to have been made by the suspects to gain entry.
According to police, the suspects used the drainage canal along Romulo Highway as a passageway and used tools to create an opening.
Police launched a hot pursuit operation and arrested five men who were allegedly fleeing through the same drainage canal in Barangay Poblacion West.
Seized from the five suspects were an improvised firearm, two hand grenades, a pressure jack, a hacksaw, two crowbars, a metal chisel and five sachets of suspected shabu (crystal meth).
Police said the suspects later disclosed the identities of three other companions who were waiting along Romulo Highway in Barangay Poblacion East aboard an Elf truck.
A follow-up operation led to the arrest of the three other suspects. Police recovered the Elf truck, a hand grenade, three sachets of suspected shabu and a rifle grenade.
TPPO director Col. Harry Lorenzo III credited the swift police response with preventing the suspected robbery and commended the citizen who reported the alarm activation. INQ /mr

articles.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
articles.summary: Russian forces were brought in to help defeat jihadists but they also defend the military leadership in Niger.

blocks.text: When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.

Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".

"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.

"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."

One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."

Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.

"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.

All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."

An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.

"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday said she fears for her life amid an arrest warrant against her over three counts of grave threats.
Duterte issued the statement as she arrived at the Quezon City Hall of Justice on Saturday morning.
“I have documented threats and harassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them,” said Duterte in a statement.
“Umalis na nga ako kung nasaan mga anak ko para pumunta sa korte pero pumunta pa rin ang pulis. I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila ako,” she added.
(I left where my children were to go to court but the police still came. I do not feel safe. I feel like they are going to kill me.)
While Duterte is facing a looming arrest, the court set bail at P120,000 for each of the three counts of grave threats. /mr

articles.title: NBI probes armed civilians seen with police at Albuera, Leyte checkpoint
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has launched a fact-finding probe into the presence of armed civilians alongside police personnel at a border control point in Albuera,…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has launched a fact-finding probe into the presence of armed civilians alongside police personnel at a border control point in Albuera, Leyte, an incident that drew public concern after a video of the September 2 encounter circulated online.
NBI Eastern Visayas Regional Director Jeremy Lotoc personally went to Albuera on Friday, September 4, where he met with Mayor Rolan “Kerwin” Espinosa at the municipal mayor’s office.
Lotoc said the NBI investigation seeks to establish what actually happened, identify those involved and determine the possible implications of the incident on peace and security in the municipality.

“While the PNP (Philippine National Police) is conducting its own investigation because its personnel were involved, the NBI wants to establish whether the incident actually happened, who were involved, and what its implications are for peace and security in Albuera,” Lotoc told reporters.
“Our focus is to obtain records and documentation, identify those who may have been involved, and determine which agencies may have been involved so we can establish what really happened,” he added.
The incident gained attention after a video showing armed civilians at the checkpoint circulated on social media, prompting the Leyte Police Provincial Office to conduct its own investigation.

As an initial administrative measure, Albuera police chief Major Franklin Romeo Parangan and police personnel assigned at the checkpoint at the time of the incident were relieved from their posts pending the outcome of the investigation.
Lotoc said he was alarmed when he saw the video, noting that the presence of armed civilians at a checkpoint could cause concern and fear among residents.
“That was very alarming,” Lotoc said, pointing out that checkpoints are normally expected to be manned by government security personnel.
He declined to comment on whether Espinosa could have been involved in the incident, saying the NBI investigation must be based on facts and evidence.
“The reason why the NBI is conducting a probe is because we want to make sure that the outcome of the investigation is fact-based and evidence-based,” Lotoc said.
Espinosa welcomed the NBI investigation, saying he trusts the agency and is willing to cooperate.
“I trust the NBI, especially our Regional Director Jeremy Lotoc. I will provide all the documents through my lawyers,” Espinosa said.
Espinosa acknowledged that one of the armed civilians seen in the video was part of his security detail.
He said, however, that his security personnel were performing their duties after they noticed a white van that allegedly appeared suspicious.

Espinosa further claimed that the people inside the vehicle were PNP intelligence personnel. He did not explain why the alleged intelligence personnel were in the area or why they were being monitored by his security detail. INQ /mr

articles.title: P3.1M worth of shabu seized in Batangas, Quezon, Laguna
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — Four suspected high-value drug traffickers were arrested on Friday and Saturday (Sept. 4 and 5) in separate buy-bust operations in the provinces of Batangas, Quezon and Laguna,…

blocks.text: LUCENA CITY — Four suspected high-value drug traffickers were arrested on Friday and Saturday (Sept. 4 and 5) in separate buy-bust operations in the provinces of Batangas, Quezon and Laguna, resulting in the seizure of more than P3.1 million worth of “shabu” (crystal meth).

In a report released Saturday, the Police Regional Office 4A (PRO-4A) said anti-narcotics operatives in Malvar, Batangas, arrested two suspects identified by their aliases “Dennis” and “Rea” at 12:10 a.m. Saturday after they allegedly sold P200,000 worth of shabu to an undercover police officer in Barangay Poblacion.

Confiscated from the suspects were two knot-tied plastic bags containing suspected shabu weighing a total of 300 grams and valued at approximately P2,040,000 based on the Dangerous Drugs Board’s assessment.
Police also recovered two mobile phones that will be examined for possible drug-related transactions.
They also seized a Nissan Terra sport utility vehicle believed to have been used by the suspects in their alleged illegal drug trade.
Both suspects are listed as high-value individuals (HVIs) in the illegal drug trade, a category that includes traffickers, financiers and members of drug syndicates.
Anti-illegal drug operatives in Santa Rosa City, Laguna, apprehended “Teroy,” also an HVI, during a sting operation in Barangay Dita on Friday morning.
Recovered from him were three heat-sealed plastic sachets containing suspected shabu weighing 50.47 grams and worth about P343,196.

Meanwhile, Quezon police chief Col. Romulo Albacea said in a report that members of the provincial drug enforcement unit arrested a suspect identified only as “Pato,” likewise an HVI, during a buy-bust operation in Barangay Silangang Mayao in Lucena City early Friday morning.
Police seized 105.9 grams of suspected shabu from the suspect, worth P720,120, as well as a motorcycle allegedly used by Pato in his illegal activities.
Authorities are continuing their investigation to determine the source of the illegal drugs.
All four suspects are in police custody and will face charges for violations of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 and other related offenses. INQ /mr

articles.title: BFAR lifts shellfish ban in Biliran Island but not in Samar, Leyte
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The shellfish ban in the coastal waters of Biliran Island has been lifted after laboratory tests showed that shellfish samples from the area are now safe for human consumption,…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The shellfish ban in the coastal waters of Biliran Island has been lifted after laboratory tests showed that shellfish samples from the area are now safe for human consumption, according to the latest red tide advisory issued Friday, September 4 by the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR).
The advisory said all types of shellfish and Acetes sp., locally known as alamang or tiny shrimp, harvested from the waters of Biliran Island are now considered safe for consumption.

However, the shellfish ban remains in effect in Matarinao Bay in Eastern Samar, covering the coastal waters of General MacArthur, Quinapondan, Hernani and Salcedo, after shellfish meat samples collected from the area tested positive for red tide toxins.

A local red tide advisory also remains in effect in the coastal waters of Leyte, Leyte, where the public has been warned against gathering, selling, buying or eating all types of shellfish and Acetes sp. from the affected area.
BFAR advised the public to strictly follow the shellfish bans because shellfish can accumulate toxins produced by certain microscopic marine algae without showing any visible sign of contamination.

Red tide is a coastal phenomenon associated with a rapid increase or accumulation of microscopic algae, also known as phytoplankton. Despite its name, the water does not always turn red and may appear brown, green, yellow or milky—or show no visible discoloration at all.

Red tide or harmful algal blooms can develop when environmental conditions favor rapid algal growth. These include changes in water temperature, sunlight, salinity and increased nutrient levels in the water. Excess nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus can contribute to algal blooms.

Some algae produce toxins that can accumulate in filter-feeding shellfish such as mussels, oysters and clams. One of the major health concerns is paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP), which can cause numbness or tingling around the mouth and extremities, vomiting, dizziness, headache, paralysis and difficulty breathing. Severe cases can be fatal.
BFAR also warns that cooking does not eliminate the toxins in contaminated shellfish, and shellfish may remain toxic even when there is no visible red discoloration in the water.

Fish, squid, shrimp and crab from areas under shellfish bans may still be consumed provided they are fresh, thoroughly washed and properly prepared, with internal organs such as the intestines and gills removed before cooking, based on BFAR guidance. /mr

articles.title: ‘Every girl now wants to be a boxer’: excitement in Katie Taylor’s home town for her valedictory bout
articles.summary:
Irish boxer lauded for her tenacity and inspiration before her last fight in front of 80,000 people at Croke Park

When Katie…

blocks.text: When Katie Taylor steps into the ring on Saturday night to defend her titles and once again enthral Ireland, there will be a bittersweet tinge. After a singular career that pioneered women’s boxing, the super-lightweight champion and Olympic gold medallist is bowing out. She is 40 and it is to be her final bout.

“The end of an era, isn’t it?” said Trevor McMahon, her brother-in-law and founder of a gym where she trains. “It’ll be an amazing night but it’ll also be a little bit sad. Everything she did, it might not ever be achieved again.”

blocks.caption: A billboard in Katie Taylor’s home town of Bray wishes her luck. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian

blocks.text: There is consolation in the manner of her farewell. Taylor will fight in front of an 80,000-strong roaring, pulsing crowd at Dublin’s Croke Park, the citadel of Irish sport, in a valedictory like no other.
Before tickets went on sale in June, some worried that a boxing match might not fill such a vast stadium. The event out in 17 minutes.

Westlife and other musical acts have joined the bill, adding to the sense of extravaganza. The national broadcaster, RTÉ, will broadcast proceedings free to air, so every home and pub can tune in for Price’s showdown with Flora Pili, an unbeaten French champion.

David Finnegan, 55, who was selling Taylor hats, flags and posters from a stall in her home town of Bray, County Wicklow, this week, said: “Business is tipping away. This is her farewell, everyone wants to be part of it.”

Catherine Hill, 45, had a precious ticket and wanted a Taylor T-shirt for the occasion. “It’s going to be amazing for Katie, the whole country and all women,” she said. “Every young girl now wants to be a boxer or an athlete. It wasn’t like that before.”

blocks.caption: Catherine Hill and her son at a stall with Katie Taylor merchandise near the boxer’s family home in Bray. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian

blocks.text: Another customer, Denise, 71, bought flags for a pub in Kerry where she planned to watch the bout. “What I love about Katie is that she’s not full of herself. She’s down to earth and still meets up with her friends here. She’s so good with the children.”
Even those with no interest in boxing have been swept up in excitement for an athlete who is adored for blazing a trail in female sports with talent, grit and humility.

Encouraged and trained by her father, Pete, Taylor began sparring as a young girl at a gym so rudimentary it was nicknamed the Tin Can. Women and girls were banned from the ring in Ireland and the UK, so she disguised herself as a boy and signed up to bouts as “K Taylor”.

blocks.caption: A mural of Katie Taylor at the site of her first gym. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian

blocks.text: Father and daughter helped to persuade Irish authorities to lift the ban in 2001, when she was 15, and were instrumental in having women’s boxing added to the Olympic Games. Taylor won gold at London 2012 and went on to headline Madison Square Garden and win an epic trilogy with Amanda Serrano.

blocks.caption: Trevor McMahon, Katie Taylor’s brother-in-law and the founder of Liberty Boxing Gym. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian

blocks.text: McMahon, whose Liberty Boxing gym hosts Taylor during her return visits to Bray, said: “The talent was always there but it was more the dedication. She knew from the get-go what she was going to do. When she comes down to train in the club, the place is packed.”
The last time Croke Park hosted a boxing match was in 1972, when Muhammad Ali fought Alvin Lewis. McMahon said Taylor’s farewell promised to be even more special.

Pili, 29, has won all 12 of her professional fights and holds the IBO world super-lightweight title. She will be no pushover but McMahon said Taylor was determined to add another belt to her titles and go out on a high. “No matter how tough the fight is, Katie always seems to rise to the occasion. If she’s beaten, you’d have to carry her out of there in a box.”

Laney O’Connell, 28, who lives on the estate where Taylor grew up, said she had inspired girls to be fit and active. “When you meet her, she’s completely normal. I don’t think she realises just how big she is,” she said. “And it’s great to see the country represented by a woman instead of a man, especially not McGregor,” she added, referencing the mixed martial artist Conor McGregor.

Anne-Marie McHugh, 58, speaking below a supermarket’s Taylor mural, hoped that Bray’s most famous daughter will enjoy a restful post-boxing life. “It’s time for her to relax,” she said. “She’s earned it.”

blocks.caption: A mural of Katie Taylor overlooks Anne-Marie McHugh and her granddaughter in Bray, County Wicklow. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian

articles.title: Tunisia: Judge orders arrest of journalist Mohamed Yousfi
articles.summary: A journalist and vocal critic of the Tunisian president, Mohamed Yousfi has been taken into custody ahead of an interview. A union called the arrest an attack on all journalists' rights.

image.caption: Tunisians took to the streets in August to call for the release of jailed activists and journalists and the president's resignationImage: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS

blocks.text: A judge in Tunisia ordered the detention of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi on Friday. Police had taken him into custody as he arrived at a radio station to give an interview, according to Zied Dabbar, president of the journalist syndicate SNJT.
Dabbar said it was unclear why Yousfi was detained outside Radio Express FM, but he believed it was related to Yousfi's criticism of the authorities.
The judge ordered Yousfi detained on charges of illicit enrichment and money laundering, the state news agency reported, citing a judicial source.
No reason provided for detention

Yousfi, editor-in-chief of investigative news website Al-Qatiba, has been an outspoken critic of President Kais Saied. Al-Qatiba is known for investigative reporting and coverage of political, economic, social and environmental issues.
Radio Express FM host Walid Ben Rhouma said no reason was given for Yousfi's detention.
"He was barred from entering to participate in the program as a guest and was taken away for questioning, according to those who stopped him," Rhouma said in a Facebook post.
The SNJT said Yousfi's detention shows the erosion of press freedoms in Tunisia, where reporters, lawyers, opposition figures and activists have recently faced prosecution.
Attack on freedom of the press
SNJT called Yousfi's arrest not only an attack on him but also on all journalists and Tunisians' right to a free and independent media.

Rights ⁠groups ​warn of efforts to close Tunisia's remaining independent ​voices since Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and dissolved it in 2022. Saied says he will not be a dictator and that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia.
In August, protesters took the streets to demonstrate in support of jailed activists and journalists, as well as to call for Saied's removal from power.
Media figures jailed this year include Zied Heni, Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies. Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced in June to four years in ​absentia.
On Thursday, lawyer Ghazi Mrabet, known for handling politically sensitive and civil liberties cases, was arrested and placed in custody, according to local media reports.
The case reportedly involves alleged drug trafficking, although there are conflicting accounts of the circumstances.
