articles.title: Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy murder case, after jury deadlocks
articles.summary: The mistrial now puts the murder case - and Clancy's future - in limbo as to whether she will be held criminally liable in the deaths of her three kids.
articles.byline: Ione Wells, Ana Faguy, Sareen Habeshian

blocks.text: "At this point, I'm going to declare that the jury is deadlocked, and I'm going to declare a mistrial," Judge Sullivan told the jury on Friday, dismissing them after weeks of testimony, nearly a week mulling Clancy's fate and the panel signalling three times that they were deadlocked.
The deadlock - known as a hung jury - does not mean prosecutors have proven their case, nor does it mean the defendant is not guilty.
A hearing was scheduled for 29 September, where prosecutors could outline their next steps in the case.
Meanwhile, the 36-year-old former nurse will remain held on the same murder charges and maintain staying in the mental health facility where she is housed now.

Prosecutors could decide from a host of options on what happens next, including holding another trial or coming to a plea agreement with Clancy over the strangulation of her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Massachusetts home.
After killing the children, Clancy cut herself ​with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to take her own life, which has left her paralysed.

Clancy does not deny killing the children in 2023 but pleaded not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges, with her lawyers arguing she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.
The mistrial came after six weeks of court proceedings and after jurors deliberated for more than 40 hours over seven days.
"There will be no decisions made today," Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said on Friday on what could happen next in the case.
He said he would meet with the rest of their legal team to decide whether they will pursue a new trial.
"The facts are Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and the evidence suggested to us that she was in control of her actions when she committed those homicides," he said.
Outside the court on Friday, Reddington said he believed 11 of the 12 jurors would have delivered a verdict that favoured Clancy, had it not been for the one holdout.
But it remains unclear what position any member of the jury took or what talks looked like in the deliberation room.

For weeks the case gripped the country and sparked debate over the topic of postpartum psychosis. Many followed along with livestreams of the trial, as family members and experts testified. Each day, more than 200 members of the media crowded the court and groups of supporters in varying sizes often gathered outside.
The widespread attention even spurred comments on Friday from US President Donald Trump, who called the case a "horrible tragedy".
"She did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse," he said at the White House. "I assume there's going to be another trial."
"But you'll find out what the price to pay is," Trump added. "There'll be a price."

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

articles.title: Trump says envoys taking plan to ‘end the war’ to Moscow, Kyiv
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump said Friday that he was sending envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv with a plan to end the four-year-old Ukraine war. It will be the…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump said Friday that he was sending envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv with a plan to end the four-year-old Ukraine war.
It will be the first time that Trump’s son-in-law Kushner and businessman friend Witkoff have visited war-torn Kyiv since Trump returned to office last year with a vow to solve the conflict.
Both US envoys have previously visited Moscow, leading to accusations that they have taken Russia’s side in negotiations.
“They’re bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” Trump told reporters when asked about the trip.
Trump would not say whether the plan involved Ukraine ceding territory as he has previously suggested but added: “We have an idea for peace.”

“I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They’ve done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we’ll do it,” he said.
The US leader blamed the war that began with Russia invading Ukraine in February 2022 on a “personality problem” between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky earlier said he had proposed observing a ceasefire with Russia while the US envoys visit Moscow and Kyiv.

“There will be no airstrikes on our part, and Russia must reciprocally ensure a ceasefire — without its own airstrikes — for the duration needed to conduct these talks,” Zelensky said in his evening address.
A senior Ukrainian official told AFP the two envoys would visit Kyiv on Sunday. The Kremlin declined to comment on the matter.
A report in the US news outlet Axios said Kushner and Witkoff would travel on Friday, meet Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday, and then Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday.
The two men have also been involved in negotiations for ceasefires in Gaza and Iran.
Trump meanwhile played down Germany’s move earlier this week to blame Russia for an attempted drone attack on an airport.
“I speak to him. I know him very well. Putin’s not looking to attack NATO territory,” Trump said in the Oval Office when an AFP reporter asked him about the German allegation.

Trump has long been skeptical about maintaining support for Ukraine and had a televised row with Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025. With Putin, he has veered between friendliness and frustration.
The US leader said on Thursday that he would ask Europeans to repay the American aid provided to Ukraine under the administration of his predecessor Joe Biden.
Trump has long demanded that Europeans shoulder more of the cost of Western support for Ukraine. /mr

articles.title: Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem
articles.summary: More than 10% of Nepal's energy generation capacity was knocked out by last week's floods.

blocks.text: Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity to India and Bangladesh.

But the very glaciers and mountains giving Nepal this massive natural advantage are succumbing to global warming - and last Wednesday's deadly floods have laid bare the risks to the nation's hydropower ambitions.
More than 1,300 people were killed, while thousands more are still missing.

The floods, which destroyed entire villages near the border of Nepal and Tibet, severely damaged 12 hydropower plants in the Trishuli River basin and knocked out more than 10% of Nepal's total power generation capacity. Operators tell the BBC they don't yet know if any of these facilities can be brought back to operation.

The state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority, which owns six of the 12 damaged facilities, has assured Nepalese households that supply remains adequate. But its spokesman Rajan Dhakal acknowledges that with climate-related disasters becoming more frequent, "the time has come for a rethink of our hydropower policy".
Only two-thirds of people in Nepal had access to electricity in 2010, and even connected households would face power cuts for up to 16 hours a day.

An expansion of hydropower infrastructure alongside efforts to tackle corruption and boost energy imports from India to fill seasonal gaps meant that by 2018, most of Nepal was enjoying 24 hours of power supply per day.

At present, there are 225 hydropower plants across Nepal with more than 3,900MW of installed capacity, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority - capable of powering some three million households simultaneously.

Hundreds more such facilities are either being constructed or in the pipeline. Most of them are built high up in the mountains, where they can seize fast-flowing currents to generate power. These projects require little to no storage system.

However, with the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warming 50% faster than the global average, they face greater environmental risks. Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier and its bedrock as the cause of last week's flash flood.

While scientists say it is too soon to draw any firm links to climate change, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority previously said more than nine in 10 disaster events recorded between 2018 and 2024 were "related to climate".
Nepal's former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising, who called the catastrophic deluge a "once-in-a-century" event, says it holds lessons for designing plants and picking sites where they are built.

"We need to design the plants [to be more] resilient to the floods and, most importantly, adopt early-warning systems as well as robust emergency evacuation measures," he told environmental news outlet Mongabay.
Potentially hundreds of hydropower labourers, engineers and residents are thought to be trapped inside the mud-filled tunnels of these plants since the floods hit.

A "rethink" of Nepal's hydropower strategy could involve reservoir-based plants that need not be situated up in the mountains, says Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority. These could allow water to be stored and released as needed, but would also involve significant economic and environmental costs.
Some question if Nepal has been too reliant on hydropower.
"We should not be putting all our eggs in one basket in these dangerous times," says renewable energy expert Kushal Gurung, who founded the clean tech firm WindPower Nepal.
"We need to seriously embrace other alternatives as well, like solar and wind. And for that we will need to revise our energy policy that is at the moment very pro-hydropower," he says.

The claim is echoed by Vivek Shastry, researcher at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who argues that "meaningful additions of wind and solar generation is a resilience strategy that can limit single-point or interconnected electricity system failures in the future".
A report from the German aid agency suggests the technical potential for energy production from solar power in Nepal is around 10 times larger, external than that of hydropower.

Puspa Sharma, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore's Institute of South Asian Studies, agrees Nepal has to diversify its energy sources, but warns this can be done "only to a limited extent".

"While there is untapped capacity in wind and solar, hydropower really is the one that gives Nepal massive competitive advantage vis-a-vis its South Asian neighbours," he says, citing various studies comparing renewable energy potential in the region.
Hydropower continues to dominate large-scale investments in Nepal, and some climate activists say the funding has continued despite known disaster risks.

The Upper Trishuli-1 project, which has been all but destroyed after last week's floods, was one of Nepal's largest foreign direct investment ventures, valued at about $647m. Its backers include the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.
The Upper Trishuli 3A, which has also been severely hit, was funded by China's Export-Import Bank.

Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says international lenders were "acutely aware of the extreme danger to which they were exposing thousands of labourers, officials, residents, rivers, infrastructure and landscape".

"Their own reports repeatedly highlighted it. But they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur," he says.

History has already shown the Trishuli River basin to be volatile, Thakkar says, pointing to how it had been hit by floods in the last two years. In September 2024, an unprecedented cloudburst over the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river basins sparked flash floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading - settlements by the river that are also among the hardest hit from last week's floods.

Then in July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet's Gyirong county burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least 11 people. That flood damaged critical infrastructure and halted trade along the busy Nepal-China corridor. The border crossing was shut for nearly six months and had only reopened on 1 January this year.
Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority admits that even if climate risk assessments were carried out correctly, "the designing of the plants may not have been done accordingly".
"Clearly we will need to improve in the way we build and operate our hydropower plants," he adds.

Private operators are already feeling the financial impact. Insurers have paid out around $40m for flood-related damage to more than 20 privately owned plants over the past three years, according to Uttam Bhlon Lama from the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.
He warns insurance premiums are rising significantly and making the cost of doing business "unfeasible".

articles.title: Duterte lawyers raise concerns over prosecution microsite
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The defense lawyers of former President Rodrigo Duterte at the International Criminal Court (ICC) are calling for the stricter authentication of prosecution evidence that came…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The defense lawyers of former President Rodrigo Duterte at the International Criminal Court (ICC) are calling for the stricter authentication of prosecution evidence that came from open source materials, as his trial for alleged crimes against humanity draws near.

According to a document released on Friday, Peter Haynes, Duterte’s lead counsel, asked the ICC’s Trial Chamber III to amend the “E-Court Protocol,” the court’s electronic system, by adding an “expert verification field” for the listing of items to be cited as evidence.
The move was made ahead of the trial which starts Nov. 30.
‘New challenge’

Haynes noted that the microsite created by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP), called “OTPLink” with the URL appeals.icc-cpi.int, for the anonymous submission of materials created a “new challenge” for the defense as it was supposedly vulnerable to tampering.

The prosecution launched the microsite in December 2024 to call for more witnesses and more documentary evidence when Duterte’s case was still at the pretrial stage. It encourages past and present police officers and other members of law enforcement agencies to come forward virtually and help in the investigation of the killings during Duterte’s war on drugs.

“There is also the obvious danger that nefarious actors will use the system to transmit falsified, manipulated, or forged evidence, which might also be circulated online; a risk identified by the Office of the Prosecutor itself,” the defense said in the document dated Aug. 31.

“[W]ith three months until the start of trial, the defense is deeply concerned that the quality and quantity of the evidence in this case risks flooding the record with unreliable and/or irrelevant material. This would be detrimental for the parties and the chamber’s search for the truth, and reputationally damaging for the court,” it noted.
The prosecution, defense and the legal representatives for victims initially agreed to add a “URL” field to identify materials from open sources, which could not be easily attributed to a witness.

But the defense argued that merely providing the URL of an “open source evidence” is not enough to prove its authenticity and avert the risk of collecting false information, adding: “The URL merely records the web location from which a piece of online content was collected; it cannot indicate its source.”

“Aside from the limitations as to what can be inferred about the source from a URL, it further says nothing of: the discovery process, which is vital to confirm its chain of custody; whether an item has been edited in any way; whether the content featured at that URL has been independently verified; whether AI (artificial intelligence) tools were used to filter the evidence, and whether there are any other indicia of authenticity and reliability,” it added.

As a remedy, the defense wants “expert verification reports” alongside the crowdsourced items to indicate information on the source, whether sender or creator if known; its chain of custody and whether it is original or a copy; its metadata, time of capture and other technical details; the steps taken to verify the information; as well as the qualifications and experience of the person who vetted the information.
“Without this information, it would be very difficult for the chamber to come to a view on the evidence’s relevance and admissibility,” it said.

The defense cited the OTP’s annual reports that more than 570,000 electronics had been collected from the microsite as of 2025 to point out the voluminous nature of the materials being gathered by the prosecution.

“Since the first status conference in this case, the prosecution has been on notice that the Trial Chamber wishes to avoid ‘unnecessary and irrelevant evidence’ being ‘dumped into the court record’,” it stressed.
This was one of Korner’s reminders to the parties during the first status conference in May to prevent a “wholesale” of documentary evidence that are deemed not useful to the case.

Based on disclosures publicly available, the prosecution has turned over nearly 7,000 pieces of evidence to the legal team of Duterte in the first seven months of the year. But according to the defense, in its latest filing, more than 25,000 items have been disclosed, with more expected to come.

The latest request by Duterte’s lawyers comes after they also urged the TC III to order the prosecution to amend the scope of the charges in terms of counts for a “more defined scope” of the crimes under the jurisdiction of the ICC.

They also asked for an exhaustive list of “underpinning acts which represent the entirety of the charges against the accused.” Duterte, who is detained in the Scheveningen prison complex in The Hague, is accused of three counts of murder as a crime against humanity in connection with the deaths of 76 people from 2013 to 2018. /cb

articles.title: Rome pushing back vs golf cart ‘invasion’
articles.summary: ROME, Italy — Beneath its splendor of monuments and ruins, the Eternal City is taking aim at a modern-day chariot: the golf cart. Even rolling along at a moderate speed, these golf carts have so far…

blocks.text: ROME, Italy — Beneath its splendor of monuments and ruins, the Eternal City is taking aim at a modern-day chariot: the golf cart.
Even rolling along at a moderate speed, these golf carts have so far outpaced regulation—with hundreds of them carrying tourists through Rome’s historic center. But the city is mounting a crackdown.
For critics, the carts are running amok, parking illegally, worsening congestion and unlocking another level of overtourism.
Some local media invoke sensational language, calling it an “invasion” and saying Rome is being “held hostage by golf carts.”
But advocates argue the carts are silent, occupy less space than tourist vans and buses, and don’t choke the air with exhaust that also stains historic monuments.
Enmity on the road
The Associated Press (AP) got a taste of the enmity during a late August ride when a black, eight-seater van pulled up alongside.
“You’re in the middle of the road!” its driver barked. “Move it!”
“Always the same! The road isn’t yours!” the golf cart driver shouted back. Both gesticulated angrily with their free hands, following a time-honored Roman traffic tradition.
Carts like this zip through Rome’s cobblestone alleys, past tourists eating spaghetti carbonara from checkered tablecloths and shops hawking tote bags stamped with clichés (“Ciao Bella!”).
“We don’t have a proper stop for golf carts, so we park where we can—as legal as possible,” driver Martin Halili said.
Little room for parking

Even before the golf cart boom, parking was a pain. Cars, vans, Vespas and motorcycles are stationed atop curbs, crosswalks and medians. Trucks double-park while unloading. Plus, an average 50,000 vehicles enter daily.

Unsurprisingly, some residents are unhappy. “This was the last straw because, unfortunately, there has already been traffic here for a long time, since there are too many categories of vehicles authorized,” Luigi la Licata, head of the Monti neighborhood association, told AP. “The golf cart is the most obvious one—and the latest—but there are many others.”
Golf cart bookings this summer grew 147 percent from 2024, according to TripAdvisor, whose subsidiary Viator is the biggest source of passengers.
Rome has as many as 500 carts, with one-fifth belonging to the Metur association of tour operators, established last December to seek common ground with locals and the city.

“Overtourism is a real problem, and we’re not denying it. And maybe we’re also part of it in a way. But if we’re part of it, then at least be part of it in a smart way,” Pascal van Duijnhoven, the association’s president, said. “We believe, especially for Rome, that it’s a solution. And we really hope that people start looking at it like this.”
EVs, carts of all types
Eugenio Patanè, Rome’s deputy mayor for sustainable mobility and transport, is striving to restore order and reduce traffic—not just golf carts.
In July, electric vehicles (EVs) started paying for admission to the historic center—a strategic shift from cutting emissions to tackling congestion.
The number of authorized vehicles is now down about one-quarter, to 350,000, and Patanè still aims to halve the number of daily entrants.
But it hasn’t been so simple to put the brakes on golf carts. For one thing, not all carts are created equal—technical specifications mean some fall under existing rules while others can roam freely.
Patanè aims to present regulation that would establish fixed tour routes, cap the number of carts of all types and create a system to select operators.
“Cities where this golf cart phenomenon is expanding truly have very few weapons,” he said, adding that “this phenomenon that has now become rampant and, in some cases, even worrisome.” /cb

articles.title: Toronto orders Live Nation Canada to repair Rogers Stadium after 'significant damage'
articles.summary: The City of Toronto has issued an "order to remedy unsafe building" to Live Nation Canada about the state of Rogers Stadium after the concert venue was damaged by Wednesday's severe thunderstorm.

image.caption: Australian rock band AC/DC perform on stage during their PowerUp Tour 2024 at the VELTINS-Arena in Gelsenkirchen, western Germany on May 17, 2024. (Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Toronto
The City of Toronto has issued an "order to remedy unsafe building" to Live Nation Canada about the state of Rogers Stadium after the concert venue was damaged by Wednesday's severe thunderstorm.
Order comes ahead of sold out AC/DC concert scheduled for Sept. 16
Rogers Stadium was seriously damaged by GTA storm. What happens now?
The City of Toronto has issued an "order to remedy unsafe building" to Live Nation Canada about the state of Rogers Stadium after the concert venue was damaged by Wednesday's storm.
The order was issued Thursday after the city inspected the open-air venue in North York that seats 50,000 people.
A sold out concert by AC/DC is scheduled to take place at the stadium, located on the former Downsview Airport lands, on Sept. 16. The show has not been cancelled or rescheduled.
Live Nation Canada, which operates the venue, said late Wednesday that no one was injured by the extreme weather but Rogers Stadium sustained "significant damage."
"Our teams are continuing to assess the extent of the damage. We will provide more information as it becomes available," a spokesperson for Live Nation Canada said in an email on Friday.
'They may not be able to get AC/DC in': councillor
Coun. James Pasternak, who represents York Centre, said safety must be guaranteed before any crowds can return.

"This stadium collapsed in a major storm event, and the question is, can they reconstruct it and repair it so that it's satisfactory, so that it's safe," he said. "They may not be able to get AC/DC in this year."
Drone photos of the stadium show bright blue bleachers crumpled and strewn across grandstands that appear to have partially collapsed.
Rogers Stadium seriously damaged by GTA storm
According to the order, Live Nation Canada must take immediate steps to secure the site, hire an engineer and repair the damage.

The order describes the damage in detail, saying it included "collapsed sections of the north stadium structure, damaged seating areas, and distorted, displaced, or otherwise compromised structural framing associated with various temporary structures.
"In addition, other structures and equipment within the stadium grounds were impacted by high winds, including overturned viewing stations, tents, and shipping containers."
The order goes on to say the damage "may pose a risk to the health and safety of persons" due to structural elements that are displaced and the potential for the structure to be unstable.

items: Rogers Stadium seriously damaged by GTA storm
'Almost a month’s worth of rain' in a day: Toronto's thunderstorm aftermath includes rescues, outages

blocks.text: The city has ordered Live Nation Canada to:

items: Prevent access to all damaged structures, temporary structures, and areas affected by the storm.
Hire a licensed professional engineer to assess all structures, including seating areas, affected by the storm, identify unsafe areas and determine the measures to be taken to address those areas.
Prepare a report by Sept. 8 identifying the damage, measures to be taken and a schedule for the work.
Carry out the necessary repairs identified by the engineer.
Submit another report by Sept. 11 confirming the status of the repairs to be taken and "whether the affected structures are safe and structurally adequate for their intended use and occupancy."

blocks.text: For at least one fan, however, there is still hope that the show will go on.
Miguel Avila, 61, a Toronto resident, said his tickets for the Sept. 16 show are in the grandstands and he is following the situation closely.
'We all love AC/DC and we're willing to wait'
Avila said he hasn't tried to get a refund yet. If the stadium is deemed not ready for the concert, he said that will not be a problem for him.
"We all love AC/DC and we're willing to wait. If the organizers decide to rebuild it, reconstruct it, we're willing to wait."
But he said the damage does raise concerns.
"It open up questions about the way it was constructed," he said.
Avila said he started listening to AC/DC when he was a teenager and hopes to see the band perform.
"I was really excited but I'm patient," he said. "Let's see what happens."
With files from Christian D'Avino and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK
articles.summary:
US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands

Donald Trump…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.
It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.
But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.

Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.

The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.

Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.

An uneasy peace has reined in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their less than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.

This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?
Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.

Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past.

The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.
And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.
In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.

“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”

Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.

It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.
Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.

Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.

He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.

The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.
Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.
Turbulence under Trump

But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.

Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.

This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.

But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.
“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”

In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.

He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.

Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.

But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

articles.title: Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
articles.summary: Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech has been found not guilty of complicity to murder journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. Almost nine years after the attack, the question of who ordered her death…

image.caption: Protesters gathered outside the Maltese Parliament following the verdict in the Caruana Galizia murder trial on WednesdayImage: Darrin Zammit Lupi/REUTERS

blocks.text: "Murderer!" — "Scum!" — "Mafia!"

As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a "terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from." He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as "obscene" and saying: "Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth."

Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia's murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver's seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.

blocks.caption: Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech was acquitted on Wednesday of conspiracy and complicity to murderImage: Kevin Schembri Orland/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A difficult trial

For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.

Fenech's arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.
His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution's argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist's murder.
Who was responsible?

The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.
But Fenech's defense called Theuma's credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.

Fenech's lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.

blocks.caption: Investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb on October 16, 2017Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The public prosecutors' argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.
Open questions

Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech's guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Caruana Galizia's family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an "atmosphere of impunity" in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.
Reforms in Malta

Since then, Malta has made progress with a series of reforms, but many say they do not go far enough. This is especially the case with regard to press freedom. In 2021, the committee of inquiry recommended that journalists be better protected against political and economic pressure and their role institutionally strengthened, yet the country is still waiting for comprehensive media reform.

Following years of discussion and a public consultation, the Maltese government brought the relevant bill before parliament in March 2026, but the legislation was not passed before early parliamentary elections in May.

In its latest Rule of Law Report, the European Commission only certifies limited progress made by Malta. It acknowledges that it has introduced some specific protection measures for journalists, but says core recommendations from the investigation into the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia remain unfulfilled.

blocks.caption: The European Commission has told Malta it needs to do more to strengthen official protections for journalists  Image: Sachelle Babbar/Zuma/picture alliance

blocks.text: Government sees progress

But the government paints a different picture. It has highlighted changes to the judiciary and anti-corruption measures, as well as better protection of journalistic sources, and additional measures to protect media professionals. This is what the EU Commission referred to as progress in specific areas.

The case has also shone a spotlight on the slow pace of the Maltese justice system. According to a report by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation, 46% of homicide cases brought to trial between 2010 and 2020 had still not been concluded in mid-2025. The foundation regards this as a structural problem, and warns that when proceedings go on for so long, it compromises the chances of an effective prosecution.
Fresh investigation?

No decision has yet been made as to what will happen now, following Fenech's acquittal. Judge Edwina Grima has ordered that the evidence presented at trial be passed on to the chief of police, who will decide whether criminal proceedings should be brought against anyone else.
On Thursday, former PM Muscat said that, according to the public prosecutors, further investigations were ongoing.

blocks.caption: Nine years on, the person behind Daphne Caruana Galizia's murder has still not been brought to justice Image: AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Institute of Maltese Journalists (IGM) has called on the authorities to pursue every line of inquiry that came to light during the trial — including, explicitly, those that lead to former high-ranking politicians. The acquittal must be respected as the outcome of the constitutional process, the IGM said, but it does not close the case.

The demonstrators outside the courthouse in Valletta are in no doubt. Someone must have issued a contract for the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia. And almost nine years after her death, still no one has been held responsible.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Yemen: Fighting intensifies amid Houthi push in the west
articles.summary: Houthi forces are trying to secure high ground and solidify their control of the entry to the Red Sea in the southwest. The Iran-backed militia abandoned a shaky truce with the Saudi-backed…

image.caption: A period of comparative calm in Yemen's 12-year civil war has been sundered amid the war with Iran [FILE: July 31, 2026]Image: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both sides in Yemen's long-running civil war have sustained losses in a new push from the Houthi militia to try to seize control of the gateway to the Red Sea in the west.
The Iran-backed Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the country, launched a ground offensive against the Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting Yemen's government-in-exile on Thursday.

No casualty numbers were formally announced but news agencies citing sources off the record concurred that both sides had sustained dozens of losses, as well as civilians who were killed amid the fighting. The AFP news agency tallied 129 deaths as of Friday.
Officials also reported shelling and artillery fire forcing hundreds of families to flee from a pair of coastal cities, Hodeidah and Mokha, one held by either side in the conflict.
Why are the Houthis pushing to control this territory now?
Yemen has been in a state of civil war for almost exactly 12 years, and a period of comparative calm broke down this July amid the war with Iran in the Gulf.

The Houthis are targeting ports and elevated terrain held by Saudi-led forces that would improve their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden, leading out into the Arabian Sea and open waters.
Always a crucial waterway, its significance has increased amid the restrictions to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Houthis claim attacks on Saudi tankers in Red Sea

The Houthis declared a blockade on ships approaching the west coast of Saudi Arabia, with access to its eastern ports already impeded via Hormuz. But they are not ideally placed or equipped to enforce their stated desire.
Nevertheless they have already fired on several commercial vessels, causing severe damage and deaths in a few cases, even with their imperfect control of the relevant coastline.
What do we know about the intensified fighting?

Military sources speaking off the record told both the DPA and AFP news agencies that both sides had sustained multiple casualties. DPA put the figure in the dozens on both sides, AFP had a more precise estimate of roughly 60 on either side.
Exchanges of fire, on land as well as using rockets and drones, were reported in two southwestern provinces, Taiz and Hodeidah.

blocks.caption: Mokha also came under aerial bombardment last month but now the Houthis appear to be trying to approach it on landImage: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Houthis control the major western port of Hodeidah further north, but large chunks of Yemen's southwestern tip in Taiz including the port of Mokha near the strait are controlled by Saudi-led forces.
"They are going for Bab al-Mandeb," Mohammed al-Basha of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report told the AFP news agency.
Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia
Fighting for the high ground, for instance on Mount al-Numan overlooking Mokha, was particularly fierce.
"The Houthis feel that if they capture Bab al-Mandab or Mokha port they will be in a better position of power to negotiate with the government and the Saudis," al-Basha said.

articles.title: In Saxony-Anhalt election, small parties will be kingmakers
articles.summary: The far-right AfD has good odds of winning an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament this state election, enabling them to govern alone. It all depends on whether other parties make the cut.

image.caption: Saxony-Anhalt is governed from the state parliament in MagdeburgImage: ArTo/Zoonar/IMAGO

blocks.text: It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt. On September 6, 2026, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time.

So far, there has not been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post-World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023.
Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote.
AfD, CDU and Left Party will get into parliament

Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties who can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party, which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR.
All other parties have cause for concern they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany.
This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU).
SPD, Greens, FDP, BSW might not make the 5% mark
The SPD is losing popularity nationwide. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago.

The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback.

The environmentalist Greens are also concerned about returning to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society.
Concern over Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW)

And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election.

The BSW never really recovered from this setback. They went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%.

Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office.
Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Small parties could prevent absolute majority for the AfD
The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood of the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone.

On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. This is because in 2018 the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party.
If the CDU sticks to this, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible.
Could the CDU form a minority government?

Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt.
The Left Party is prepared to support Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term.

"In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF.
He pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony, where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party.

Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Germany's civil society alliance takes on the far right
articles.summary: Trade unions, churches and human rights activists are worried about the rise of the far-right AfD. How can civil society protect people who are threatened by far-right extremism?

image.caption: In 2024, hundreds of thousands across the country rallied in protest against right-wing extremismImage: Stefan Boness/IPON/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage.

For Felix Pankonin, locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes, a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property. Pankonin's bicycles have been vandalized, and he has received threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted.
Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony.

The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political adviser at DaMOst, the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, said right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years.

"We have completely different security protocols now. After 6 p.m. no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand," she said.

Kuperan's work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the AfD, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial.

blocks.caption: Ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, numerous business owners with a background of migration went on strike against racism and fascism, and in support of a free and democratic societyImage: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Saxony-Anhalt, a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities.
Green Party politician becomes target of hostilities

Miriam Zeller, a city councilor in Stendal, a city of 37,000 in northern Saxony-Anhalt, is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the election. Zeller told DW that the hostility against her was even more intense when the Greens were in power.

Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia.
"It can't get any worse than this," said Zeller.

blocks.caption: Miriam Zeller, a Green Party candidate, has also felt the impact of the shift to the right in her private lifeImage: Miriam Zeller

blocks.text: However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job.
For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real.
Alliance for Democracy: Educating people on how to defend themselves
The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists — people like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller.

The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying.

Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace.

Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over 5 million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear.

"This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works."

That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader has called for more commitment from politicians.

"We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," she said.
Threats, abuse to German mayors hurting local government
Teaming up to hlep 'bring this injustice to light'

"Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," said Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association(LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people (LGBTQ+) since 1990.

"Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann told DW.
The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlin has deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now.

The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, said Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace.

"That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl said.
Will the alliance also be able to help in rural areas?

Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas.

Green Party politician Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas.
For his part, Lehmann is determined. "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
articles.summary: The Togo-sponsored resolution was backed by 164 nations - the US the only nation to vote against it.

blocks.text: The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.
The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made.
The Mercator map shows the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing bigger.
In an effort to correct this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection.
In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, saying it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa".
Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency: "A fair world begins with a fair map."
Earlier he had told a UN briefing: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."
The UN vote is non-binding but will see changes to the maps used by institutions around the world.

articles.title: Argentine couple to return Nazi-looted painting to rightful owner
articles.summary: The late-baroque Portrait of a Lady was lost for 80 years until it was spotted in photographs of a house for sale near Buenos Aires.

blocks.text: A painting which was stolen by the Nazis and only recovered in Argentina last year must now be returned to the heir of its rightful owner, a court has ruled.
The late-baroque Portrait of a Lady was lost for 80 years until it was spotted in photographs of a house for sale near Buenos Aires.

The house belonged to Patricia Kadgien, the daughter of a Nazi fugitive who had fled there after the Second World War, and she has now agreed to return the painting in exchange for not being prosecuted for concealing it from the authorities.
Portrait of a Lady was among over 1,000 artworks looted from the collection of Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker after the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands in 1940.

His daughter-in-law and sole heir Marei von Saher intends for the painting to be exhibited on a temporary loan at the Holocaust Museum of Buenos Aires to spread awareness of the issue, Argentine newspaper Clarin reports.
Von Saher has previously said her family "aims to bring back every single artwork robbed from Jacques' collection, and to restore his legacy".
This painting was first recognised in August 2025 by the Dutch Algemeen Dagblad (AD) newspaper on an estate agent's website of a property in the coastal town of Mar del Plata.

It was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father Friedrich Kadgien had been a top adviser to Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's deputy. Goring plundered thousands of works across Europe.

articles.title: Cape Breton hit by over 200 millimetres of rain, leading to washouts and flood risks
articles.summary: Torrential downpours have dropped up to 200 millimetres of rain on Cape Breton, causing washouts and flooding in Richmond County and Eskasoni. While eastern and central Nova Scotia face ongoing rain…

image.caption: Heavy downpours and thunderstorms are expected to bring rainfall rates of 10 to 20 millimetres per hour. (CBC)

blocks.text: A slow-moving weather system is dropping significant rainfall on northeastern Nova Scotia, especially Cape Breton this weekend.
Environment and Climate Change Canada has issued orange and yellow alert level rainfall warnings for these regions.
Heavy downpours and thunderstorms are bringing rainfall rates of 10 to 20+ millimetres per hour with the risk of localized flooding and hazardous travel conditions.
More than 21,000 Nova Scotia Power customers were without electricity late Saturday morning, with more than half the outages located in Cape Breton.
Cape Breton

The system has already dropped very heavy rainfall across the island with widespread amounts of 100-200 millimetres being recorded as of Saturday morning. Some private weather stations have already exceeded 200 millimetres in Richmond County with reports of washouts and localized flooding.
The community of Eskasoni picked up 20-30 millimetres per hour overnight and was also nearing the 200-millimetre mark as of mid-Saturday morning.

Rain will continue at times heavy for the Island through Saturday. Generally another 15-to-30 millimetres is expected throughout the day. However, with downpours and thunderstorms, another 50 millimetres locally isn't out of the question. The greatest risk for higher totals will be in Victoria County and also in Cape Breton County near the Atlantic coastline.

The rain continues Saturday night with generally another five-to-15 millimetres, however higher local amounts are still possible. Once again, Victoria county and coastal Cape Breton county will be at the greatest risk for these higher amounts overnight.
The system is also bringing winds gusting 60-80 km/h to the Island, which have brought some power outages.
Sunday both the rain and wind look to ease, however lighter rain and showers will continue with winds gusting to 50-60 km/h.
Northeastern regions

Guysborough, Antigonish, Pictou, as well as northern Colchester and Cumberland counties have also already picked up a lot of rain. Widespread totals of 40 to 70 millimetres have been recorded, with localized amounts nearing 100 millimetres in some areas as of mid-Saturday morning.

Periods of rain at times heavy with the risk of thunderstorms will continue in the east today with generally another 10-to-20 millimetres, however heavier amounts are possible locally, especially near the Northumberland Strait.
The periods of rain will continue tonight and right into Sunday with totals of 70 to 150 millimetres possible by the end of Sunday.
Central regions
Periods of rain will continue throughout Saturday and into Saturday night with lingering showers in the forecast for Sunday.

Generally, additional rainfall totals of 5-10 millimetres are expected for most of the central region by Sunday evening. However, as noted above, higher amounts look more likely for northern Colchester and Cumberland counties.
Temperatures in central areas will struggle with highs in the mid-teens for Saturday and Sunday with northerly winds gusting 50 to 60 km/h.
Monday should bring a mix of sun and cloud with a lingering chance of showers and milder temperatures.
Western regions

Further west, areas like the western Annapolis Valley, South Shore and Tri-County can expect just some lingering showers for Saturday and Sunday. However some sunny breaks are also likely for this region, especially Annapolis, Digby, Yarmouth, Shelburne and Queens counties. This region will see the mildest conditions, with highs in the mid-to-upper teens for Saturday and Sunday. Winds gusting 40–50 km/h will keep the fall feel in the air for both days.
Monday here will be great with lighter winds, lots of sunshine and temperatures popping into the upper teens and low 20s.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukrainian security headquarters in drone attack, Zelensky says
articles.summary: The unmanned aerial vehicle struck without warning in the heart of the Ukrainian capital.

blocks.text: Russia hits Ukrainian security headquarters in drone attack, Zelensky says
Image source, Reuters
A Russian drone has hit the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) during a strike in the heart of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The unmanned aerial vehicle crashed into the SBU headquarters on Friday afternoon, targeting a room used by security chief Oleksandr Poklad.
It is not clear whether Poklad was in the building, but Zelensky said he had since spoken to him to order an "appropriate, tangible response".

"The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," Zelensky confirmed. It suggests Russia's new drones are growing in accuracy and signals Moscow could step up strikes before possible US mediation talks this weekend.
"All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram.

"I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response."
Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building.
Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses".
"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices.
The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa.
In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets.
In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Firefighters work to put out fires in the building following the Russian drone strike

blocks.text: Firefighters work to put out fires in the building following the Russian drone strike
The strike on the SBU building is a rare example of Russia successfully hitting a government building.
Previously Ukrainian offices have remained unscathed despite attempts from the Kremlin to stifle defences to its advances.
The SBU - which is just over the road from the St Sophia cathedral, the oldest building in Kyiv - is a key part of Ukraine's war efforts as it conducts deep strikes to damage Russian infrastructure.
The drone came during yet another air raid alert. There was a brief whine before an explosion echoed across the roof tops and smoke rose into the sky.
Despite the ongoing exchanges, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, reports say, as efforts to end the war continue.
The envoys will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, and then will hold talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in Kyiv, Axios said, citing US officials.
Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, without a breakthrough so far.

articles.title: Nigeria: Suspected oil thieves dead after inhaling fumes
articles.summary: A Nigerian environmental group says that at least 37 people died trying to siphon crude oil off a ship illegally. Police acknowledged a fatal incident but gave fewer details, saying investigations…

image.caption: Ships often dock to load and discharge produce at refineries in oil-rich Nigeria, in thie case at the Dangote refinery in Lagos in April 2026Image: Sodiq Adelakun/REUTERS

blocks.text: A Nigerian environmental NGO says that at least 37 people died in an attempt to tap oil from a loading vessel in the south of the country illegally.
Most of them died as a result of inhaling hazardous fumes, the Youth and Advocacy Centre said.
Nigerian authorities were yet to issue a death toll but had acknowledged a fatal incident in which people were killed, apparently while trying to steal crude oil.
What do we know about the case?
The incident took place overnight on Thursday in Okrika in Rivers State in the oil-rich Niger Delta in the south of the country.

The environmental group said it happened at a jetty as a vessel was loading oil from the Indorama Eleme Petrochemical through the Port Harcourt Refinery. The people who died were "suspected oil thieves" trying to siphon the commodity off into boats at an "illegal tapping point."
The Youth and Advocacy Centre NGO said that other people were still missing, potentially lost in the water, quoting a network of volunteers.
Police acknowledged an incident but said they continued to investigate the details.
"The Rivers State Police Command can confirm the deaths. The victims were allegedly attempting to steal crude oil," said spokesperson Blessing Agbabe.
Africa's fuel crisis: Is Dangote the answer?
Oil theft is fairly common in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, Africa's biggest oil producer, with oil mining areas hotspots for poverty and environmental degradation.
The Nigerian government estimates that oil theft causes losses worth several billion dollars annually and has been trying to clamp down on the practice.
The tapping process can also cause leaks and environmental damage.
If confirmed this would be the worst fatal accident on record connected to attempted oil theft since at least October 2023.
However the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps said that the casualty figures circulating remained unverified, saying it was working with other security agencies to clarify the details.

articles.title: Australia’s housing prices are trending down. See which suburbs have had the biggest falls
articles.summary:
Cotality says prices have declined in most capital cities over winter. Search the data to see how they have changed in your area

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s property market is facing a rare price correction, as rising interest rates and less favourable tax settings for investors accelerate a downturn.

Most capital cities recorded winter price falls, according to Cotality data, with Sydney leading the decline. That weakness is expected to continue, as higher inflation could lead to further interest rate hikes, denting demand.
But the recent price falls are not uniform.

In general, suburbs that previously recorded the biggest price increases also cooled the fastest. More affordable homes are also more likely to hold their value, given they are in demand by first home buyers aided by the government’s low-deposit scheme.
Those who have owned their properties for longer are also likely to be sitting on significant gains, even after the recent falls.
In some cities, including Brisbane, Perth and Darwin, home values are still up more than 10% over the past 12 months.
And the falls have not done much to make Australian homes more affordable for prospective homeowners, given rising mortgage repayment rates have cut borrowing capacity.

articles.title: Vlogger, sports car owner summoned over registration issues
articles.summary: MANILA – The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has issued show cause orders (SCOs) against the driver and registered owner of a sports car and its LTO-accredited importer over irregularities in…

blocks.text: MANILA – The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has issued show cause orders (SCOs) against the driver and registered owner of a sports car and its LTO-accredited importer over irregularities in the vehicle’s registration.

In a statement on Friday, LTO Chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao said the respondents are expected to appear before the Intelligence and Investigation Division (IID) of the LTO Central Office on Sept. 8 to submit their sworn statements and supporting documents.

The driver and owner must explain the allegations related to “Imitation and False Interpretation,” as well as why the driver’s license should not be revoked for being an “Improper Person to Operate a Motor Vehicle.”

The importer, meanwhile, must explain why it should not be held liable under Memorandum Circular No. AVT 2014-023, particularly on the allegation of “Commission of Fraud and Misinterpretation in the Filing of Application and its Operations,” including “Stocks and Sales Reporting.”
As a precautionary measure, the driver has been ordered to surrender his license to the IID and will face a 90-day preventive suspension pending the investigation.
The LTO also ordered the surrender of the sports car for verification and investigation.

“Simple lang ang paninindigan natin: dapat tama ang dokumento, tama ang rehistro, at tama ang proseso (Our position is simple — documents must be correct, registration must be correct, and the process must be correct),” Lacanilao said.
He also reminded motorists to be discerning about the vehicles they buy and warned dealers against deceiving the public.

“Sa mga motorista, maging mapanuri sa mga sasakyang binibili natin. Sa mga dealer naman, huwag nating lokohin ang ating mga kababayan. Kung may mali, itama natin at huwag tayong makilahok sa anumang uri ng panloloko (To motorists, be discerning about the vehicles we buy. To dealers, do not deceive our countrymen. If something is wrong, let us correct it and not participate in any kind of fraud),” he said.
He said the LTO will continue to intensify monitoring, validation, and enforcement of motor vehicle registration irregularities to promote a more orderly, transparent, and accountable system.
The public is encouraged to report any suspicious activity or irregularity to the LTO for appropriate action and investigation. (PNA)
